Like the Night that never ends
by DreamsofArachne
Summary

After James's death, Francis finds himself on his ship, two years before, the horrors still
ahead of them. He is determined to avert the disaster this time, but will he be able to?
Caught between two timelines, Francis soon realises that even with hindsight, things are far
from easy and he must make difficult decisions if they're all to survive, not to mention come
to terms with his own feelings...

Chapter 1: The Beginning
"God wants you to live."
As Francis sat beside James's body and closed his eyes, he felt strangely numb. It was the
pure agony of it, so much pain that his mind was dulled to it.
He wanted to say words, a prayer, but the sound that came out of his mouth was not in any
way discernible as human.
It wasn't strong enough to be a scream, nor quiet enough for a whimper.
Francis realised he was gripping James's hand, limp now, lifeless.
He should do something. He was still the Captain, the men needed him, and there was always
something to be done.
But James was dead.
Francis couldn't move. He couldn't breathe.
Some part of him thought, if I just close my eyes and wish it away, it will go away. James
will be alive again, and strong, and insufferable, and Francis would love him for it.
Francis blinked, James's ravaged face slipping out of focus. He was exhausted, and not in the
way of tiredness. It was something that went deeper, down to his bones.
He had to make himself let go of James's hand, before he pressed a kiss to the knuckles,
tasting salt.
He didn't have the capacity to wonder at the gesture now, same as he didn't know why he
leant down and rested his head on James's still chest.
Trying to find a heartbeat, perhaps.
Francis closed his eyes then. Just for a second, he told himself.
"God wants you to live."
James's words seemed to taunt him, for in this moment, he didn't want to live. Not in a world
without James in it.
He thought of James's request then, to give his body to the men.
This would not happen, Francis would make sure of it. James would be honored in death and
no one would get their hands on him or else they would have Francis's murderous wrath to
contend with.

He would guard James for the night, sit vigil at his side.
Perhaps Mr. Bridgens would be back for his medicines, but that was only a far away thought
in Francis's mind.
Francis raised his head from James's chest, smoothing down his clothes with his hands. James
should be afforded all dignity there could be.
Francis looked at the waning light of the latern, and the world began to fade.
He felt a strange pounding inside his ears, as if he was about to faint in reality, but he was so
raw with grief that he welcomed any respite from it in that moment.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
After all his years of service, Francis was well acquainted with the feeling of being on a ship
on water. He would know it immediately.
It sometimes felt like he had spent more time icebound, the ship locked into place, or the bow
forced up by the ice.
Still, Francis had never been able to shake the a certain sense of wrongness, of something not
being as it should, when he woke up on a ship in ice.
The ice was another living being, almost. It groaned and screamed and pressed upon the ship,
and if Francis caught himself thinking about it, he saw that he was trapped in a trapped thing.
It had never quite gone away, and when he'd left Terror he remembered thinking that he
would leave her with this feeling, and that that wasn't right.
However, as Francis jerked out of sleep now, he didn't pay attention to what his senses were
telling him, he was too busy with his thoughts, and the fact that James's body was gone.
"James!", he exclaimed, more out of shock than any conscious effort to call to his dead
friend.
He looked around, wildly, but it was nearly dark. The lamp must've gone out.
The next thing Francis realised was that he was lying down, not sitting up any longer. He was
also wearing a nightshirt, and -there he finally saw it- he appeared to be in his berth aboard
Terror.
Francis tumbled out of bed, completely disoriented.
Was this a dream?
The strange thing was, he could remember with complete clarity what had happened before
he had fallen asleep, at the same time there was nothing dreamlike about this where he was
now.

Still, Francis tugged up his nightshirt and pinched himself once in the thigh, hard, expecting
to wake up.
He'd wanted to keep vigil at James's side, and damn it he was going to do it.
When nothing happened, he cursed. Never once did he entertain the notion that James's death
had been the dream, appealing as it was.
No dream could've conjured up that kind of despair, that kind of raw grief together with the
hit on the head that was the real.
Also people might call Francis a pessimist afflicted with melancholy (James had called him
thus...), but even he would've struggled to come up with a scenario where things had gone
wrong that badly as the one he had lived through in the last weeks.
The horror of the Carnivale, followed by the long walk, the creature after them, Hickey's
mutiny...
Francis got up an stumbled out of his berth, waiting to wake up at any moment. The cabin
was empty, light streamed through the windows.
A half drunken glas of whiskey was on the table, as if to taunt him. Francis, however, was too
stunned to pay it much notice.
Because they were moving. The ship was moving. Francis went over to the window to see.
"Jopson!", he called, not lifting his eyes from what he could see.
Francis still expected to wake up when his steward burst through the door.
"Captain?"
"Wh- what time is it?", Francis asked, as opposed to what he really wanted to know, which
was which date do we have.
"Just past second bell on the morning watch, Sir."
Well, that told Francis precisely nothing. He stared at Jopson. Maybe if he did it long enough
he would finally wake up.
"And the day?"
"The 22nd of September."
Poor Jopson probably thought Francis was drunk. Well, Francis might as well go for broke,
then.
"The year?"
Jopson didn't even twitch, though there was a slight eyebrow raise.

"1845."
Francis felt dizzy. This meant they were somewhere in the Barrow straight, heading for King
William Island.
Everything ahead of them. The winters in the ice, Tuunbaq, the long walk... And James. Oh
God, James.
Francis pressed his eyes shut, willing himself to wake up, now. Anything else would've been
cruel in the extreme.
When he opened his eyes, Jopson was still standing there. More importantly, he was still
standing there, in his cabin on Terror, apparently in fucking 1845.
He needed to ask. There was no way around it.
"And Ja- Commander Fitzjames?"
Perhaps Francis should've directed the question more casually, but Francis found that he
wasn't able to.
Now, Jopson did look confused, though he answered readily: "He is on the Erebus with Sir
John."
"Alive?", Francis asked, and his voice almost cracked.
"Alive and well, last time I heard, sir."
Francis let out a breath. This couldn't be. And yet, it was. He turned away from Jopson, trying
to get a handle on the situation. On himself, especially.
Once more, he willed himself to wake up, wake up now, before he never wanted to leave
again. But who was he kidding? He was already yearning for it.
"The men?", Francis asked brokenly. "The ship?"
"All is well, sir. Has something happened?", Jopson inquired cautiously.
Holy Mary.
It wasn't just James, but all the men they had lost, now alive and well again. Presumably. This
was around the time that boy had died...
Francis forced himself to remember. So much had happened since then, even though he made
it a policy to know everyone who served on his ship.
The name eluded him, however. They had conducted and autopsy and found nothing, but
Goodsir had later assumed he had died because of the lead.
The lead in the cans.

Francis ran a shaking hand through his hair. Already things were going wrong, but perhaps"Sir?"
Jopson stopped that blasphemous thought before it could take root. Slowly, Francis turned
around again. Jopson looked worried, now, though he was still professionalism personified.
"It's nothing, Jopson.", Francis said, trying for calm. "Just... a bad dream."
Jopson didn't appear to quite believe him, Francis saw that very well.
"A bad dream about... Commander Fitzjames?"
Francis was only capable of a curt nod. James, pleading for death, was before his eyes again.
His throat under his fingers, as he forced the poison down.
"It's time I get dressed.", Francis said, when once again the memory of the horror failed to
wake him.
Jopson nodded and went to fetch his things.
Francis resisted the urge to call him back and hug him close. Jopson had still been alive,
before he had woken up here, but the number of things they had been through as well as his
grief made him sentimental.
Well, that was one word for it.
~~~~~~~~~~
Francis was shaved and dressed, and the mundaneness of the act helped restore some of his
senses.
It still didn't undo the unease creeping down his spine, nor his memories before he'd woken
up here.
They also didn't go away as he walked through Terror, unable to help touching wooden
planks that were the walls with the tips of his fingers.
He had been alone, when he'd said goodbye to her, the passageways and decks empty, save
for the few they left behind. And the ghosts, he supposed.
Now, however, the ship was positively bustling with the sounds of life.
The first ship's boy he passed, who saluted him as Captain, was Evans. The one who had
gone out on the ice with him and had been taken by Tuunbaq.
Francis prided himself in his self control that his step only stuttered a little. He soon passed
more and more, most of them dead in his memory, some not, and each sighting was ripping
the wound in his heart open anew.

It got so bad that Francis wished himself alone in his cabin again, nursing a drink. Then he
stopped short with the realisation that he could actually do that, in fact, had been doing that
for most of the journey.
But no, he had to be on deck at least once, before he woke up again.
As he stepped up the ladder, Francis heard the familiar laughter of Thomas Blanky.
God, Thomas. Francis almost raced to him, but he was stopped by the sight of the clear sky,
the crisp wind in his face. He looked around, at the usual activity on deck, everything in
order.
He went to the railing, and saw the water, packed with icy shoals, and when he glanced
ahead, he could glimpse Erebus in front of them.
"This dream is starting to piss me off.", Francis muttered, as he had to push away the thought
of James, perhaps being on deck right now, looking to Terror.
But had ever felt a dream this real to him? But it couldn't both be real, what he remembered
and what he was experiencing right now!
Could it?
Well, Francis thought, he would find out soon enough.
He spoke to the nearest midshipman: "Signal Erebus. I request and ice report."
Sir John would probably invite himself and James to dinner over that, as Francis knew that
Sir John had a craving for beef tongue.
Then perhaps, he may be wrong. As soon as he'd spoken the words, Francis kind of hoped he
was.
Never mind seeing Sir John again after their ugly parting and his even uglier death, meeting
James again, alive and well, would sure undo him.
With dismay, Francis realised that his hands were shaking when he pulled out his telescope.
He took a deep breath, then looked at what Erebus was signaling.
"Tell Mr. Diggle that Sir John and Commander Fitzjames will be joining us for dinner
tonight.", Francis said to Jopson, who had also appeared on deck behind him.
And that was that. Francis knew he had been through this exact moment before, though he
couldn't recall everything. The sense of deja vu was overpowering, and he had a vague
feeling of swimming against the current.
He didn't miss Jospon's slight hesitation before he turned away, as if he'd wanted to say
something, but Francis was soon distracted by Thomas Blanky, sliding down the rigging onto
the deck.

Francis stared at him, knowing he was supposed to say something, but he was too overcome.
"I saw that you will have guests tonight.", Thomas said.
Francis nodded and stepped forward, clapping the other on the shoulder.
"It's good to see you, Thomas."
Blanky frowned at him. "We just saw each other before you went to bed. Are you alright?"
"Fine.", Francis replied in a choked voice. "Just fine, I think."
"Francis, you look like you just saw the ghost of my dead grandmother. Will you tell me
what's going on?"
Of course, Thomas was far too observant for his own good.
"Nothing is the matter.", Francis tried to assure him, then had an idea. "I'm just not looking
forward to this dinner, as you can imagine."
"Ah, well, keep to three courses and then you have it over with."
Not with Fitzjames there. Francis thought it, but he couldn't say the words.
He was supposed to complain about James now, he knew, and it might help to get Thomas to
stop looking at him like that. As if he suspected what was going on, which, surely he didn't,
since Francis didn't even know himself.
~~~~~~~~
It was a long time until dinner, and Francis kept himself busy. When his reactions seemed
slow at times, his demeanor pensive, no one remarked on it.
He quickly realised this was probably because the others thought he was drunk.
Francis knew how easy it would be, how infernally easy, to just have a drink right now,
which was another reason he kept milling about the ship, asking everyone for status reports.
Francis knew that this evening the crew would probably wonder why the captain had chosen
to insert himself into every mundane task that needed doing, but that was of little
consequence.
He just knew that if he returned to his cabin, he would be drawn to the full bottle of whiskey
on his shelf, and just maybe convince himself that this didn't matter, since it was all a dream.
But the more time he spent in this strange... reality, the less likely it seemed.
But what did this mean? What about the other things he experienced?
Maybe he was going mad. James's death had finally driven him off the deep end.

But this wasn't what going mad felt like, he was certain. He had spent the last months in a
situation that would bring anyone to the edge of sanity, and at no point had he even conceived
of something like this!
Everything went marginally well, until he ran into Cornelius Hickey caulking a sprung plank

The secluded nature of the place was probably the only reason Francis hadn't seen Hickey
before now, but to be fair, his mind was occupied with a lot of things right now, so that he
hadn't thought of the mutinous caulker's mate.
Francis had actually hoped for some quiet time with his ship - away from his cabin though,
for obvious reasons- and he thought no one would be down here.
His eyes first caught the stacks of tinned food to the side of the room and he felt a twinge of
apprehension. Their slow poison.
Francis realised that to this point, he had not tried to actually use his knowledge to change

If this was no dream, on the other hand...
He needed to try. The first thing he could do was to issue an order to stay off the tinned food

"Captain."
It was then that he noticed Hickey, who had stood up and straightened, the brush with tar still

He looked particularly unassuming this morning, though Francis was hard-pressed to know

Suspicious though he had been, it had been far too late that Francis had realised the true
depths of perfidy in that man. Had the ice brought it out in him? Or had he always been this

"What are you doing here, Mr. Hickey?", Francis asked, only years of command training
keeping his voice steady.
"Repairing a sprung plank, sir.", Hickey replied, and Francis believed to see in his eyes the

Francis wished he would ask, so he could have a reason to punish him for disobedience.
Lock him up, for God's sake, even throw him overboard for all the pain he caused.
It was a treacherous thought, since Francis felt responsible for every single member of his

But all he could think about when he looked at the man now was Lieutenant Irving, and Mr.

He hadn't disobeyed, hadn't brought Lady Silence onto the ship, hadn't been flogged, hadn't

No, he was just another member of the crew, doing his job.

"As you were.", he forced out and left the room.
Really, was peace nowhere to be found? Francis sighed and listened to the sounds of the ship,
the groaning wood, the distant voices, the bells...
Peace was all around him, Francis realised. It was his mind which was at war, reeling from

By the time Sir John and James were due to arrive, Francis felt numb and exhausted from his

Francis knew that if the symptoms of withdrawal started, he would have the certainty that

doing, talking to Jopson?"

They shook hands, and Sir John smiled. "Francis."

"Well, it seems to be getting thicker farther ahead, sir.", Thomas replied. "Have you brought

Francis jerked. He realised he must be staring at James like the second coming of Christ, but

Christ almighty, Francis thought. How am I going to make it through this evening?

James Fitzjames was extremely, extremely confused.
Thankfully, that was an emotion he could hide pretty well by now. He was painfully aware of
his lack of Arctic experience next to the rest of command, and he did his damndest not to
make it show.

It was a delicate dance; trying to seem as assured as an Arctic veteran, to seem as if he
belonged here, at the same time opening his ears for anything new he might learn.
Still, in private, James experienced a mixture of cheerful optimism and crushing doubts,
depending on his mood. He never expected anyone to ask how precisely he secured his spot
on this expedition, but deep down he knew it, and that was enough to make him feel
inadequate.
And there was no one who brought out these feelings more than Francis Crozier, Captain of
the HMS Terror, Arctic veteran, and James's personal nemesis.
Well, maybe "nemesis" was the wrong word. James just had the feeling that Francis saw right
through him, all the flimsy pretense and frippery he cloaked his name in, and there was
nothing James could do about it.
He had tried to charm him, at first. But Francis Crozier was the equivalent of a block of
frozen ice with no intention to thaw, when it came politeness and conversation.
James had now convinced himself that Francis was simply a melancholic, who for whatever
reason, didn't really want to be here.
He certainly had no passion for the glory of finding the passage, had advised caution at every
meeting so far, and all in all was a misery to be around.
Yes, James was certain that he had figured out the Captain of the Terror by now, and he knew
they would never be friends.
Which was why it was so confounding that James's confusion this evening was entirely due
to Francis Crozier.
When they had greeted each other on Terror, Francis had looked at James like he had never
seen him before, with mixture of pain and reverence in his expression that James was sure he
had read wrong.
Perhaps Francis was drunk, he thought. Rumor had it that he liked his whiskey, such James
had even heard on Erebus.
But Francis's voice was steady, his movements sure and not at all sluggish. His eyes were
clear.
He talked to Sir John normally enough, and Little and Hodgson, as they appeared. But
whenever he looked at James, something passed his eyes the other couldn't quite decipher.
And he did that a lot. Looking at James, which was unusual in of itself.
James wondered more than once if he had food on his face and spent an inordinate time
dabbing his mouth with his napkin.
After a while, James asked himself why he was so affected by Francis's sudden regard. It
must be some instinct left over from the times he had tried to impress him.

Still, James was his usual boisterous self at dinner, and he even started another rendition of

numerous others.
Once he had realised that Francis refused to be dazzled, James had, in a kind of stubbornness,

Often, this annoyance ended with some kind of terse comment on Francis's part, a comment

And still he always did it again. Sometimes, James didn't understand himself.
This evening, however, the person he decidedly didn't understand was Francis, who seemed
to hang on to his every word, with a downright misty eyed expression on his face.
Was this some cruel game Francis played, seeming enraptured only to denounce him later

James was so distracted by Francis that he almost lost his sentence more than once, and the

When James arrived at the shot - "a single musketball, the size of a cherry" - Francis's eyes

James could almost feel the scar itching.
"They got me back to the Cornwallis, where our own Dr. Stanley dug out the bullet...", James

Surely not!
James also noticed that he hadn't taken a single sip of his glass of port. What on earth was

And what did it have to do with James? He had no idea, and he didn't like the thorough

"I chatted with Mr. Reid about the ice today.", Sir John said, making James belatedly realise

James felt relieved, for now he was at a leisure to watch Francis without drawing attention to
himself or the other.
However, the next moment, Francis was looking right at him, and James felt his throat dry.

There was so much... affection in that gaze that James felt dizzy with it. Pained affection, yes,
but affection.
Was this a dream? Had he finally gotten through to Francis Crozier of all people?
But how in the world had he done that? James remembered the last time they'd seen each

James had been telling his story of the Euphrates expedition, and Francis had never glanced

At a pause in the conversation, Francis had interjected: "Wonderful story, James, really, but
Dr. McDonald was just telling us about changes in the crew's diet to prevent scurvy."
This had been uttered with such annoyance and bitter sarcasm ("wonderful story, James...")
that even James couldn't pretend this wasn't a blatant hint to shut up, and do it permanently.
What had changed between then and now?
Francis finally looked away, and asked Sir John a question about the ice.
Right, the ice. A very important subject James ought to pay attention to.
But he couldn't take his eyes off Francis.
Suddenly, there was a commotion and calls for doctor. It seemed that a young midshipman
had started coughing up blood.
Everyone was alarmed, and Dr. McDonald swiftly went to take care of the lad.
They regrouped in Francis's cabin.
James almost waited for Francis to say it was scurvy, to be his usual pessimistic self, but
Francis just stared into the middle distance and was silent.
Sir John cleared his throat. "I don't think it is scurvy.", he said. "None of the three who died at
Beechey showed any signs of it. And if even if it is so, we will be in the Pacific before it has
a chance to don it's undertaker's weepers."
At this, Francis gave a low scoff. Finally, back to normal, James thought.
"You're not confident?", he asked him. "After all that we've achieved? I don't know why.
We've all but found the passage in a year. We're not rowing drekars, after all."
"In this place, technology still bends the knee to luck, James.", Francis said.
There was something about the way he said it. Tired, resigned, deeply sad in a way James
could not comprehend. And he looked at James again with such pain in his eyes that any
smart retort died on his tongue.

At this, Dr. McDonald knocked. He thought it was consumption, and Sir John wanted Dr.
Stanley over on Erebus to examine the boy and take him over with them.
"If you don't mind.", Francis said. "I would like to go over to Erebus as well. I need to have a

Sir John just nodded, but James didn't hide his surprise. Francis was extremely prickly about

"What precisely about?", James asked. "Are you still worried about scurvy? We just said-"
"A private matter.", Francis interrupted him resolutely, looking at the middle distance again
and making James feel like a horrible person for prying.
Perhaps he wanted to do something about his dependence on drink, James thought. That
should reassure him, since he had already complained to Sir John multiple times about
Francis being a lushington.
Instead, James felt irritated, because he was sure there was something he was missing.
If Francis trusted any physician on board, it would surely be Dr. McDonald, who had served

There was a sundog in the sky when they got on deck, and Francis stared at it, that strange
expression on his face again.
"Try to shake the brown study.", James told him, doing his best not to let his irritation show.
"All is well."
Francis turned to him. "Yes, James.", he whispered, and James almost blushed and looked
down at what he saw in his gaze. "All is well, you're right."
This had to be a side-effect of the drinking. Good God, how was that man even capable of

James's irritation only grew as they rowed back to Erebus, Francis still and pensive next to

Sir John was talking to Mr. Reid, who had conferred with Mr. Blanky, and James realised that
if there was a moment for a half way private conversation, it was now.
"Are you quite alright, Francis?", James asked. "You seemed... a tad distracted tonight, I'll
say."
"There's a lot on my mind, James.", Francis said. "But I am very glad to see you. Very glad
indeed."
James frowned at him. "Are you mocking me?"

Francis looked surprised, shaking his head. "Of course not. Why would I mock you?"
Why did he sound so guileless, as if any of his behavior tonight was normal? James felt
profoundly out of his depth, which didn't help with his annoyance.
"Forgive me for saying so, but it's clear that you do not have the greatest affection for me,
Francis. And it's fine. The feeling is mutual."
That had been the wrong thing to say, and James cursed himself for his honesty. He wasn't
even sure he disliked Francis. Well, he most definitely disliked Francis, but he had to admit
that he spent an inordinate amount of time being upset by him for someone pretending
indifference.
And irked him, how much he wanted to hope, how much he wanted to greedily soak up the
the sudden kind regard in Francis's eyes.
How much it hurt, when Francis recoiled from him at his words.
"Right.", Francis replied, his jaw set. "I forgot."
"Forgot what?"
James knew he was doing the equivalent of poking a hornet's nest with a short stick, but
damn him, he couldn't stop.
To his surprise, Francis barked a laugh. "What an insufferable, annoying, irritating pest you
really were."
"Were? Are you implying that I'm ever not?", James asked, put out that he was even trying to
decipher what the bloody hell Francis was saying now.
"You have no idea.", Francis said, still amused. "No idea..."
As he trailed off, he got that melancholic look again. "James, I need to ask you something."
James sighed. "I'm listening."
He still couldn't contain his astonishment when Francis grabbed his hand. "Have you ever
had a dream, a dream you were so sure was real, about something that happened in the past?
Something you regret?"
This caused James to wonder if this was about Sophia Cracroft. Sir John had told him about
Francis's attachment to his niece, the two failed marriage proposals. Though James had long
since determined he was not the marrying sort, he did have a certain kind of sympathy for
Francis.
Certainly, if he had been in Francis's place, he would've hardly been deemed suitable either,
at least if Sir John had known about the circumstances of his birth James worked so hard to
conceal. Thinking of it now made James apprehensive, because there lay the root for his

misgivings with Francis. The fact that somehow, Francis seemed to know his shameful secret,
and was judging him for it.
"I can't say that I have.", James replied.
"But if you had, would you... try to change it? So it would not happen this way?", Francis
said so urgently that James believed that he owed him some kind of serious attempt at an
answer.
"Well, if it's a dream, you can do whatever you want, can't you?", said James. "If you have
the possibility to turn it from a nightmare into something more pleasant, why not grab it?"
"That's true. But I don't know if I can change it. Though I have to try. By God, I have to try."
James had the inkling that they were not talking about a dream after all.
"Is this about your worries about the expedition again? Good God man, we've all but found
the passage-"
They had arrived at the Erebus, and James immediately knew that something happened by
the shouts on deck. Francis let go of James's hand, James realising belatedly that he had still
been holding on to it.
Something was wrong with the propeller, and they had lost a man, Billy Orrin. As Dr. Stanley
was still examining the sick boy, who had been brought over on a different boat, Francis
joined Sir John and James in the great cabin to hear Lieutenant Gore's report.
It wasn't probably wasn't overly serious, but James would be lying if he weren't feeling a
major dent in his optimism due to all these events, the lost man especially.
He half expected Francis to say "I told you so" or even give him some smug look, but of
course, Francis never rejoiced in the tragedy he prophesied. He didn't seem to react at all,
except by looking deeply sad.
Good Christ, James couldn't stand him in that moment!
He felt immediately bad for thinking this, though.
All in all, Francis had been kind to him this evening, had shown no sour temper and barbed
words. Even when he called James insufferable, there had been definite affection in his tone.
Still, James was sure there was something he was missing when it came to Francis, and he
was going to get to the bottom of this, because he knew he wouldn't be able to leave it alone
anyway.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Chapter 2: Francis
"Dr. Stanley has retired to his cabin.", Goodsir told Francis in a hushed tone.
Sickbay was empty save for the sleeping form of David Young on one of the beds.
Francis felt a pang, knowing he wouldn't be able to save him.
So far, he didn't know if he could save anyone, but he had to try. There must be some reason
why he was experiencing this, and Francis thought that perhaps that reason was to help him
stop the disaster from ever happening.
He still had no idea why fate, or God, or some force of the universe had chosen him for this,
as he had already been warning everyone at this time, and no one had listened.
Surely it would've been more wise for Sir John to have such a foresight, or James?
James was exactly the reason Francis had almost given into despair. Of course his altered
state would be dismissed as melancholy, just as his warnings.
If there was only a way, some way to get through to him!
"Shall I fetch him?", Goodsir asked now.
"No need.", Francis said, with a look at Young to make sure he was really sleeping. "It's you I
came to see."
Goodsir blinked in surprise. "Me? What on earth for?"
"I have a theory.", Francis said. "And please, promise me to hear me out till the end. This is
to be treated with the utmost discretion."
Obviously intrigued, Goodsir nodded, then guided him to a chair at the back of the room.
"When he dies, you're going to perform an autopsy on Mr. Young here.", Francis murmured
in a low voice. "To look for signs of scurvy. You're going to find none. None pointing to
consumption, either."
"How do you-"
Francis held up his hand, and Goodsir fell silent. "You're going to have a mystery on your
hands, doctor. People will keep coming to you with strange symptoms, fatigue, irritability,
concentration and memory problems... You're will be confounded by the causes, desperately
trying to search for a solution."
Goodsir looked at him with ever widening eyes, but he didn't have the look of someone
believing to be talking to a crazy person. Yet.

"Well, doctor, I will save you the trouble now.", Francis said. "It's lead poisoning. The lead in
the cans we brought, it's building up inside us, slowly poisoning us. We already need to pick
out bits of lead if we open a can, as you know. If we're to have any hope of surviving, we
can't use the cans anymore."
Goodsir took off his glasses and ran a hand over his face. "I- I don't understand. How do you
know all this, Captain?"
"I just do.", Francis replied, feeling helpless. "The proof is in the cans."
"I suppose there is a certain logic to your words...", Goodsir began. "But pardon me for my
candor, Captain, this is most... unusual."
"You don't have to believe me. Just promise me that you'll investigate it. Please.", Francis
whispered as he tried to inject every bit of authority he had into his pleading.
"If there is even the slightest possibility of what you're saying is true, the whole expedition is
at risk.", Goodsir said quietly.
"Exactly."
"But why... come to me with this? I'm a mere assistant surgeon. Surely Dr. Stanley is more
suitable to-"
"No."
Francis thought of the fire, the screams at Carnivale. He thought of Dr. Stanley going up in
flames before his very eyes.
"I believe I can count on you, Dr. Goodsir.", Francis said gravely. "Your work is meticulous,
and you have an open mind. Please, consider my words. For the sake of the men."
Francis knew he should've perhaps tried something else, but he hadn't had time to think of a
better plan. And perhaps honesty was the best policy in that regard.
"I will.", Goodsir promised him.
~~~~~~~~~~~~
Even though he could've stayed on Erebus for the night, though not without turning some
poor officer out of his quarters, Francis had himself rowed back to Terror.
It should've felt good to be on his ship again, and there was sense of something righting itself,
but soon that all evaporated in light of the lonely night Francis had ahead of him.
A night with room for all manner of dark and hopeless thoughts...
James had still been with Sir John when Francis had said his goodbyes, and Francis had felt a
rush of his old hatred at James all but sitting at Sir John's feet like a prized lapdog.

He had just wished to touch James one last time, even if it was just a squeeze of the hand.
It confounded Francis, how starved he was for it. James's skin, warm and alive...
As it was, it seemed to be an insurmountable gulf between them, and Francis entirely blamed
Sir John for it.
Why did the bloody man always have to come between him and his-lovers, he'd almost thought.
Francis had narrowly stopped himself from blushing and turned away with one last look at
James, done up in all his finery, sitting at the corner of the room.
Once he was back on Terror, he called for Jopson. Anything to stop himself from being alone,
besides, there was something that needed to be done.
Jopson helped him undress, and Francis had to surpress the sudden urge to ask after his
mother.
He thought of all the weeks Jopson had nursed him through withdrawal, bringing them closer
than Francis had thought possible.
This couldn't have all been for nothing.
"Jopson, I want you to take all the whiskey you can find and hide somewhere where I can't
get to it.", Francis said.
This was the second time this evening that Francis has been met with a surprised stare that
carried more than a suggestion of him acting very strangely indeed.
"Are you sure, sir?", Jopson asked. "If you go off it now..."
"You know very well that I haven't drunk a single drop all day, and still I'm feeling right as
rain."
A slight exaggeration, but it was still true.
"To be honest, I don't quite know how that's possible, sir."
"Trust me, you don't want to know.", Francis said.
He had infinite belief in Jospon's trust and discretion, yet Francis knew he couldn't just tell
him the truth. Even him. Not before Francis himself had figured out what the hell was going
on.
"Was that what you saw Dr. Stanley about then, sir?", Jopson asked tentatively.
Of course! Francis eagerly jumped on the excuse. "Yes, he seems to have an effective cure for
that kind of... malady.", he said.

Jospon's face betrayed nothing. He stood there stoically as Francis gave him all of his drink
reserves.
"Hide also all the whiskey in the spirit room.", he told him. "I don't want temptation to haunt
me every time I go down there."
After Jospon had left, Francis lay on his bunk, not sleepy in the least. That is, he was tired,
but he was also scared of what would happen if he fell asleep.
Would he wake up back with James's body, James dead again, horror reality?
No, Francis had to keep himself awake. After some useless fretting about the tins and
Goodsir, then James's death, Francis decided that he was going to drive himself mad if he
kept thinking about that.
And then, his thoughts, already occupied with James, strayed back to his momentary lapse
when he had compared James to Sophia.
Well, he hadn't so much compared them as the situation with them, he told himself.
Both attached to Sir John, both too good for him- though "good" was perhaps the wrong
word.
And also, he wasn't very well wishing he had a similar attachment to James as the one he'd
had to Sophia!
Yes, his soul had felt split in half at his death, butThey were brothers to each other. That was all. Brothers.
James had said so with tears in his eyes...
Francis groaned and covered his face with his hands. This wasn't helping.
What really would help would be formulating a plan for the command meeting tomorrow,
after they would have found out about the bent propeller...
Francis still remembered it as the moment all of their folly had come to a head, when Sir
John had decided, against all advice, to continue on their course.
Could Francis change his mind this time?
He knew well his original idea, to abandon Erebus and sail around King William Island.
Well, Sir John would never abandon Erebus, that much was clear now.
Could there be an alternative plan?
Francis got up at that to consult his charts and maps. He was itching for a drink to go with it,
but glad that Jopson had stowed away the temptation.

Of course, the best course of action would be to stop this expedition entire and head back
home before they got stuck in the ice, but that was even less likely to be considered over
abandoning Erebus.
If he had to convince Sir John, he needed to get others on his side.
The problem was, the only person in reach right now was Thomas Blanky, and he was on
Francis's side already.
What would really make a difference would be the help of James, Francis realised with a
start.
But James was also beyond his reach. At least for the meeting tomorrow, but later... There
must be some way to get him on his side.
Francis heard James's words in his head, so loud as if they were spoken directly beside him.
"It's all vanity."
God, he couldn't think of James, James as he had been in his last days.
Francis stared at the charts until his eyes watered. If he could do nothing tomorrow, and they
would get stuck in the ice, they needed to walk out as soon as they could, not wait until they
were sick and mad.
Francis looked at the path from where they would be stuck to Fort Resolution, willing the
miles to shrink before his eyes.
It was a few moments later that he realised that he'd dozed off, and jerked awake.
He needed to get dressed again, this wasn't working.
~~~~~~~~~~~~
The command meeting was on Erebus again. Francis fidgeted in his dress uniform as he
waited for everyone to trickle in.
James was sitting across from him, sipping his tea and doing a bad job of pretending not to
look at Francis.
Francis wondered what he was thinking. He remembered well James's words during the
meeting, his words about melodrama; though James had apologised for them later, that
wouldn't do them much good now, would it?
Sir John began the meeting, and it played out exactly like Francis remembered, telling them
that Erebus was compromised, that the ice ahead was increasing, but that he wasn't worried
about continuing on their course.
"The situation is more dire than you may understand.", Francis began.

Should he really say the exact same thing again? For all the good it had done?
At least James kept his sly comments to himself for now, just watched him with a frown.
"So what are you suggesting?", Sir John asked after he'd finished. "That we overwinter
here?"
Francis paused for a beat. He looked at James, who stared back in confusion.
"No. The exact shape of King William Land is unknown. As we discovered with Cornwallis
Land, it could very well be King William Island, with a chance to sail around it's Eastern
shore."
"But the east would add miles. We might not be out this year after all.", Sir John said.
Francis tried to phrase his next words carefully. "But only because Erebus is lame... Sir John,
I know what I'm proposing is unconventional, but I think we should abandon Erebus, and
consolidate all our coal on Terror. I truly believe this is our only chance."
"Yes, we should go for broke.", Thomas, blessed Thomas, said next to him.
"If it is a dead end, we can overwinter in complete safety out of the pack, in some sheltered
harbor. We retrace our steps come spring, tired of one another, no doubt, but alive. Please."
Francis knew, knew in his heart that it wouldn't work, but he still tried. He looked at James as
he said it, and James seemed to see something in his gaze, for he frowned and looked down,
his cocky assurance nowhere to be found.
Had he actually reached James?
"That is an interesting speculation.", Sir John said, making Francis realise that perhaps he
should've focused on him, instead. "But of course we will not be abandoning Erebus, nor
Terror, should she suffer some minor misfortune."
Francis balled his hand into a fist under the table, his nails digging into his palm.
"Hear me, please. If the leads close up, it won't matter if we're two hundred or two thousand
miles from safe water. We will be stuck in the ice, and it's already a colder winter than last.
We will have no idea whether thaw will come come spring."
Except that Francis already knew it wouldn't.
"As a trusted friend once put it, this place wants us dead."
James cleared his throat. "Who was this friend? Did he also write melodrama?"
So he was back on track then. Francis could've howled with frustration, but instead he banged
his fist on the table.

"Sir John, myself, Mr. Blanky and Mr. Reid. Only four of us at this table are Arctic veterans.
There be no melodramas here."
Francis was pretty sure he had said the exact same thing the first time around, but this time he
did it with the clearer intention to wound James in his frustration. He now knew how insecure
James was when it came to his rightful place on the expedition.
God, why did he have to be such a thick-headed, stubborn idiot?
"Just live men or dead men.", Francis said, and he almost choked on his own words.
James's death was before his eyes again. "God wants you to live."
James had looked back defiantly, but now his eyes widened. "Francis, are you..."
"It's certainly good to see color in your cheeks again, Francis.", Sir John said. "But we are
two weeks from finding the grail. It is my firm belief that God and winter will find us in safe
waters by the end of the year."
"If you're wrong, we're about to commit an act of hubris, we will not survive.", Francis
replied as he wanted to scream at the man and shake him until he realised the truth.
He should've done it differently, Francis now thought. Suggest something like overwintering
in a safe harbor, like he had toyed with doing.
He dimly heard how Sir John said they would put Terror in the lead position and continue on
their course.
Christ Almighty, how incompetent was Francis that he couldn't prevent this, given a second
chance?
There must be another way, Francis thought. There must be.
~~~~~~~~~~
As soon as the meeting ended, Francis was out the door, heading back to Terror. He needed
to think. More importantly, he couldn't look at James anymore without being driven to
despair.
"Wait, Francis!", James called in the passageway behind him.
Francis pretended he hadn't heard and stalked towards the ladderway. James followed.
"Why don't you stay?", James asked. "They'll bury the boy. Plenty of time for you to...
socialize a bit."
Francis stopped so abruptly that James walked into him from behind.
He backed away as Francis turned around. "Sorry.", James said, a slightly strained smile on
his face.

"Why would I want to socialize with you?", Francis bit out, even as the words hurt him more
than they must James.
"Oh, I don't know. Maybe because you've been staring at me like I've grown barnacles ever
since yesterday.", James said, lowering his voice a bit. "Will you tell me now what the blasted
hell is going on?"
"I don't see why I owe you any kind of explanation.", Francis replied curtly, turning away
from him.
James grabbed his arm. Francis was confounded by his sudden closeness, even as he tried to
get away.
"Have you... some kind of medical problem, perhaps?", James asked in a low voice. "Is that
why you went to see Dr. Stanley?"
Francis avoided James's searching gaze, for he just didn't feel strong enough to bear it.
"We can talk about this in private, if you prefer.", James added, seeming to realise that
anyone could walk up to them and overhear them.
"How about we don't talk about it at all?"
Francis knew if he was alone with James right now he wouldn't be able to keep himself
together. He didn't even want to think what he might do.
Throw himself onto his chest and weep? That was a distinct possibility...
Francis decisively extracted himself from James's grip and began to ascend the ladder, when
suddenly he felt a rushing inside his ears.
It was a little like the vertigo one experienced walking on land after a long time at sea, only
ten times more strong.
"Francis, wait!", James said again behind him, and that was the last thing he heard before a
horrible blackness descended on him.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
This time, Francis knew he was back in an instant. He didn't know how, but he could feel the
despair clawing at his heart in a way that wasn't just remembrance.
He was back.
He was lying with his head on the able where James's body had lain, and Francis knew that it
could've been no ordinary sleep that stopped him from waking up and seeing James's body
removed.
"Captain!"

It was Mr. Bridgens, who approached him and put his hand on his shoulder.
"You were completely dead to the world, unresponsive. I worried..."
"It's alright, Mr. Bridgens.", Francis said, trying to project an assured air and not the creeping
horror he was really feeling.
He had failed to stop it. He had failed to stop it, and that was why he was back here, he was
sure of it.
And he had failed to save James.
Francis could still feel the touch of his hand on his arm, his words "Francis, wait!", and
indeed in his perception it had only happened seconds ago.
Daylight was shining through the tent, and he saw that he would now have to bury him.
Francis spent the next moments in a haze, thinking desperately of some way, any way to go
back.
There was still time to avert the disaster. Even if the inevitable happened and they got frozen
in the ice, they could walk out a soon as possible, like he'd determined last night.
They would have a real chance of making it, then.
Francis covered his face with his hands. He wanted to scream his desperation to the heavens,
but he knew he needed to keep it together.
When he went out, James's body was covered, being sown in.
Francis stood there, knowing that he should say something, perhaps use this moment of grief
for one of unity, but he couldn't.
He refused to credit this truth, still. Refused to believe that he had really lost all chance to
save him.
"Do you wish to speak, sir?", Lieutenant Little asked him.
"I said a service with him last night, just the two of us.", Francis said, his voice sounding
raspy to his own ears. "Let the others pray over him, if they like."
Francis took a shaking breath. "Hide him in the landscape, Edward. Make him invisible. I
don't want him found... and pawed."
Francis only heard dimly Little's assent. He stood there, over James's body, and tried to pray.
But what he was really doing, he realised, was waiting. Waiting to be sent back.
Yet nothing happened. Everything stayed as it was, and James was still dead.
It was a bright day, and they would probably have to contend with sunburn later.

Francis felt the sun was a cruel star here, distant and cold, and in this state of grief he
would've preferred darkness.
It was Thomas Blanky, who finally drew him out of his reverie. He approached Francis and
put a hand on his back, silent for a moment, no need for words.
"Golding sighted the creature. We ought to hear his report.", Thomas said in an apologetic
tone.
Francis nodded, and followed Thomas doggedly like an errant child.
Then he stopped. "Wait."
Francis, wait...
Thomas turned to him with a frown. "What is it?"
"Something happened, Thomas. Something I can't quite explain..."
He was interrupted by Golding, jogging towards them.
He explained that the creature was tracking them, just as Lieutenant Little caught up with
them.
Francis told him to gather the men before he took care of James's body.
He forced himself to think, as the others turned away, except for Thomas.
"We'll need higher ground. Put all the sick in the middle, and face it down with all the ammo
we've got."
"I got a strategy, Francis.", Thomas said. "You cut inland a bit and I drive it back out onto the
ice."
Francis shook his head, refusing to consider it.
"Not possible."
As the fight unfolded and Thomas showed him his leg, Francis wondered if this was
punishment, meant specifically for him, for not preventing this.
It was an egomaniacal thought, but he couldn't help it.
Not Thomas, as well.
"What do you need?", Francis asked, after he had shouted and raged.
No God listened.
~~~~~~~~~

Before they said goodbye, Francis said to Thomas: "I still need your advice on something."
"Happy to help.", Thomas replied. "Though I can't see what advice could make any of this
easier. From old me, at least."
Francis shook his head. "There might be a way, a way to change it. A way that none of this
ever happens. I don't know how, and if I will be given a second chance, but if I am, I would
like to know what you would do."
As quickly and as reasonably as possible, Francis explained to Thomas what had happened to
him. He figured that at this point, he might as well be thought of as a madman.
Thomas wouldn't hold it against him.
"I tried, I tried to change it.", Francis said desperately. "That horrid command meeting about
the propeller, I tried to convince Sir John of the alternative plan. Anything but his planned
course. But he didn't listen, he didn't-"
For the first time since Francis had started his tale, Thomas said something: "Of course he
bloody well didn't! That's exactly what happened the first time!"
"Well, what in God's name was I supposed to have done?", Francis asked.
"Something different, for starters.", Thomas replied. He hobbled closer to Francis and put a
hand on his arm. "Let me be honest Francis: if it's really true what you're saying, you need to
change it. And you're not going to do it by doing the same thing! You need to get creative to
find a solution. Think outside the box."
"What do you mean?"
Something about Thomas's tone seemed to convey something that was better left unsaid, but
Francis hadn't the equanimity to decipher it.
"Bloody hell, Francis, have you ever thought that as long as Sir John is in command of the
expedition, there will be no saving any of us?"
~~~~~~~~
Francis pulled with the others, further and further. More and more were sick, now, and it was
looking dire.
Well, that was an understatement. It really always seemed to be getting worse from what
Francis thought was the worst point.
Someone shouted "man down!", and they stopped.
Francis turned to see who it was, but suddenly he felt the rushing in his ears again. He walked
a few steps, stumbling in the light of the sun, but his surroundings began to fade away.

"Oh, thank God!", he muttered, as his feet went out from under him and once more blackness
descended.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Chapter 3: James
There was really no warning. One moment, Francis was briskly climbing the ladderway to
the hatch, and the next he was falling and James scrambled to catch him.
One of Francis's feet was caught in the stair, and while he fell he twisted around. There was a
cracking sound as the bone broke, just as James caught Francis's head and saved it from
crashing into the wood.
James lost his own footing, and they ended up in a heap at the bottom of the ladderway.
"Francis?", James said urgently.
No answer.
Lieutenants Irving and Hodgson, over from Terror, had caught up with them and rushed to
help.
James propped himself up on an elbow and looked down at Francis, who he expected was out
cold.
Instead, Francis's blue eyes were open, and he stared unseeingly up at him. James shook his
shoulders.
"Francis? Francis, wake up!"
No reaction. James felt unease creeping down his spine, meanwhile people gathered around
them.
"Help me get him away from here.", James said to Hodgson and Little.
When they extracted Francis's leg from its entanglement with the stair, Francis moaned in
pain. James saw his eyelids flutter, and he seemed to be back with them.
"Francis, you took a fall.", James said to him as he heaved him up by the shoulders, Hodgson
and Little to either side of him. "We're carrying you to sickbay."
"James?", Francis whispered.
"Yes, I'm here. You're going to be alright."
"Am I back? Am I really back?"
Back where, James wondered, but Francis sounded so lost that he just agreed in soothing
tones.
Goodsir was in sickbay, sewing up the corpse of David Young.

He immediately helped them get Francis on the free bed and went to examine him.
Francis was conscious, though in a state James could best describe as not quite there. His
voice was weak and brittle, the exact opposite of his assuredness back at the command
meeting.
James felt like as few as possible should see Francis like this, and so he told Little and
Hodgson to leave and fetch Dr. Stanley.
"James?", Francis whispered again, completely ignoring Goodsir, who had begun to ask him
questions about the fall. "James, are you here?"
"I'm here.", James assured him, puzzled though he was, even more so when Francis reached
for him with his hand.
Moments ago, Francis had done anything he could to be rid of James's company, and now...
On instinct, James took Francis's grasping hand. Its grip was strong, not feeble like he
expected. Francis looked at James, and his eyes had that same expression again as when
James had told his story about getting shot yesterday.
James could only stare back, very confused, though for some reason his heart was hammering
in his head.
Goodsir had begun to examine Francis's body, and their eye contact broke when Goodsir
reached the broken leg and Francis scrunched his eyes shut, giving a howl of pain.
"I think it's broken.", James said, rather unnecessarily.
He felt a stab of sympathy for Francis. He had actually broken his leg once, on the Euphrates
expedition, and he didn't like to remember the incident for all the pain it had caused. He had
tried to maintain good cheer, more for himself than the others, but Francis would probably
scoff at the story at how he had arranged his toilette in front of Dr. Helper in order to recieve
visitors.
What happened next was that Francis cursed very colorfully, but he stopped when Dr. Stanley
came into the room, closely followed by Sir John.
"I see you've already started the examination, Mr. Goodsir.", Stanley said archly. "Well, then,
what have we here?"
Francis seemed rather embarrassed by the whole ordeal now, but James was just relieved that
he was apparently his old self again.
Only when Sir John looked at him strangely did James realise that he was still holding
Francis's hand, and he quickly let go.

He wanted to argue, and he did feel wary to leave Erebus. Also, this apparent "perfect

Dundy hummed. "By the time we see each other again, we might have found the passage."

The one of William, Elizabeth and the children -why the hell not.

It was true, that during the long winter at Beechey, James and Le Vesconte had sought each

It was a shame, a damn shame that they weren't as close as they used to...

Francis at first absolutely refused to be lowered into the boat like David Young had been,

Francis had been carried on deck sitting on a chair at his own insistence. It looked completely

At least he would have ample time for that, now.

Again.

Next, a happy Neptune zapped past Jopson's legs to greet James.
James eagerly petted him, as he had a fondness for the ship's dog.
"Why don't you settle in, James?", Francis said. "We can take dinner together later."

Chapter 4: Francis
Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Francis had barely time to think after James left, before Mr. Hickey came in. Perhaps it was
good this way, he was at least glad that they didn't arrive at the subject matter of Sophia.
Francis didn't want to think about her right now on top of everything else.
Of course, his thoughts, rebellious as ever, didn't obey his own orders. He had promised her
that he would bring Sir John safely back.
Back then, it seemed obvious that Sir John's safety and the safety of the crew were one and
the same thing, and so Francis hadn't put much thought into the wording of the promise.
Now, however, Francis saw the sinister perfidy of it, precisely because it wasn't one and the
same thing.
And if he couldn't find another way, he may have to break his promise in the most terrible of
ways.
But first, he had to deal with Mr. Hickey. Hickey had been at the back of his mind the entire
time since he'd been back, even with everything else going on.
Francis knew it wasn't just to condemn a man for crimes he had not yet committed, but that
didn't mean he couldn't keep an eye on Hickey.
The caulker's mate arrived in his cabin with a slightly puzzled air, but if he was nervous he
didn't show it. His eyes fell on Francis's propped up leg, and Francis immediately hated this
sign of weakness, though he projected every bit of authority he had at the other.
One would see how much good it would do him this time around.
"You wanted to see me, Captain?"
Francis nodded. "How did the burial go?"
"Well, we buried him.", Hickey said.
Francis nodded again. "And how is the mood among the crew?"
"Well for the most part. We grieve for Young, of course, but rumor has it that we will have
found the passage soon."
You have no idea, Francis thought. "I see that trust in Sir John is absolute."
"And trust in you, sir.", Hickey said. "You've been to the Arctic before, after all."

"So was Sir John. But I'm glad to hear it."
Francis looked at Hickey for a moment, hoping he would squirm under his gaze. It would be
easier if Hickey was intimidated by him, but Francis suspected he never had been.
There was something world-wise about Hickey, some sort of understanding of life that
caused him to have no respect for his superiors.
Francis had the vague feeling that if he wanted Hickey's trust, he needed to earn it; it wasn't
already given because of his position.
"What if I were to tell you that the rumors were wrong, Mr. Hickey?", Francis said. "That we
will have to spend another winter in the ice?"
Hickey frowned. "Then I suppose we'll have to keep warm and trust that the ice will thaw
come summer."
"And if it doesn't thaw?"
Hickey gave a little laugh. "Captain, do you know something that we don't?"
"I'm merely speculating, Mr. Hickey."
They were both silent a moment. Francis could see the cogs turning in Hickey's head, trying
to figure out what he was after.
"We trust you to get us out of the ice, sir.", Hickey said.
"Do you really?"
Hickey smiled again and fidgeted a little, but it wasn't an expression of shyness. "Why
wouldn't we?"
The question hung between them. Why indeed, Francis thought. If only he could know the
reason Hickey had turned against him. Well, perhaps it could still be ferreted out of him.
Francis leaned back on his seat. He once more regretted that he couldn't stand up. That
blasted leg. He supposed it could've been worse; Private Heather's unresponsive face came to
mind, but still. Francis barely remembered breaking it, just falling, falling, and finally James's
face before his.
Francis had been taken by the urge to pull him close and never let go more than once this
evening.
Who knew when he would be back... in the other time.
"Mr. Hickey,", Francis began. "As you can see, I've suffered an accident while over on
Erebus."
Hickey nodded.

"Because of this, I won't be able to interact with the crew the way a Captain should, at least in
the next few weeks. So I wanted to ask you if you'd be willing to observe the men's mood,
and report it back to me, as I can no longer gauge it myself."
"You mean, spy for you, sir?", Hickey asked, obviously surprised.
"Nothing so nefarious. I just wish to know what is going on, in every sense of the word. And
I think you are the right man to tell me. You get along well with everyone, wouldn't you
say?"
"Reasonably so, yes."
Francis forced a smile. "Good. Feel free to tell me if there's anything troubling you."
"I will, sir.", Hickey said.
He wore an expression of confusion that reminded Francis of James in the last days, or
Goodsir when he told him about the cans.
Really, I need to be careful., Francis thought. A rumor that the Captain of the Terror is a
madman would be worse than him being just a drunkard.
Francis reached out his hand. "Shall we shake on it, Mr. Hickey?"
For a moment, Hickey looked at Francis as if he was some kind of witch, forcing an innocent
virgin to join her coven. Francis bit back a laugh.
Then, Hickey approached and took Francis's hand, giving it a firm shake.

James appeared for dinner on time, in his dress uniform, which confounded Francis for two
reasons: Firstly, he hadn't donned his, thinking he and James were past all formalities
anyway; but there he had mixed up the two timelines again, hadn't he?
Secondly, his first thought when James had ducked through the door had been: 'Good Lord,

Francis had thought so from the moment he met James, and in the beginning that had only
fueled his resentment.
As he had gotten to know James in their shared trials, the bitterness of the thought had
disappeared, but never the thought itself.
Even when James had been wasting away, his beauty was never quite taken from him.
Still, when Francis compared him now to how he had been then, near death, James was
positively radiant. His hair, that damned hair, luscious and thick, his eyes glowing, his skin
without blemish.

It hurt to look at him, really, though not because of any resentment. Francis could see James

"I'm not cross with Sir John.", James said. "He only wants what's best for all of us."

"I don't understand you, Francis.", James said. "I don't think I ever did. But especially not

He was absolutely exhausted, he realised.

"Except for my blasted leg, of course."
And the fact that I want to weep every time I look at you.

"So you can play nursemaid to me? You know, someone else might take that as an insult."

Francis could well understand Sir John's reason for sending James over to Terror. He wanted

Another part of him was hurt, though. It was almost as if James's presence was taunting him

It was true, Francis regretted not having made friends with James sooner. All that time they'd

"I know. And still, I feel..."
So alone, Francis thought. So very, very alone.
"If you ever think it becomes unbearable, you call me, sir.", Jopson said earnestly. "Day and
night. I am here."
"Thank you, Jopson."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
"Bloody hell, Francis, have you ever thought that as long as Sir John is in command of the
expedition, there will be no saving any of us?"
Francis could hear Thomas's words as clearly as if he'd just spoken them.
"You think I can't make him see reason?", he had replied.
"I think that you've been trying to make him see reason for a whole damn year, and nothing
came of it.", Thomas said.
"So what are you suggesting?", Francis asked desperately. "I can't very well kill him."
Thomas just looked at him, indicating that that was exactly what he was suggesting.
"No. I can't.", Francis said. "I can't-"
Thomas put his other hand Francis's shoulder. The other was already resting on his arm. "I'm
not saying you have to, necessarily. You just need to make sure that you're in command

before everything is lost this time, and you're not going to manage it by making the same
mistakes."
Francis looked at Thomas, another friend he was about to lose, because of Sir John's folly. He
thought of James, cold and dead, and all the other men.
Would he be willing to pay for their lives with Sir John's?
"Francis, we're at a point where extreme measures have to be considered. If there is truly a
chance to do it again, it has to happen differently."
"I agree.", Francis said in choked voice. "By God, I agree."
"I can't believe I'm saying this. I was sceptical when you wanted to abandon the ships with
the rescue party. But now.. you have to abandon the ships as soon as possible, if you get stuck
in the ice. And there is no way in hell that Sir John is going to sanction that."
"You'd have me organise a mutiny?", Francis asked.
"If that's what it takes."
Francis knew that Thomas was right. When it came to one life, measured up against all the
others, there was no question.
"Thomas, I wish you would stay. In case I'm back there again, and here, I would take your
advice.", Francis said, unable to say that the parting would hurt more than he could bear.
Thomas smiled. "What for, hm? You already have old me in the other time, that ought to be
enough. Besides, somebody needs to save you from Tuunbaq."
"Perhaps there is a way to stop that from happening, too."
"I know you'll think of something.", Thomas said.
Francis was exhausted, but he couldn't sleep. The conversation with Thomas kept playing
before his inner eye.
Francis had made another attempt to talk to Sir John, right after his leg had been broken, but
to no avail.
Sir John had dismissed all his worries, and tried to soothe him with the coming glory of
finding the passage, and when that didn't work, he said that Francis needed to focus on
resting on account of his leg.
Francis had never felt so desperate. "Don't you see?! We're all going to die, all of us, if you
don't-"
Sir John blinked at him in surprise. "If I don't what? Take your advice? Is there anything that
you know about the Arctic that I don't?"

He still sounded calm, but Francis saw that all this was going to lead to was the dressing
down Sir John had given him when he'd suggested sending out the rescue party.
In fact, Sir John was already beginning to act annoyed at his input, and Francis could see that
further speaking up was beginning to hurt his case more than he could help it.
Thomas was right, he needed to try other ways of changing everything.
Perhaps Francis shouldn't even contemplate the uglier possibilities open to him. Murder,
mutiny and the like. He was sure there were others who would say that such disobedience
was worse than death, that it was adhering to the rules of conduct that separated good
Englishmen from lawless savages.
Francis, however, knew he was not above such actions in these circumstances. He'd rather
never have found out about that, but it was what it was.
If it meant bringing the men home, saving James's life, Francis would do anything. No price
was too high, no blemish on his own soul too much.
Though he still held on to the hope that it wouldn't have to come to that.
There might still be a way to change Sir John's mind, even if he didn't listen to Francis
himself.
There would be an entire winter's time to try other things, if they proceeded on this course.
Still, Francis may couldn't change the course, but he could change the speed at which they
met their doom. For the reasons of conserving coal, and for Erebus to keep up, he'd greatly
reduced Terror's speed.
His hope was that he might talk to James and convince him before they were stuck in the ice.
Francis tried to relax and sleep, if only for his own sanity, even if there was still the fear that
he would wake up in the other time.
Along with his thoughts, the fact that with his leg he couldn't toss and turn greatly bothered
him, and soon he was itching to move.
Francis gave a great sigh. Even the movement of the ship failed to soothe him, knowing it
was on the course to its own doom.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Somehow, Francis must've fallen asleep, because he woke late the next morning. Still on the
ship, James still alive.
And his damned leg - still broken, as he noticed when he fell out of his bunk turning over.
One of the wooden staves broke, and Francis instinctually jerked his leg, which caused the
world to white out in pain for a moment.

The crash alerted Jopson, who immediately called Dr. McDonald, and together they got
Francis into a sitting position.
Consequently, Francis wasn't even dressed and already in a bad mood, and James coming in
positively chipper did nothing to lift it -except for the brief shock of seeing him alive and
well, that is.
"You know, I almost broke my leg once.", James began.
"That must've been horrible for you.", Francis said sarcastically.
"It was.", James replied completely seriously. "My legs were all I had at that time. I was
walking through the Mediterranean to deliver the India Office mails the Euphrates was
carrying-"
"As riveting as this story sounds, could you perhaps wait with its delivery until I'm at least
not sitting before you in my bloody nightshirt-"
"I just came to lend a helping hand!", James said.
"Not needed!", Francis bellowed, vaguely alarmed.
The thought of James's hands on him was disquieting, if only for the reason that Francis
found himself yearning for his touch. He didn't want to get misty-eyed again - he didn't know
precisely how to win James over to his side yet, but he was sure it wouldn't help if Francis
were to cry in his arms.
"Are you sure? Charlewood twisted his ankle once when we were on the Excellent and I
helped him with everything-"
"James, I thank you for the offer, but I-"
"Perhaps I can distract you from the pain, then.", James said. "I could tell you a story while
you are dressed."
"Don't you have something better to do?", Francis asked desperately.
He was aware of how their positions had been reversed in the other time, how he had seen
James in the indignity of illness. Perhaps it was only just that James take care of him for a
change. The only difference was that Francis felt completely healthy, and part of him refused
to accept that he needed any help at all.
"Where is it best to lift you, Captain?", Dr. McDonald asked before James could answer. "On
your bed or the chair at your table?"
"I'm certainly not going to spend the day lounging in bed like some sort of-"
"The chair it is, then.", McDonald said.

As Jopson and McDonald heaved him onto the chair, Francis did his best to ignore James,
who very much wasn't going away.
He was of course impeccably dressed, his damned hair brushed, and looked a vision, which
Francis tried not to notice.
Thankfully, there was knock on the door and Thomas Blanky strode in, demanding to know
what everyone was doing here this "fine morning".
Francis looked at his friend, trying to communicate with his gaze that he wanted everyone out
while he was dressed, especially James.
He could've just ordered such, but he didn't want to hurt James's feelings, damn it all.
"Commander, would you come on deck? I need your opinion on the ice ahead.", Thomas
said.
James frowned. Of course, Thomas Blanky didn't need anyone's opinion on the matter of ice,
least of all James's, who probably knew as much about ice as he did about broken legs, which
was to say, not much.
Still, James went after Thomas out of the cabin, and Dr. McDonald followed after Francis's
leg was secure.
Francis breathed a sigh of relief once he was alone with Jopson.
"I hope you're not put out that you didn't get to hear Fitzjames's story.", Francis told his
stewart.
"It seems to me that you are the one who'd rather have heard it, sir.", Jopson said as Francis
got his waistcoat on.
Francis scoffed. "What makes you say that?"
"It's just, well, whenever Commander Fitzjames is in the room, you look at him as if you'd
want him to stay forever, as opposed to only a few days ago, when you seemingly couldn't
wait to be rid of him."
Francis wondered once more if he should tell Jopson the truth, for all he seemed to have
almost pieced it together himself.
But no, the sheer absurdity of what was going on stayed him, as well as the responsibility that
came with knowing. The responsibility to stop it.
He'd really already laid enough at Jopson's door, it wouldn't do to add more.
Dressed, he took tea, had a smoke, just as Thomas Blanky came back in, wrapped in his
various layers.

"It's getting colder, too. I don't think we'll make it to King William Land, to be honest.", the
icemaster proclaimed.
"I know we won't make it.", Francis muttered.
"Well, we have provisions for another winter, if the ice doesn't crush us."
Francis nodded.
"What's going on between you and Fitzjames, then?", Thomas asked.
"I wish I knew.", Francis said truthfully.
Thomas pulled his pipe out and began to stuff it. "You know what I've been wondering? How
a man who was a sailor since he was thirteen can break his leg on a bloody ladderway."
"Isn't a friend supposed to make me forget that humiliation rather than dwell on it?"
"I will once I understand what is happening to you."
Francis sighed. "Nothing is happening to me, Thomas. I'm perfectly fine. Disregarding the
leg."
"How did you break it, then?"
Francis decided to be as honest as possible. "It was just after the meeting. I was arguing with
Fitzjames-"
"About what?"
"What does it matter? Anyway, I was climbing the ladderway, when everything went dark
before my eyes. I don't know why, it just happened... And the next thing I knew, I was being
carried, Fitzjames looking down on me..."
Francis reasoned that this was almost the truth, exempting his stay in the other timeline.
Where he had said goodbye to Thomas for the last time...
Francis looked at his friend, and was once more overcome with the urge to pull him close,
vowing internally that he would make it right.
Even if it meant...
"So you're telling me that James Fitzjames, who you can't stand, made you swoon like a lady
seeing the man of her dreams?", Thomas yanked Francis back to the present.
"Of course not!", Francis said indignantly, finding with dismay that he was blushing. "How
can you even suggest-"
Thomas just looked at him, eyes gleaming with merriment, and Francis stopped his bashful
stuttering to hit him in the arm.

Thomas laughed, and suddenly Francis had to laugh too, feeling something light in his chest,
until he remembered laughing with Thomas thus when he'd made his absurd request of forks
and a rope.
Francis stopped to wipe the tears from his eyes. "I'm glad you're here, Thomas."
"Where else would I be?", Thomas asked.
