Chapter 5: James
James's first days on Terror went by without incident, and he didn't even have much time to
stare longingly back at Erebus very often.
He also slowly began to realise that while he missed what he'd come to think of as his ship,
he didn't miss Sir John's company, which made him feel slightly guilty.
It wasn't that Sir John was in any way disagreeable in nature -he certainly was more so than
Francis, even the new Francis who was acting strangely at times- or that he didn't have any
regard for James, rather the opposite.
However, James realised that it was he himself who had always put a lot of effort in his
interactions with Sir John -more so than the usual effort of being a polite, decent human
being. He had played his role of being unassuming and worthy of his position, polished to
perfection and it had been exhausting.
Here on the other hand, James didn't have to bother, except for the normal amount of
pretense- and even that faded in the company of Francis.
James still had the feeling that Francis new the game he played, saw through him in a way so
few people had. In the beginning, this had terrified him, but now he was less alarmed.
It was the affection with which Francis treated him, grudging and sometimes clumsy, but
definitely there.
James was still confounded as to why Francis suddenly liked him now, and he wanted to get
at the truth, but at the same time he wasn't going to complain about it.
Francis could still be as acerbic as ever, but his barbs were less cruel and more good-natured
teasing, now.
James found himself responding to it quite naturally, and he quite liked their back and forth.
James caught himself beginning to look forward to his conferences with Francis, even though
he was in terrible mood during most of them.
Sitting still didn't suit Francis, and he was also dreadfully melancholic about their future, still.
However, James had admit that more than Francis's dire feelings pointed towards a hard
winter.
The ice increased per day, same as the cold, and James didn't need to be an expert to know
that they had a difficult time battling the elements.
It was as if the mood of the ship's Captain was starting to effect everyone else on board, and
James was soon heartily sick of it.

He decided that it would be to the good of everyone to cheer Francis up a bit, and he was
determined to use his new position in Francis's affections to do so.
The next time he went down to the great cabin, he took time to study the selection of books
on hand. It was three days after the funeral of David Young, the ice was slow yielding, yet Sir
John maintained their course south southwest.
"Are you looking for something specific?", Francis asked.
Of course, it was too cold for him on deck, especially since he couldn't move around, and his
own sleeping berth was too small to admit people for meetings, so Francis had took up shop
here, so to speak.
"Yes.", James said, studying the spines, before turning to Francis, who raised an eyebrow at
him.
"Well?"
"The Complete Works of Shakespeare. I think I heard mention on Erebus about this library
having every classical book one could think of, so it ought to be there."
"Would you have us put on a play, James?"
"No. Not as such, anyway.", James said cryptically.
He didn't want to tell Francis his plan before he found the book. Francis might hide it, or
outright refuse.
"We do have it, but someone must've taken it, because it's not here.", Francis said.
"One of your officers?"
"Anyone is allowed to read the books here, really.", Francis said with a shrug. "What the
devil do you want with Shakespeare, anyway? You hardly need any more theatricals in your
life."
Mere days ago, this might've been a taunt, designed to sting, but now it sounded fond,
teasing. James couldn't help the warmth that spread in his chest.
"Francis, there can never be enough theatricals.", he said seriously.
Francis sighed. "That shouldn't surprise me, coming from you."
"We used to put on plays while docked in Malta, when I was a midshipman.", James began,
thinking back to those times with a pang, especially at the warmer climate.
Back then, he hadn't known what "cold" really meant.
James stopped scanning the shelves to look at Francis. "Our Captain had a fondness for the
bard, and with nothing better to do, we put on productions of Romeo and Juliet, Richard III,

Julius Caesar... It was great fun."
"I can imagine.", Francis said with a gentle scoff. "Ready for the stage as you are with all
your stories and flamboyance."
"Why, thank you."
"That wasn't a compliment."
James smiled at him. "I think it was."
For a moment, their gazes were caught in each other, and James suddenly felt his throat dry.
His heart was also racing, and at the same time he wished to gaze forever into Francis's eyes,
so shockingly blue.
Realising what he was thinking, James looked down, heat in his cheeks.
This wasn't... a good idea at all. In fact, it was extraordinarily foolish.
"I'm going to look for that book now.", James mumbled, practically fleeing the room.
Francis didn't call after him, and James wondered if he'd noticed it too. Hopefully not, or else
Francis would probably readily sent him back to Erebus, no matter what Sir John said.
James paused. Wasn't that exactly what he wanted?
James leaned against the bulkhead and took a few deep breaths to calm himself.
It had only been a look. Fleeting, really, not indicative of anything. Even if Francis suspected,
there was no proof.
Also, it came to him, it was only the unnatural nature of his desires that made him able to
read gazes with such accuracy, to imbue them with so much meaning.
If Francis suspected, did he perhaps have experience with this subtle art as well?
For now, James decided to hope that Francis was still hopelessly in love with Sophia Cracroft
and couldn't even notice anyone's affections besides her, as much as he didn't actually want
that to be true.
For the rest of the day, James avoided seeing Francis, which thankfully wasn't difficult.
To distract himself further, he also looked for the book, drawing up in his head a list of
possible candidates who could've taken it.
Lieutenant Hodgson was now berthing on Erebus, seeing as the flagship had ample space in
its officer's quarters on account of James's absence and the deaths at Beechey.
There was the possibility that Hodgson had taken the book with him to Erebus, and James
had to say, even though they had served together on the Cornwallis, he had no idea if

Hodgson was the kind of man who read Shakespeare in his spare time.
Disregarding that, James asked Little next.
"Shakespeare?", Little asked. "No, haven't seen it. To be honest, I don't really have the
necessary leisure to read in my spare time."
That didn't surprise James. Little seemed very tense on a good day, and not in the everrighteous way of Lieutenant Irving, but in a more melancholic way. He seemed perfectly
suited for his job at Francis's side, in that aspect.
"I think perhaps you should read Shakespeare once in a while.", James told Little. "He can be
quite funny. Might cheer you up a little."
Little frowned. "Yes, sir."
"That wasn't an order.", James hurried to assure him. "Just a suggestion."
"I will consider it."
"Wonderful!", James said, forcing a smile onto his face.
Good God, that man was more dreary than Francis in his worst moods!
Next on the list was Lieutenant Irving, though James didn't have very high hopes where he
was concerned.
All the while, the ice continued to close in on them.
James could feel Terror straining against the onslaught, the moan of cracking ice against her
hull, pierced by the shouts of the men.
It was an eerie feeling, because the ship seemed ready to split apart at any moment. James
remembered it from the winter at Beechey, and was glad for it, since that meant he didn't
catch a fright every time the ice shrieked around the ship.
Lieutenant Irving was on deck, in deep discussion with Thomas Blanky.
"We'll have to try and burst the ice open physically soon.", Blanky was saying. "Ah,
Commander, we're just trying to think of a plan."
James discussed it with them, and a tiny part of him wondered if they shouldn't turn back
now, before they were frozen in.
The ice could also crush them, he knew. Francis hadn't said so at the command meeting, he
had been talking about being frozen in, so perhaps that was the liklier possibility.
"Has Erebus been signaling?", he asked.

"Only to let us know to continue forward at all costs. And also to ask about why we're so
slow, but the Captain won't enhance the speed, no matter what, he said.", Irving said.
James nodded. Different from Francis, he had actually been down on the engineering deck,
where the coal was shoveled, to find out if there were some problems Francis was responding
to, but apparently their coal reserves were the same and nothing had changed.
When James had reported this to Francis, he had just said: "All the same, there is no need to
rush things. Also, Erebus still needs to keep up."
His tone had brokered no argument.
"You do realize that Sir John is going to demand to know what the hell you're doing sooner or
later.", James said dryly. "And that I'm going to be the one who is going to have to explain it
to him, probably."
"I am aware."
James wondered if Francis had copied this sort of brushing off from Sir John himself.
"Well, I'm sure Sir John is going to invite himself to dinner soon.", James said to Blanky and
Irving.
They were walking up and down the gunwale to keep warm. From the winter at Beechey,
James knew it would only get worse.
He tried to summon the sense of adventure he'd had when signing up for this expedition,
when he had written John Barrow's son that he would gladly walk to the North Pole.
He did feel it, but there was also a strange kind of foreboding clinging to him, and he couldn't
get rid of it. Maybe he had been spending too much time around Francis.
"Shakespeare?", Irving said when James asked him. "He has a rather coarse sense of humor,
don't you think? Not to my taste at all."
"So you haven't taken the book?"
"No. I wouldn't be caught dead with it."
James regarded him in the fading light of dusk. "What do you read? Besides the Bible, of
course."
"I don't see what is wrong with reading the Bible."
"Of course, I wasn't implying any judgement.", James said, deeply wishing that Irving had
gone over to Erebus after all.
Between him and Little, Hodgson could hardly be worse than them.

Of course, Sir John had a fondness for reading the Bible, in fact, he had often requested
James read it to him in the late hours.
James, eager as ever to ingratiate himself with Sir John, had done so, though he had to say
that the Bible wasn't to his taste.
"I dare say you're a bit bored of it.", Sir John had remarked one evening. "Perhaps you're too
young to find refuge in the Bible's pages."
"Perhaps I'm too much of a sinner to find refuge in the Bible's pages.", James had replied
lightly.
"Oh, nonsense!", Sir John had said, puffing on his pipe. "And even if it were true, a sinner
will find the most refuge of all, if he is only penitent."
"That's true.", James had answered.
Perhaps that was the issue with him and God, he mused. He wasn't repentant of his sin, at
least the one that mattered most.
The only reason he had ended things with Dundy had been because of fear of discovery, not
regret of doing the deed itself.
It was almost time for dinner with Francis, and finally James had the idea of asking the
stewarts what had become of the book.
Since Jopson was so busy tending to Francis, James went to Billy Gibson, who now also
tended to him in place of Bridgens.
Gibson was in the carpenter's workshop, though Mr. Honey was nowhere to be seen. Instead,
Mr. Hickey was sitting on the worktable, smoking and chatting animatedly with Gibson.
James only recognized the caulker's mate because he had passed him on his way to speak
Francis, after Francis had made his cryptic remark about rumors about him.
When James came in, Hickey jumped off the table and straightened.
"At ease, gentlemen.", James said. "Where is Mr. Honey?"
"He went to fetch something.", Hickey said, putting a belated "sir" at the end.
"Do you want us to look for him?", Gibson asked.
"No, it's actually you I wanted to see.", James said to him.
Hickey threw Gibson a look -ah, there we are with those fleeting looks again, James
thought-, before he turned to leave.
"So, I'm looking for the Complete Works of Shakespeare.", James told Gibson. "I thought you
might know who took it from the shelf."

"I have no idea, sir.", Gibson said. "We really ought to have some sort of system to know who
took a book."
James nodded. "On Erebus, Mr. Bridgens knows the state of the library at all times. Granted,
it's not as many books, but-" He stopped, having a realisation, and smiled. "I think I know
who has taken the book.", he said. "If you'll excuse me..."
Since he hadn't seen the Captain of the foretop on deck, James thought he might find Henry
Peglar near, and he was right. He was in the crew's mess, reading.
Not the Complete Works of Shakespeare, since the volume was too thin for that, but James
still believed he was on the right track.
"I'm sure Mr. Bridgens misses you.", James said to him. "I know how often you visited each
other during the winter at Beechey, despite the treacherous weather."
"I miss him, too.", Peglar said freely. "I would really like to ask him some questions about
what I'm reading. He recommended it to me."
"What are you reading?"
Peglar showed the book to him. "Seneca. Letters from a Stoic."
James gave a laugh. "Mr. Bridgens really isn't one for light subject matters, is he? I remember
having to read it as a boy. Barely got through the thing, it was so boring."
"I do like it.", Peglar said. "It's just, I don't know much about the Romans, and sometimes I'd
like to for context. I'm sure John knows more about them."
"I know he does... Say, Mr. Peglar, you wouldn't happen to know what happened to the
Complete Works of Shakespeare, would you?"
Peglar's cheeks colored a little in the yellow lighting. "I have it, sir. I asked Mr. Jopson if I
could take it. Until a few days ago I was reading Richard III."
"Then you wouldn't mind giving it to me?"
"Of course not! I'd meant to return it, I just forgot..."
"I performed in Richard III once, you know.", James said. "In port at Malta."
"Really? Who did you play?"
"One of the young princes. They said my hair was perfect for it."
James wondered what sort of comment Francis would make at that, and had to smile.
~~~~~~~~~~~

At dinner, Francis wasn't in a good mood, but James was just kind of relieved that he didn't
seem to remember their last parting.
Or was he a tad disappointed, too?
Dangerous waters, he thought to himself.
"You think we will get stuck in the ice.", James said.
"I know that we will get stuck in the ice.", Francis grumbled. "Once again, I failed to bring
my point across."
James didn't say that Francis had brought his point across, as he said it, perfectly, it was just
that no one was willing to listen to him.
"Well, even if we do, what's one more winter? Thaw will come come spring."
"And if it doesn't?"
James looked at Francis, seated next to him, his leg propped up on a stool. He looked good,
James thought. Undefeated. His question wasn't melancholic brooding, it seemed to be
genuine curiosity.
"I suppose we can manage another year in the ice, then.", James said.
"And if thaw doesn't come then? If we're stuck in the ice indefinitely, our resources
dwindling, the resources we do have spoiled, and all of us getting more ill and less sane each
month, what then?"
Francis's tone stopped James from making any kind of flippant reply. Why did that man
always have to ruin the mood? Though, a tiny part of him said, if he was right...
"Well, then...", James began, trying to scramble for an easy solution, and finding none, ended
on: "...then we're royally fucked, I suppose. Pardon the language."
"Exactly.", Francis said. "So it would do to make sure that doesn't happen in the first place,
doesn't it?"
"That's true.", James conceded. "But what I'm bothered with is that you absolutely refuse to
consider other possibilities. It is as if you already know -know with certainty- that everything
is going to go wrong."
Francis nodded, looking sad. "It's not just the reality of being in a place as hostile as this,
though that's certainly a factor. We are absolutely dependant on the resources we brought, and
we can't survive in this place like the Netsilik people..." He trailed off in thought.
"What else is it, then?", James asked.
"It's our entire attitude, the hubris of it. It's disregarding everything experience tells us,
instead assuming that we can just sail through these waters like it's nothing. It's endangering

every single one of us, and it needs to stop."
Francis was speaking of "our attitude", but James could tell that he really meant Sir John.
Part of James, loyal to their leader, wanted to scoff and brush Francis off, yet another couldn't
help seeing that there was a grain of truth to Francis's words.
Hadn't the Arctic intimidated him from the beginning, even as it fascinated him?
As if to agree, the ice made the ship groan again.
"Well, what do you suggest, now that we're on this course?", James asked.
Francis chewed and swallowed, considering. "Wait out winter in some sheltered harbor, if we
can still turn around, if it's not too late. Or here, or wherever we're stuck, and then, if thaw
doesn't come, walk out. Back to Fort Resolution."
James was speechless for a moment. "Abandoning the ships? Both of them? You can't be
serious!"
"It will be a difficult sacrifice.", Francis said. "Believe me, I know. But it will leave us alive
by the end of it."
James thought of Sir John, having a quiet dinner by now, accompanied by nothing but the
shouts of the men and the ever present ice.
He and Francis didn't even think in the same dimensions.
"I can't believe Sir John would ever agree to such a course of action."
Francis nodded. "He wouldn't... At least when I propose it."
James looked at him carefully. It was hanging in the air between them, what if he, James,
were to propose it? Preposterous, surely. James didn't share Francis's opinions, in fact, he
thought Francis entirely unsuited for the whole expedition, and also he couldn't stand him!
"I would never ask him such a thing.", James said stiffly.
Francis put down his fork, and in a move that left James utterly stunned, covered James's
hand with his own.
"James, I only wish to save us. Save you. There's is no malice intended, and I speak from
experience, not overwhelmed with melancholy, as you might think. I know Sir John cherishes
you more so than he does me, for various reasons, and so I dearly hope that you might help
me."
James was, once more, utterly speechless. He realised that all he thought before about
despising Francis might have been true only days ago, but now it wasn't. This new, strange

It was all well and good to hate someone who hated you back, but Francis, strangely enough,

"Does it matter? I know you said it."
Francis sighed. "I did. I won't deny it- But that was before I knew you- what I mean to say is,
that was before I gave up the drinking, while I was still bitter about- a private matter..."
"Sophia Cracroft.", James said.
For some reason, he had been feeling like she had been hanging between them for a while

"Yes, Sophia Cracroft.", Francis muttered. "She is the reason I'm here, but not the reason II'm trying to save us."
"Don't you have the hope that once you've returned us all to England, she will not reject you a

James only belatedly realised that perhaps Francis would be cross, knowing that Sir John had

But Francis didn't seem greatly surprised, if a little morose.

Perhaps this was the reason for Francis's change in behavior, then. But it didn't entirely

"I'm sorry about saying that about you.", Francis said. "I was wrong. You're very much

James was very aware of how Francis hadn't let go of his hand, the way he had leaned close they had both leaned close and James could see the dusting of freckles on Francis's skin and
feel his breath on his face.
"Speak freely.", James repeated in a gravelly voice.
"Aye.", Francis said. "Sir John doesn't want to accept the possibility of failure. His own pride
stands in the way, perhaps his memories of previous expeditions... I'm not saying that we will
fail, but it is dangerous to not even contemplate it. It is equally dangerous to go into this

"Like Erebus?"
"Like Erebus, or even Terror. And lives, James. We're already fewer than we were when we
set out. All we can do is put aside all vanity and make sure the number of dead stays as low

James nodded, hating how he was beginning to see Francis's point, as well as how his

It occurred to him that Francis had prepared these words, set him at ease over the last days so

If Francis really believed their situation was as dire as he had made it out to be, wouldn't

James swallowed as Francis gripped his hand tighter, his fingers curling around James's palm.
"James, please, see that I-"
The expression in Francis's eyes became too painful to bear, so much so that James withdrew
his hand and stood up, even though he wasn't done eating.
"There is still something you're not telling me, though.", he said, looking anywhere but
Francis.
"I've told you everything I freely can.", Francis whispered.
"What's that supposed to mean?" His voice sounded harsh to his own ears.
"James, look at me, please."
I can't bear it., James thought, shaking his head. The way you look at me, I can't bear it.
He heard Francis shuffling in his own seat, huffing in frustration. "You must know that I'm
speaking the truth out of my own heart.", he said at last.
James cleared his throat. "I know.", he said. "I do know. But I don't understand-"
"Will speak to Sir John for me?", Francis continued with the relentlessness of an incoming
locomotive.
James took a breath to steady himself, and then sat down again, picking up his cutlery.
"I don't see that I have any choice at this point."

Chapter 6: James
James was walking. He liked to walk, though the landscape seemed a little dreary. It was also
familiar, but there were no landmarks to jostle his memory.
Just endless rock, nothingness, really.
After a while James realised that he was tired, and it wasn't the normal tiredness after a long
walk, but something deeper. Seeping into his bones.
He tasted blood in his mouth, and his side hurt, and he was just so tired. Yet he knew he
needed to keep walking.
The pain got worse and worse after he noticed it, and he staggered a few steps and came to a
halt.
Keep walking.
James gritted his teeth and continued. Speaking of teeth, his gums felt strange, not just from
the bleeding. It tasted of rot, too.
James felt a gnawing hunger, and he felt weak, and he knew there would be a point, soon,
when his legs wouldn't carry him anymore.
But he needed to keep walking.
He bit on something hard and spit it out. It was one of his teeth.
James fell, and he couldn't breathe, couldn't~~~~~~~~
James sat bolt upright in Lieutenant Hodgson's bunk, breathing hard. For a moment, his
throat was closed up, and he couldn't get air into his lungs.
He thought he was actually going to die, still half in the dream, absolutely terrified, until
slowly, the pain lessened and his breaths actually brought nourishment again.
James jumped to his feet and only dimly noticed a book falling to the floor.
He fumbled for his desklamp, and somehow managed lighting it with shaking hands.
He needed a moment to find the mirror in the unfamiliar surroundings, and addled as his
mind was, but when he had it he almost didn't want to look.
He did it anyway, expecting to find himself wasting away, but it was his normal, healthy
visage that looked back at him with fearful eyes.

He checked his gums, his teeth, and there was nothing amiss. Finally he tugged up his
nightshirt to look at the bullet wound.
It wasn't open and bleeding, there was just the healed scar.
James breathed a sigh of relief, even as he couldn't quite believe it. He didn't think he had
ever dreamed this vividly before, and even now he remembered every detail.
It seemed wrong to call it a dream really, when it was so much like a memory.
James didn't want to go back to sleep, he was terrified to even extinguish the light, and so he
started to dress.
He could've called Gibson, but contrarily James also didn't want to see anyone, unmoored
and shaky as he felt.
Well, almost.
He wondered if Francis was awake.
On his way out, his foot bumped into something. It was the Complete Works of Shakespeare,
he had been reading in before falling asleep.
James tugged the book under his arm and went to the Great Cabin. It was empty, and James
could hear Francis's light snoring from behind his door.
He felt a tad disappointed, though also relieved that Francis was at least able to catch a little
sleep.
With nothing better to do, James lit another lamp, sat down and began to read.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
James lost track of time. He wasn't really reading, and he wasn't sleeping. The nightmare kept
playing before his eyes, the entire creeping horror of it.
He didn't understand himself. Of course, he recognized the symptoms of scurvy, and every
sailor he knew was at least vaguely afraid of it...
But this, this was as if it had actually happened to him, and he was remembering.
The fugue state he was in didn't lift, and so he went up on deck. It was a clear night, and the
stars were out.
Such beauty had always struck James as strange in the biting cold. The Arctic could be very
beautiful indeed, but it was a harsh kind. Deadly, even.
He thought back to his talk with Francis. He would speak to Sir John, try and persuade him to
change course.

James already felt deeply uncomfortable about it. He had made it his mission to please Sir
John, to make him like him, and this seemed directly opposed to that.
But of course, a little discomfort was nothing if it was a matter of their survival.
He wondered if his nightmare had been a subconscious response to Francis's words, proof
how they had shaken him.
Still, there was something about Francis that didn't add up, something that unsettled James.
And so, he was glad to row back to Erebus the next morning, if only to feel the slightest bit of
normalcy again.
He was to take breakfast with Sir John. For a reason he didn't quite understand, James didn't

In his fear, he had wanted nothing but to see him, though in general he didn't comprehend his
complicated emotions for Francis at any given time.
Dundy was waiting for him on deck, along with many others of the crew who were glad to

"And, has Captain Crozier driven you mad yet?", Le Vesconte asked.

Harry Goodsir, with whom James had always gotten along, was also part of the crowd, and

"Have got some new scetches to show me?", James asked.
"In a manner of speaking.", the young assistant surgeon answered.
Sir John greeted James one deck lower, shaking his hand vigorously and exclaiming how he'd
missed him.
"Likewise, sir."
"Let's eat. Everyone back to their duties!", Sir John ordered.
Lieutenants Hodgson and Gore, as well as Dundy, joined them for breakfast. James was still

That was one of the questions James had feared the most, but he was prepared for it.
"Francis believes that the slow course in our best interests. It will only add a few days to our

A vague answer, yet it was what sounded best and most like Francis was not directly

"That is all well and good, but winter is fast approaching. If we want to be in the Pacific by

James shouldn't have left the question hang in the air like that, but for a moment his words

He looked at the Lieutenants, hoping to find some agreement. Hodgson seemed thoughtful,

"Well, I see, Francis has been hard at work.", he said calmly.

Chapter 7: Francis
Chapter Notes

"How do you know it?"
Francis knew that James wasn't asking about his experience, or what the ice indicated. He
was asking for the truth.
But Francis couldn't give it to him.
They were very close to each other again, and Francis tried his best not to seem affected. The
urge to touch James was nearly overpowering, to feel his warm skin beneath his fingers...
There was also the fact that Sir John hadn't been swayed, and it drove Francis to despair,
which he suspected was behind these strange desires.
He couldn't have failed again! Not when he'd done everything as carefully as he could, had
talked to James with the utmost sincerity when the time had been right, had stopped himself
from confronting Sir John himself once more.
They still had time, he told himself. An entire winter, now, for they would maintain this
course.
"How do you know it?", James said again.
Francis couldn't help himself, he reached out and touched James's cheek. It was mistake,
reminding him of touching James similarly when he lay dying, forcing the poison down his
throat.
James, meanwhile, visibly froze, mouth hanging open.
"Do you trust me?", Francis asked.
The question was sudden, desperate in its urgency.
"How could I?", James said. "I don't- I don't know what's happening to you."
Francis's thumb brushed the other's chin, the line of his jaw.
"I shall have to earn it, then.", Francis breathed.
James swallowed. His usual confidence was nowhere to be found, and he looked rather like a
hare caught in a trap.
Francis knew he should pull his hand back, but he was reluctant to do so.

"Francis...", James began, seemingly unsure how to finish.
Suddenly, Francis felt the rushing in his ears again. He first thought it was his excitement, but
the sensation quickly grew so overpowering that Francis knew it was the pull of the other
time.
"No.", he muttered. "Oh, God, please no."
It was to no avail. James's face before blurred out of focus, and finally darkness descended.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Francis didn't need to open his eyes, for they were already open. Jopson's face was before
him, looking worried.
Francis blinked a few times, then immediately felt for his leg. If it was broken now, that
would be an inconvenience indeed.
It did hurt when he stood on it, a bit like an echo, but it definitely wasn't broken.
Jopson, however, looked much the worse for wear, and seemed only barely be holding
himself upright.
"Who collapsed?", Francis asked. "Aside from me?"
"Harry Peglar, sir.", Jopson said.
Francis nodded, trying to keep his composure. They were dropping like flies, and still had so
far to walk.
And James...
Oh, why did it hurt so much every time?
"Is everything alright, sir?", Jopson asked. "Do you need rest?"
"I'm fine.", Francis replied. "We'll make camp soon, and then-"
There were shouts behind them, men pointing to the sky. Francis followed their fingers, and
yes, there was a white bird flying in the sky.
Francis couldn't believe his eyes. There hadn't been a single living thing in this landscape
except for them and the dead Netsilik family.
Perhaps this bird was a sign of things to come, of game to be had.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
They made camp and split the meat of the bird, woefully little, but perhaps there would be
more soon.

Francis wanted to be alone, but as soon as he was, he felt he couldn't stand it. He was
immediately confronted by his failures, too many to list, and he saw it before him clearly: all
of them dead by the end.
He jumped to his feet, shaking his head. Such thoughts lead nowhere, and there were still
lives to be saved.
There were also the mutineers still out there, and Goodsir. Francis had the sense he hadn't
seen the last of them.
It somehow didn't feel right to spend time alone, mourning the dead, when there were people
still alive. Like Jopson.
Decisively, he took a stool, some water and a cloth and went to his former stewart's tent.
Jopson tried to rise when he came in.
"At ease, Jopson.", Francis said.
"Is there something I can do for you, sir?", Jopson asked, and Francis didn't let show how that
broke his heart a little more.
He set the stool on the ground and said: "Aye. You can lie there, not feeling well, while I try
and cheer you up by telling you the story of how anyone ever let me ride a cow."
The words had the desired effect; Jopson smiled.
"I know that story ends with you head first in a compost heap.", Jopson said, chuckling
weakly.
"Well, would you like to hear it or not?"
Francis took the cloth and dipped it in water, starting to wash Jopson. It really was the least
he could do.
What he wanted was to bring Jopson to safety, to give him food and his home, which was his
task as his Captain. But right now, this would have to do.
He thought of James when he started talking. He would've made this story a veritable drama
with four acts, Francis was sure.
However, Francis would be more than happy if he made Jopson laugh at least once.
Jopson did laugh, though he looked sad by the end of it.
"Thank you, sir.", he whispered.
"It really is the least I could do.", Francis said sincerely. "I will sit with you until you fall
asleep."

Jopson looked lost for words. Francis knew he was afraid, as every single one of them was
afraid.

Jopson soon had him set up in the great cabin again. The ship was groaning against the ice,

Francis knew it was probably true. His withdrawal had been far worse, and Jopson had never

Would Jopson be dead when he returned? It didn't bear thinking about.

"In a manner of speaking."
They were moving forward at Sir John's proposed speed again, and Francis had been too

"Wonderful.", Francis snapped. "You can go tell Commander Fitzjames that this all could've

Starved."
This was the most personal thing Hickey had ever said to him, though it could've been a

Francis hadn't had a wealthy background either, as a solicitor's son, but that was still miles

He'd known what it was like to starve, way before they had ever walked over King William

"Friends who worked at factories?"

"Friends who starved.", Francis clarified.
Hickey blinked. "To be honest, sir, yes I did. It was no fault of their own, they were as
hardworking as any man, it's just that life sometimes deals a difficult hand."

Francis nodded. Of course he would say that, but perhaps he wasn't even lying. Francis

There was food, there was a place to sleep, and the pay was good, even for a mere caulker's

James was late for dinner. This anomaly was enough to make Francis feel terribly nervous

He remembered the words he had almost blurted out in sickbay, and the sentiment behind

Francis felt like he had been punched in the gut. It was true, when he'd signed up a part of

Such words from someone Francis had almost told he loved him went down like bitter

James stood up, throwing his cutlery on the plate.
"I find I don't have an appetite anymore, nor any wish to spend time in your company. Good

"Well, I already know them by heart, and I can't help but think that the endless repitition of
them is not making the men more obedient, but bored of them.", Little said.
Irving considered. "What is your opinion on this, Commander Fitzjames?"
"I can't say, really."
Between Sir John pontificating and a reading of the Ship's Articles, James would choose the
Ship's Articles every time, for the simple reason that that was over more quickly.
Sir John was a gifted speaker, that was true, but James couldn't take much pleasure in his
sermons, for various reasons.
Not that the Ship's Articles were any better in that regard, and James did wonder why Francis
liked so much to have them read.
Otherwise, he didn't seem more strict than the average Captain, and in his personal
interactions with the crew, some of which James had witnessed at this point, he didn't seem to
do things solely by the book, but brought a more human element to his judgement.
James couldn't know if this was a recent development, for not too long ago, James had been
convinced that Francis shut himself off from his duties with a glass of whiskey always in
hand.
"I haven't been on the ship long enough to see how the crew's discipline is affected.", James
explained to Little and Irving. "Say, do any of you know why Francis chose the Ship's
Articles for Sunday service?"
Perhaps James had misjudged Francis. Perhaps he liked to hear "if a man commits sodomy
with a member of the crew or a member of the ship's livestock, that man shall be put to
death" every week, because he thought that was justice.
Irving and Little exchanged a look, fleeting, but James caught it.
Irving cleared his throat. "Captain Crozier knows the value of discipline, and order, and he
wants every man to live by the articles, not just in body, but in spirit as well."
When Irving walked a few steps toward the railing, Lieutenant Little inclined his head
towards James and muttered: "Just between you and me, the reason is convenience, nothing
else. In front of us, the Captain doesn't pretend otherwise, so I thought it would be alright if I
told you."
James nodded, hiding his relief. "That can't sit well with Sir John, though."

Little looked at him with dismay. "Are you going to tell him that?"
"Not at all.", James hurried to assure him.
The last thing he wanted the crew of the Terror to think was that he was Sir John's spy, and
really, James was living proof that Sir John didn't need to know everything.
James eyed Little and wondered if he too had had the privilege of hearing the "pet poodle"
comment, if he maybe even was Dundy's mysterious source.
However, James was very certain at this point that Hodgson was the one who informed Le
Vesconte, Little being far too loyal and Irving being too stuck-up. As for the rest of the crew,
James hoped that Francis had enough of a handle on himself not to make such comments in
their presence.
James thought that Dundy and Hodgson must get along - they all knew each other from the
Cornwallis but only vaguely in James's case, though he had still championed Hodgson's
appointment to this expedition.
He was there to greet Sir John when he arrived with a good portion of the rest of Erebus's
crew, apparently everyone who could be spared.
The mood was subdued, with the exception of Neptune, who was excited about all the new
strangers on his ship. When Bridgens hugged Harry Peglar in greeting, Neptune jumped up
the steward's leg and nearly caused him to lose his footing.
"That means he likes you.", James told Bridgens.
"Neptune remembers you because you kept sneaking him bits of food under the table last
year at Beechey.", Peglar said with a laugh.
"Well, he is such a good boy, aren't you?", Bridgens replied, scratching Neptune behind the
ears.
James smiled and turned away to give Bridgens and Peglar some semblance of privacy in
their reunion.
As it was, Sir John was demanding his presence at his side.
"I will give Divine Service on Terror today.", he said. "Do you think Francis can make it on
deck?"
"You'll have to ask him that."
"James!", Dundy called. "How I missed your ugly mug on Erebus!"
James grinned and pulled his friend into a hug. Ever since James had earned the epithet
"handsomest man in the royal navy", Le Vesconte liked to tease him this way.
It made James feel maudlin, now, thinking as he did about the hard winter ahead.

"Let's proceed to the Great Cabin.", Sir John said.
Francis was sitting in his usual place, his leg propped up, and bent over a map. He looked up
when they all entered, Sir John, James, Mr. Blanky, Dr. Stanley, Dr. McDonald and the
Lieutenants Gore, Le Vesconte, Hodgson, Irving and Little.
It was cramped, and indeed James was glad Mr. Reid had stayed behind to oversee the
preparations on Erebus.
Sir John sat down next to Francis and beckoned James to sit next to him, but it turned out that
Sir John had left too much space between himself and Francis and so James ended up
between them.
A supremely awkward position James couldn't help but see as a symbol of his discomfort.
Francis acknowledged him with a nod, then consulted the map again.
After some shuffling around everyone was quiet and looking to Sir John.
"Gentlemen, I won't mince words. We have a hard winter ahead. We have fixed our position
as carefully as possible, for we expect to move with the pack. That needn't be a bad thing, as
Mr. Blanky can attest."
"Aye.", said Mr. Blanky. "When I was serving on the whaler Pluribus, we got stuck into
Baffin Bay. With the pack ice, we drifted seven hundred miles south until we reached the ice
line and could sail to safety."
"But this is the absolute best case scenario.", Francis, ever dutiful, put in.
"Aye.", Mr. Blanky said again. "I don't know this ice, sir. This isn't like the Lancaster Sound,
which I know like the back of my hand, and pardon me for saying, the composition of this ice
worries me."
"How so?", Sir John asked.
"Pack ice is always tricky. And our position, with Arctic Canada to the south, King William
Land to the southwest, and Boothia peninsula to the northeast, may prove... problematic in
the future, when it comes to the ice flow. I have a feeling we're in for trouble."
Lieutenant Gore cleared his throat. "With all due respect for your feeling, Mr. Blanky, you
yourself say that you don't know this ice. It could very well be that we're out by next summer,
the passage that much closer."
"Very true.", Sir John said. "But even if Mr. Blanky is right, there is hardly much that we can
do about it now. What I want to discuss are our plans for readying for winter."
In the following discussion, James didn't contribute much, though he had already been part of
similar meetings at Beechey.

As it happened, he had talked a great deal in those, and only later realised that he had
sprouted complete nonsense that likely had only been indulged and then quietly discarded
because of his high position.
Francis had watched him with annoyed bemusement, he was sure.
"James, I want you to continue to stay on Terror and help where you can. After all, Erebus is
only a short walk away now.", Sir John said toward the end. "Lieutenant Hodgson, I give you
the choice of returning to Terror, if you like."
"Thank you, sir.", Hodgson said.
"There is another matter.", Dr. Stanley put in.
"What is it?"
"My assistant surgeon, Mr. Goodsir, has raised some concerns over our canned provisions.",
Stanley said. "Somehow, he has gotten the idea that they are...
tainted. Poisonous, even."
"Hm. And there is merit to this theory?", Sir John asked.
"I can't say.", Stanley replied. "Mr. Goodsir is convinced of it, but I have my reservations. He
has some curious notions that aren't at all English, in my opinion, and seems overly excitable
on the whole."
James was saddened that Stephen and Goodsir didn't get along, though not surprised. Goodsir
lacked the traditional values Dr. Stanley lived by.
James didn't know what his own relationship with him would be, had Dr. Stanley not saved
his life at Zhenjiang.
"Perhaps Mr. Goodsir should consult with Dr. McDonald on this, as he seems to be the expert
on tinned provisions.", James suggested.
Dr. McDonald nodded. James would like to pick his brain about what was wrong with
Francis, but that wasn't possible, of course.
After he had fainted a few days ago, James had entertained the notion that perhaps Francis
was being so nice to him because he was dying of some mysterious illness, yet surely Dr.
McDonald would be more alarmed if that were true.
"That's an excellent idea.", Sir John said. "Even if it's nothing, anything about our provisions
is worth investigating, of course."
Something about all this made James pause, but he couldn't rightly figure out what.
He turned his head to look at Francis, but Francis was staring at the map again. James
remembered Goodsir's cryptic remarks to him on Erebus, though he had thought they
pertained to the nebulous medical issue Francis had.

James hoped that Francis had at least told Dr. McDonald what was going on during his
examination.
It was only during Sir John's Divine Service that James remembered what Francis had said to
him during that fateful dinner days ago.
Francis was wrapped in his slops, sitting on a chair with his leg propped up next to Sir John,
a glare fixed on his face.
Sir John's words were ringing over everyone's head as they stood crowded together on
Terror's deck, fidgeting to keep warm.
For this sermon, Sir John had chosen the story of Job, a particular favorite of his as James
knew from their shared Bible readings.
Part of James thought that it really was convenient to chose a story that had as a moral that no
matter what you did, God's mercy and grace was a absolute.
But if it invigorated the men, he was not going to complain.
"And Job said: the Lord has given, and the Lord has taken away, blessed be the name of the
Lord..."
James looked at their faces, by chance spotting Goodsir next to the stone-faced Dr. Stanley.
What if this business with the tins had to do with Francis as well?
James let his gaze drift to the man in question, who was doubtlessly freezing, and also paying
as much attention to Sir John's words as James was.
"And if thaw doesn't come then? If we're stuck in the ice indefinitely, our resources
dwindling, the resources we do have spoiled, and all of us getting more ill and less sane each
month, what then?"
The resources we do have spoiled.
Was that just a conincedence? Or had Francis noticed something wrong with the tins, and
then, for whatever reason, outsourced the problem to Goodsir? Or, more likely, had Goodsir
simply shared his worries with Francis? But why would he do that?
James again had the uncomfortable feeling that something was going on that he didn't
understand, and it wasn't just an intriguing mystery he could solve for fun, but a deeply
serious issue that threatened the very existence of this expedition.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
James didn't get a chance to speak to Goodsir before Sir John's party left for Erebus again,
there was just too much to do, but he reasoned they were now just a short walk apart.

He went to Hodgson's cabin and spotted The Complete Works of Shakespeare on his table.
Maybe it was a sign that he should enact his previous plan.
Determined to do so, he went to dinner with Francis.
"So you found the book you wanted.", Francis remarked when James set the volume on the
table and sat down.
James nodded. "I thought we could read it together.", he said casually.
"Read Shakespeare? Why?"
"For fun, Francis. I know this is a foreign concept for you, but you might try to enjoy
yourself."
Francis considered. "As long as you don't expect me to act."
"I'm sure you'll get into it.", James said with a smile. "What did you think of today's
sermon?"
"Do you want an honest answer?"
James had only asked for the honest answer. He wanted to know how Francis regarded Sir
John now. Sir John, who hadn't once admitted that he had been wrong, who acted as if it was
the fate of God that they were stuck now, rather than his own poor decision making.
"Of course.", James said.
Francis sighed. "I know the story of Job is particular favorite of his, and I suppose it is rather
telling of his character. And perhaps... it shows his flaws rather aptly as well.", he said
carefully.
James took a bite of salted meat and chewed. "How so?"
"Sir John views himself as Job. He lives a blameless, devout life, and he believes that any
hardship that befalls him is just God testing him, and in the end he will triumph for keeping
his faith in the Lord."
"And you believe this sort of view is dangerous and short-sighted, bordering on hubris.",
James said. At Francis's surprised expression, he added: "I do pay attention to what you say
to me, even when I don't agree."
Francis gave him a brief smile. "It's not just bordering on hubris, I think. It is hubris, plain
and simple. The Arctic doesn't care if you're devoted to God, and it doesn't listen to your
prayers as you freeze or starve. Mistakes aren't proof of our faith, they might kill us all
instead."
James had to say that he agreed much more with that line of thought than Sir John's, but he
was also ashamed of having followed Sir John so loyally despite this in the past.

Not just followed, he thought. Ingratiated, flattered, sucked up...
"What would you have given the sermon on?", James asked. "And don't say the Ship's
Articles."
"What have you against the Ship's Articles?", Francis echoed Irving.
"Nothing. I just want to know what you would give a sermon on, I suppose. The Ship's
Articles don't count, because you just read them as they are."
"That's exactly why they are the best subject.", Francis maintained. "They are powerful
enough to stand on their own."
"Are you afraid of public speaking? Or simply lazy?", James teased. He couldn't help
himself.
"What are you hoping to accomplish with these asinine questions, Fitzjames?"
Francis sounded amused despite himself.
James pretended ignorance. "Why, to get to know you better, like we agreed. What else
would I want?"
Francis eyed him up and down. James felt a hot shiver down his spine.
"What else indeed..."
James cleared his throat and looked at his food, trying his very best not to remember the
dream.
"You know what?", Francis began. "I'll tell you what I would give a sermon on, if you tell me
what you think of Sir John. Honestly."

Chapter 9: Francis
Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

"You know what? I'll tell you what I would give a sermon on, if you tell me what you think of
Sir John. Honestly."
Francis supposed that was inane enough a question. What he really wanted to ask James was
more along the lines of: Would you be interested in helping me remove Sir John from
command at all costs?
The truth was, since they were stuck in the ice, Francis had no idea what to do next. That is,
he knew what had to happen, but how to get there was a complete mystery to him.
There was part of him that still didn't want to contemplate the reality of what he had to do.
Maybe, if he thought about James's death again, and that of the others, Jopson's ravaged face,
maybe then he would get himself together.
But today, he had needed to keep a straight facade, without melancholic despair. It wasn't all
bad: Yes, they were stuck, but James was talking to him again.
He hadn't made a move to speak to James before, because he didn't want to smother him with
his worries. It all had to be handed delicately, so James stayed sympathetic to his cause.
Also, Francis was a little stumped on how to handle all the personal tension between them, he
freely admitted to himself, if no one else.
After he had first met Sophia, he had been feeling much the same way. It was her who had
guided him through their conversations Francis otherwise would have had no idea how to
continue. When he was alone, he found himself going endlessly over what he'd said, berating
himself for not being wittier, cleverer, more agreeable.
With James, he had similar thoughts, but they were overshadowed by his potent fear of the
horrible future awaiting them.
James eyed him carefully. "You're not trying to get me to talk ill of Sir John, are you?"
"I simply asked for your honest opinion.", Francis said. "I won't betray your confidence, if
that's what you're worried about."
"Somehow, I'm not.", James replied thoughtfully. "But as I said, I don't know if I- if I can
trust you. I wish I could, but..."
Francis wondered when during their tumultuous relationship he had earned James's trust. It
must've happened, after all, James had trusted him with the secret of his past. He had trusted
Francis to end his life.

Oh, how that thought hurt, like a splinter in his heart.
"It's just a question, James. I'm not asking you to leap into the ocean blindfolded.", Francis
said. "Or to help me kill a man."
James gave a nervous laugh. "I should hope not. But you're my superior officer. And he is
too. It's not just a question, it's a test. And I'm not sure I want to take it."
Francis hadn't considered that element, just as he hadn't considered James and himself as
anything else than equals for the longest time. Of course, James had been his Second even in
the other time, but the necessities of survival, the direness of their situation, had soon
eradicated all differences of rank between them.
"I don't mean to put you on the spot. I just wish to know what you think, because surely you
have seen that we might need to convince Sir John of certain... facts together, and I would
know your mind about him."
James nodded slowly. "Alright. Sir John. I greatly admire him, of course. What he has
achieved in the Arctic alone is monumental. Moreover, he is a good man. There was never
any malice in our interactions."
"But?"
James fiddled with his fork and cleared his throat. "Why would there be a 'but'?"
"Forgive me, but your words indicate there is."
James stared at him, his eyes wide. Complete silence engulfed them, the ice was temperate
today.
"He cares about appearances.", James whispered at last. "More about them than the truth.
And he doesn't know, doesn't care to know, what might upset his worldview."
James sighed as if he had just performed a great labor, then smiled.
"There. Is your curiosity satisfied, Captain Crozier?"
"Do you care about appearances?", Francis asked, trying to make sense of the significance
behind James's words.
James shook his head. "You owe me an answer first. So tell me. What would your sermon be
on?"
On the whole, Francis had always thought of Sunday Service as an onerous duty, and he
supposed the whole ship knew it. But talking to James now, Francis wondered if he might be
missing an opportunity.
He remembered Hickey's mutiny very well, and aside from keeping an eye on Hickey, he
might do other things to prevent it from ever happening.

One of those would be to be a better leader to his men in the first place, to inspire their
loyalty and bind them to him through showing that he cared.
He had shut himself off to drink for far too long, and Sunday Service might be the key to
winning at least the trust of his crew; and since the mutineers, to his shame, were mostly
made up of Terror's men, it could prove invaluable.
He doubted he would reach Hickey with this (with what in God's name one could reach
Hickey he was still not clear on), but maybe some of the others.
"You know what?", he said to James. "I'm going to give you my answer, in the form of my
sermon next Sunday. We're done with the Ship's Articles for now."
James looked surprised, and he smirked. "Admit it: you have no idea on what to hold the
sermon on."
Francis raised an admonishing finger. "Yet.", he maintained.
They finished their meal in companionable silence, though it quickly made Francis overthink
things again.
Had he pushed too far, asking James his opinion on Sir John? But surely he needed to start
somewhere, in case he was going to ask him much worse later on.
No, I must deal with Sir John on my own., Francis thought. I can't drag James into this. If it
can be helped.
He still had the vague hope that the poisoned cans might sway Sir John, and Goodsir seemed
to be close to results, thank God.
After they were done eating and Jopson had cleared the plates away, James yawned.
"Are you for bed?", Francis asked.
"Oh, don't think you can get out of reading Shakespeare with me like this!", James said,
rubbing his hands together.
"Must we?"
"We must.", James stated resolutely.
The truth was, Francis was actually looking forward to this, and his resistance was more for
show.
It drove him up the walls, keeping his leg still, and the last days without James's company
had been absolutely dreadful. Jopson had offered to read to him, but Francis wanted to give
his stewart at least semblance of time ot himself between helping him with dressing, using
the chamber pot, and bringing him things.

He had conferred with Edward, but they had never been two for inane chatter to pass the time
and mostly stuck to ship's business.
Of course, there was Thomas, yet he had been busy with the ice situation.
Also right now, everyone was busy with the ice situation, and Francis hated that he couldn't
help. He certainly wouldn't have suggested something like reading Shakespeare to James,
who he didn't want to cheat out of much needed rest.
When he said so now, James made a dismissive gesture. "I'm not too fond of sleep these
days."
"Why that?"
"Nightmares.", James said with a shrug.
Francis felt a pang of sympathy. "I know what that feels like."
James gazed at him strangely. "Really? What do you dream about? If you don't mind me
asking."
Francis was caught by the haunted look in James's eyes, the flush to his cheeks. There
seemed to be a non-verbal conversation going on that Francis couldn't decipher, and before
he knew it, he was turning red as well.
Too late he realised that James might interpret that as his dreams being somehow illicit and
improper.
As it was, he didn't really want to tell James about his dreams, dreams that weren't dreams at
all; all of them starving, dying, being torn apart by the creature, themselves and the cold.
Their endless march into nothing and James, James seizing to breathe under his fingers.
Francis cleared his throat. "Weren't we going to read Shakespeare?"
"Of course, of course.", James said, pulling the book close from the edge of the table like a
life line.
He was sitting across from Francis, at a polite distance, but now he stood up and approached.
"I thought we could each read a part.", he said. "And since I don't believe you have a comedic
temperament, I chose a tragedy. Not too tragic though, I don't want to sink your spirits
further."
"Which play is it?", Francis asked.
"Julius Caesar.", James announced. "Do you know it?"
"I know of it.", Francis said.

His education had been substantial enough, though Francis knew it was nothing to brag
about. He remembered reading some of Shakespeare's plays and finding them tedious, mostly
because they didn't seem to come to life under the eyes of his strict teachers.
Julius Caesar though hadn't been one of them.
"It's about Caesar's assassination, isn't it?", Francis asked.
He remembered dimly that James Ross had once seen a production and told him about it.
"Exactly.", James said. "I actually performed in it, on the St Vincent.", he added proudly.
He looked ready to give another performance right now, standing there in the low light.
Francis recalled his friend's rendition of the plot, and frowned. "Is that the right play for that
sort of environment? As I remember, Caesar's murder isn't necessarily condemned by the
play."
James nodded. "It's a bold choice, to be sure. Though you could say that the murderers are
justly punished by the end of the play. As it was, our Captain, implicitly trusted his first
Lieutenant, who played Brutus. And Cassius had to make sure he was as evil as possible."
"And Cassius is...?"
"Brutus's friend, who convinces him to murder Caesar. You'll see.", James said. "Let's get
started!"
Curious, Francis inquired: "Who did you play? Caesar?"
James gave a fetching little laugh. "No one quite so important, I'm afraid. Remember, I was
only a midshipman."
"Who then?", Francis asked, genuinely interested.
James cleared his throat again. "Calpurnia, Caesar's wife."
"Ah.", Francis said, suddenly picturing James in a dress and finding the idea powerfully
attractive, so he quickly surpressed it. "And she is...?"
"Mostly worried for Caesar. She tells him not to go to the Senate on the Ides- the day he is
killed, that is." James grinned. "I got to fall to my knees before the second Lieutenant, who
played Caesar, and beg him not to go."
"That must've been quite the fetching sight.", Francis said, aiming for mocking, but he
sounded a bit too breathless for that.
James's grin deepened. "Perhaps I'll do it again if we get to that point in the text."
Francis felt his throat dry, a part of him warning that this was dangerous territory. The nature
of his regard for James was already confusing enough, what he didn't need was James on his

knees before him!
"Let's see about that.", Francis said, willing himself be calm.
What happened next was that James seated himself directly beside him so they could both
look into the book, and Francis tried not to feel flustered by his proximity.
He remembered Sophia in Van Diemen's Land, always seating herself a little too close next to
him and near driving him mad with it.
Oh yes, he was comparing James and Sophia again, but he could hardly stop himself at this
point.
Meanwhile, James seemed to be in a great mood, and once he had found Julius Caesar in the
assortment of plays, told him to read a certain Marullus.
"It's just the first scene.", James murmured, almost whispering into Francis's ear. "You'll get
used to it."
When he retreated, James's hair brushed Francis's neck, and Francis shivered. He had to force
himself to focus on the play as James started to read.
"Hence! Home you idle creatures, get you home? Is this a holiday? What, know you not,
being mechanical you ought not walk upon a laboring day without the sign of your
profession? Speak, what trade art thou?"
James affected a voice Francis suspected he would use to write up some poor crewman for
disobedience, but before Francis got used to it, James read the next character in a completely
different tone.
"Why, sir, a carpenter."
There was a pause. Only when James looked at him questioningly did Francis realise that he
was supposed to read.
Francis cleared his throat and started: "Where is thy leather apron, and thy rule? What dost
thou with thy best apparel on? You, sir, what trade are you?"
In yet another different voice, James answered: "Truly, sir, in respect of a fine workman I am
but, as you would say, a cobbler."
James had told Francis that he wasn't supposed to act, yet it felt very strange to just read the
lines while James was putting on such a performance.
The anger with which Francis read his next sentences was more due to this than him
genuinely representing his character, who also happened to be angry.
They went back and forth for a bit, until Marullus went into a speech about why Caesar
shouldn't be celebrated, and Francis at this point was practically spitting his words.

Realising, this he stopped, and James looked up from the page at him.
"You're doing marvelously!", James exclaimed. "Go on!"
Francis was just about to tell James where he could stuff his stupid bard, when he saw the
unadulterated joy shining in his eyes. Well, if it would make James happy... And Francis did
enjoy his proximity, even flustered as it made him feel...
"... The lifelong day, with patient expectation, to see great Pompey pass the streets of
Rome...", Francis continued, haltingly at first, but after a moment, he found himself warming
to the words and pressed on with more ease, putting all his anger into the speech.
There was something liberating about it, that was of no doubt.
When they were done with the scene, James grinned at him.
"That wasn't so bad now, was it?", he said.
"It's tolerable, I suppose.", Francis replied stiffly.
James eyed him, considering. "You've never acted before, haven't you?"
"Not in that way, no."
"How do you mean?"
Francis decidedly did not want to talk about his melancholic tendencies with James
Fitzjames. Well, he didn't want to talk about them with anyone, really.
But something about their companionship, sitting so close together, did invite those sort of
confessions.
"I feel like I'm acting, I suppose, every time I go to a dinner of the Admiralty, or any sort of
social function.", Francis said. "It's why I detest such things."
"You like being yourself, then?"
"I don't know how to be anyone else. I don't want to be anyone else. But I imagine it's
different for you."
"Why?", James asked.
Oh, right. James had told Francis about the circumstances of his birth, his need to put on an
act, in the other time. Francis cursed inwardly. He could hardly tell James that he knew, now.
"Because you like to act!", Francis said quickly. "And got a talent for it too, clearly."
James looked relieved for the briefest second, before he covered it up with a smile.
"There are many different kinds of acting, I should say. Acting for the stage, Francis, is not
the same as acting in front of the Admiralty. I think you've got a talent for the former too, and

a taste for it."
Francis gave a gentle scoff. "Now, now, let's not go so far as that. I consent to reading more
Julius Caesar with you, for the moment. That is all."
James's smile deepened, became more genuine. There were sitting so close that James
could've rested his head on Francis's shoulder; as it was, the brush of James's arm against his

"Then let's continue!", James said. "The next scene is with the main characters, hm..." He

"The role of the villain.", Francis said, sceptical. "Of course you would say that."
"You know, there is a question whether Cassius actually is a villain. So it appears to me, at
least."
"Because he has honorable motives?"
"And because he loves Brutus.", James explained, eyes glowing. "Of course, if you put on
this sort of play for the crew of a ship, there can't be any question whether Cassius is evil.
Our third Lieutenant, he made a great show of it. I think the ship's boys were afraid of him
for weeks. But when I read the play on my own..." He trailed off, thoughtful.
"Hm." Francis considered James. "Then I will read Cassius. But I do wonder what your
Captain was thinking, putting on that play in the first place."
