Another one he couldn't save.
At least Hodgson was alive, not dead as they'd believed.
He gave Edward his orders, certain he would see him again, Edward would not be content to
leave him with the mutineers, but still it kind of felt like a final goodbye.
And perhaps it was, what was happening was ample proof that everything was going wrong.
"We will live.", Edward repeated, and Francis tried to see it; tried to believe it.
~~~~~~~~~~
They beat him and bound his hands, though Francis could hardly feel it. He was worried
about dropping into the other time now, thinking they might kill him if he couldn't walk.
As they walked, Francis tried to remember the way they were going, which was no easy task
in this landscape.
They arrived at Hickey's camp, and Francis saw them, the mutineers, or at least those who
had, for whatever reason, gone with Hickey; Diggle and Pilkington and Tozer- he saw neither
Gibson nor Goodsir anywhere, and was worried for the latter.
Finally, there was Mr. Hickey himself, who was standing with his back to him.
Oh, Francis did wonder.
If he'd had Hickey killed in the other time line, would they be here now?
He could find a way to kill Hickey without much trouble, as his Captain. As it was, ever
since his mutiny, Hickey had been a subject of much gossip back in his camp, and Francis
had heard more than one damning rumor about him.

He could hang Hickey for sodomy, even if he was too careful, Francis could manufacture
proof.
It was a great hypocrisy to even think it, Francis was aware, but these were desperate times.
Still, he felt less certain about this than the need to kill Sir John, ironically.
Their overall situation wasn't Hickey's fault, and it stood to reason that if Francis executed
him, there would just be another one of his kind.
There always was.
And it might damage his rapport with the men even more if he were to execute Hickey for
behavior that Francis would have at best had someone lashed for before.
Once he had been released of the irons, he walked over to Hickey.
Hickey seemed to know him without looking at him. "Do you know what day it is, Mr.
Crozier?", he asked. "What day of the week, I mean."
"No.", Francis said, puzzled to where this was going.
"It's a Wednesday." Hickey paused. "You and I once shared a drink on a Wednesday. Do you
remember that day?"
"I do. You had a dog turd in your hand."
It was meant to sting, but all it did was remind Francis himself of Neptune, whom Hickey
had butchered.
"The toast was 'Ourselves'. That was fitting then. And so it is again today."
Francis looked and saw Goodsir in the middle distance. Still alive, thank God. Francis
thought of the assistant surgeon in the other timeline, how relieved and impressed he'd been
that Goodsir had investigated the tins right away.
"You misunderstand the toast, Mr. Hickey. It was meant as a joke. Not a very clever one."
Hickey looked at him with that damned smile of his, then turned away.
"Mr. Des Voeux. Have Goodsir tend to Mr. Crozier's injuries. And make sure he is not
harmed again."
Francis looked at Hickey walking away, and suddenly had to think of James's gait. He was
puzzled for the barest second, then he saw that Hickey was wearing James's boots, the J.F.
clearly visible on the leather.
Francis felt impotent rage rise in him, rage so blinding that he almost stumbled forward and
threw himself at Hickey, not even wanting to kill, but wanting to hurt; hurt worse than the
pain James had felt when he died, when he-

Francis made a step towards Hickey, and only then realised that the rushing in his ears wasn't
just his wrath.
He just had time to feel Des Voeux grabbing his shoulder before blackness descended.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Francis woke in sickbay once more, but this time no one was with him, just a lone illuminator
glowed on the table. It was good, because Francis realised that tears were streaming down his
cheeks.
Francis felt powerless to stop them, and he cried quietly for a few minutes, until he heard the
door opening.
He wiped his eyes to see Goodsir approaching.
"You're awake, Captain.", he exclaimed. "Let me go get-"
"No.", Francis said. "Please, give me a moment..."
Goodsir's eyes widened even further. "Of course, sir. Is there anything I can do to help?"
"You already did your best, Harry.", Francis mumbled, the first name slipping from his lips
before he could stop it.
"I've tried, sir.", Goodsir agreed. "I do believe you're right, that we have to turn back. Others
think it too, I'm sure of it."
Francis wondered again at the idea of a mutiny. Could he pull it off? But that would be
infinitely more complicated, not to mention that Sir John would never just peacefully resign
command to him, even if the majority of both ships was on his side.
And any return would see him hanged, which might have been a acceptable sacrifice, would
not everyone who had followed him suffer the same death.
Where James's loyalties would fall he didn't want to imagine.
"Maybe we might sway Sir John yet.", Francis said to Goodsir.
Goodsir nodded. "Of that I am sure. If can only convince Dr. Stanley of the direness of our
situation, I'm sure much will be won."
Well, if the other reality had proven anything, it was that Stephen Stanley didn't have the
spirit to handle the truth regarding the tins, and Francis was just relieved that here he had
chosen denial instead of setting everyone on fire.
"Captain?", Goodsir asked.
"Yes?"

"Would you tell me how you knew? About the tins, I mean?"
Francis looked at him, knowing he owed him a debt. Would Goodsir believe him? Perhaps.
The assistant surgeon certainly had the most open mind Francis had ever encountered.
He opened his mouth, but before he could say anything, James burst into the room.
"I heard your voice, Francis, but I didn't dare hope you would be back with us...", James
exclaimed, rushing to his side.
To his mortification, Francis felt tears burn in his eyes again. He turned his head away from
James, lest he see them.
"Francis-"
"What's this?"
Jesus buggering Christ, Dr. McDonald and Sir John were the next ones to enter the room, and
Francis could barely keep himself together!
Francis felt James's hand on his neck and stifled a sob.
"Please...", he whispered. "Please leave..."
It was Dr. McDonald who saved Francis from further embarrassment, sending everyone out,
including Sir John and James.
Then he pulled up a chair and sat down at the table, grabbing Francis's hand. "It will pass.",
he murmured in soothing tones. "It will pass, Frank."
It did pass, slowly. Dr McDonald held his hand through it, offering comforting words and his
handkerchief once the worst was over.
"Alexander, I'm so sorry-"
"Don't apologise.", Dr. McDonald said. "I believe you've experienced an epileptic fit, and this
state of fearful confusion is quite normal for the aftermath."
Francis nodded weakly. "Thank you."
"It's nothing. Though I am greatly worried about you."
Francis tried to think, and also stop himself from insisting he was fine. That wouldn't be
received well, he had the inkling.
"Do you believe... this illness impacts my ability to act as Captain of this ship?", Francis
asked, hoping he wouldn't have to deal with such a thing as well.
"Not as of yet, no. You are of sound mind. Though it is probably best for morale if you're not
seen in your state after a seizure.", Dr. McDonald replied. "What gives me hope is that the

seizures don't seem to be close together, but several days apart."
Francis wondered if he should at least attempt to tell Dr. McDonald the truth, but then he
would probably not declare him fit to captain his ship anymore, he was sure.
Goodsir might believe him, maybe Thomas, but even though he was more open minded than
Stanley, Alexander primarily believed in what he could see.
He wouldn't take Francis's word for it.
"Can I let the others in or do you still need a moment?", Dr. McDonald asked. "I could barely
get Commander Fitzjames out of here. You must've become fast friends during the last days."
Francis swallowed down the lump in his throat at that.
"We did.", was all he said. "And yes, you may let them in."
James wasn't the only one waiting to see him; of course, Sir John was still there, and also
Neptune had scratched at the door at times.
The ship's dog had taken up a habit to keep Francis company in the great cabin and on the
floor to his berth, and was now eager to make sure that his master was alright.
James rushed almost as eagerly to his side again, but he visibly stopped himself from taking
Francis's hand when his gaze fell on Sir John.
"I'm glad to see you sitting up, Francis.", Sir John said. "I don't like to see you running
yourself ragged for care for your ship."
"I'm not-"
"You are, I can see it. And James told me this has happened before. Why no one saw fit to
inform me sooner is a great mystery to me."
Both Francis and Sir John looked at James with reproach, and James said: "I'm sorry.", to no
one in particular.
"This will pass.", Francis assured Sir John. "I'm sure of it."
"What do you say, doctor?"
"He will need to be extremely careful not to take another fall. Thankfully, his leg will keep
him mostly out of harm's way for now. But epilepsy is nothing to joke about."
"Of course not.", Sir John said. "James, I want you to take extremely good care of Francis in
my absence. Keep him safe."
James flushed a little. "Yes, sir."

Sir John smiled and patted Francis on the shoulder. "Cheer up, old fellow. It's only Caesar's
illness!"
"I beg your pardon?", Francis asked, startled.
"Caesar's illness. He famously suffered from epilepsy as well.", Sir John said.
Francis remembered Cassius saying that Caesar had the falling sickness in Shakespeare,
come to think of it.
Sir John didn't want to discuss the tins, believing the subject too strenuous for Francis right
now.
"We have all winter to disagree about it.", he said resolutely. "Now you must rest."
Francis didn't want to rest. He didn't want to think, though he knew he had to.
At his insistence, the crutches were brought and he limped back to his berth himself, Jopson
and James to the side of him, and before and behind him when the gangway was too narrow.
Neptune zapped ahead, the only one happy to be up at this hour of the day.
Once Francis was sitting in his berth, his gaze fell to James, who hovered in the doorway,
uncertain.
"I'm really- really glad you're alright.", he said.
Jopson had told him the same thing before going to bed. Francis had barely stopped himself
from giving him a bone-crushing hug.
It was the transition between the timelines that so affected him.
"I'm glad you're ali- here, too.", Francis said.
"Really? I should think you are cross with me for not supporting you better in the meeting.",
James replied, leaning forward in confidence. "Rest assured, I am on your side, Francis. I do
want to find the passage, but not at the cost of our lives. I just think we need to consider
carefully how to change Sir John's mind."
"Oh, James.", Francis muttered, almost crying again.
That had been the capacity in James that Francis had only noticed far too late, his ability for
self-reflection without vanity. James may be flamboyant, boisterous, and even vain in other
ways, but never in this.
It was something Francis couldn't say he did as well himself. Especially on the drink, he
knew he could be as stubborn and obstinate as Sir John if he really put his mind to it.
James took his hand at last, watching him be overcome. Hopefully, he would make Francis
supposed "seizure" responsible for his mood.

"Yes, we will change his mind. Together.", James said with a reassuring smile.
Francis nodded, giving James's fingers a firm press. He didn't just want to hold James's hand,
he thought. He wanted to touch him all over, his warm skin, proof of being alive. He wanted
to press his lips to his chest, over his heart, he wanted"Is there anything else you need?", James asked, echoing Jopson from moments before,
though his tone was much more... familiar.
Francis imagined asking James to stay, to get into bed with him.
He imagined James agreeing, smiling that smile of his and pulling him close.
But no. Disregarding the fact that James probably wouldn't agree, Francis couldn't trust
himself to keep silent about his time switching, couldn't calculate the things he would say to
James with his tongue so loosened.
"Good night, James.", Francis forced out. "What's left of it, at any rate."
James nodded and withdrew his hand. "Good night, Francis."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Francis did fall into a fitful sleep, absolutely exhausted as he was. He dreamed of Hickey
wearing James's boots, and woke almost cursing with rage.
He remembered what he'd thought about executing Hickey, or rather, not executing him.
But right now, Francis wanted Hickey dead more than anything.
Hickey was too perfidious, too evil to ever truly fall in line. He would do it again, the mutiny,
the killing, all of it, and Francis could only stop him by taking his life.
Another life to save all the others... surely that was an acceptable sacrifice?
But deep down, Francis knew that it wasn't that simple.
He wasn't just doing it for the men, this was also him satisfying his personal need for
revenge.
And so what?, he thought angrily. Hickey has me at his mercy in the other time, and I have
him at mine in this; why shouldn't I punish him?
The one who dug up James's corpse and desecrated him, stolen his possessions, not to
mention murdered peopleFrancis knew this kind of anger from his drinking days, but paradoxically, he now yearned
for a glass of whiskey to help him calm down.
He looked at his braced leg and groaned in frustration.

How he hated, hated, hated this!
He rung for Jopson and his stewart appeared promptly.
"Time to dress for the day, sir?"
"First, bring me a bottle of whiskey.", Francis growled. "You hid them, you know where they
are. Get me one."
He glared at Jopson, daring him to disobey.
"Sir, you've told me to hide them for your own good.", Jopson reminded him.
"I don't care. I want a drink, now."
Jopson looked at him with a worried frown. "Sir-"
"Bring it to me at once, before I write you up for disobedience!"
Oh, how Francis already hated himself for this...
Jopson stared at him for a moment longer, before he nodded and went away. Francis closed
his eyes and leant against the wooden wall. He'd thought he was strong enough to bear this,
but he couldn't.
He just couldn't do it anymore.
He heard the sounds of footsteps, a door opening. A voice: "Francis?"
It was James.
"Go away!", Francis called.
More footsteps, then James appeared in the doorway in his nightclothes. His mere presence
was enough for Francis to almost start crying again.
"I said, go away!", Francis yelled, afraid.
"Not until you tell me why you want to start drinking again.", James said.
"I'm going to skin Jopson alive."
"No, you're not.", James said, approaching carefully, as if Francis was a skittish horse.
"You're going to tell me what is going on with you. And then we're going to think of a way to
help you that doesn't involve whiskey."
"Damn you, James, can't you just leave?", Francis hissed.
James shook his head. And then he stepped even closer and put a warm hand on Francis's
knee, which served to make Francis stop short rather effectively.

"Tell me.", James said again, a gentle command.
Francis was powerless to stop his tears of anguish and rage, and he buried his face in his
hands and sobbed.
Next thing he knew, strong arms enveloped him and he was pulled close against James's
chest.
Francis cried even harder, overwhelmed by the other's proximity, by him being alive. He
hugged James back with abandon, thinking of killing and Hickey in James's boots and his
impotent rage, while James murmured comforting words and stroked his hair.
Finally, there were no more tears, but Francis stayed in the embrace because he could listen
to James's heartbeat through his night shirt.
He belatedly realised that James had climbed into his berth, his knees bracketing Francis's
legs, and that they were - for this climate at least- practically half naked.
Still, it was James who drew back after a while to look him in the eyes. "Better?", he
murmured.
Francis cleared his throat, not really knowing what to say.
"I still want a drink.", he muttered.
James's hand that had been in his hair moved down to his cheek. "Talk to me, hm?"
Francis sighed, and James backed away from him while clearing his throat. Francis
immediately missed his nearness.
"I wish I could kill Mr. Hickey."
James's eyebrows shot up. "You... what?"
"You know, I actually could kill him. I will kill him. I just need a reason... He will give me
one, I'm sure of it."
James was silent a moment, then said: "Well, normally the reason to kill someone comes
before the actual urge... Or what did Mr. Hickey do to deserve death?"
"I wish I could tell you.", Francis said grimly.
"You're serious? You actually want to execute a member of your crew for... what? I certainly
don't see what Mr. Hickey could've done, save some minor disobedience..."
"Minor disobedience?", Francis repeated with a scoff. "Oh, you have no idea..."
James looked greatly disconcerted, but Francis knew if he didn't talk about this to someone,
he would seek refuge at the bottom of a glass.

"What did he do to you?", James suddenly asked, his gaze fire. "Did he dare... harm you in
some way?"
"Not just me.", Francis said. "Not just me, which I could bear, but- James..."
"You talk in riddles.", James said gently, putting a hand on Francis's arm again.
"It's not so much what he did.", Francis tried to explain. "But what he will do in the future if I
don't temper him."
James frowned. "Does he possess some kind of damning knowledge about you? Is that why
you give him special attention?"
Francis said nothing. He couldn't tell James the truth, he realised, not even necessarily
because James wouldn't believe him, but because James wasn't born yesterday. He would
come to the same conclusions Francis had, and then he would have to be part of the plot to
kill Sir John.
Goodsir would've maybe not thought of it -and Francis didn't have the time for details with
him anyway- but James definitely.
"You know, it occurs to me that Mr. Hickey seems to be the sort of man who preens under
attention, any attention you give him. Perhaps if you can... rid yourself of your association
with him, much will be won.", James said, bringing Francis back to the present.
"I can't just ignore the problem he represents.", Francis replied. "And it is my right as his
Captain to punish him for his actions."
James considered this. "Even actions he hasn't committed yet? Because forgive me, Francis,
but that sounds an awful lot like tyranny, not leadership."
Francis sighed angrily. "Then perhaps actions he is committing right now will do! I know, for
one, that Mr. Hickey is practicing sodomy on this very ship. That offense is punished by
death, according to the Ship's Articles."
James sucked in a breath. His hand tensed on Francis's arm before it fell away completely.
"I had not thought you such a hypocrite, Francis.", James said quietly.
Fear like ice in Francis's veins. "What's that supposed to mean?"
"You know damn well what I mean, don't pretend!", James hissed, enraged. "What is it that
Hickey did to you? What is it that would drive you to punish him so unjustly, to have him
hang for something you indulged in yourself?"
Francis stared at James, shocked. How could James have found out about his indecent
thoughts towards him? More importantly, how could James know about those awkward
fumblings of his youth that could constitute sodomy to an unkind eye?
"It wouldn't be unjust!", Francis whispered harshly.

He longed to yell, but just like James he didn't think it wise to keep his voice above a
murmur.
"Oh, yes, it would be!", James fired back bitterly. "For that offense, it would be, and you
know it. The sheer hypocrisy of it! Really, Francis, I've never been so disappointed in you,
that you would even consider-"
Francis had arrived at the conclusion that James couldn't have known about him that way, so
he must be thinking something else. But what?
"I'm just doing this to keep order on my ship!"
"That's a lie, and we both know it!", James hissed. "You were the one who seduced Mr.
Hickey -he might be bold but he would never have initiated anything- and now, because of
some trifle of an offense, you want to murder him -and it would be murder, make no mistake"
Seduced him? Francis stopped short.
"James, you don't think that Mr. Hickey and I- engaged in some kind of congress, do you?",
he asked.
James scoffed. "What, you're going to deny it now? After everything you said?"
Oh.
Well, that certainly explained why James was so angry.
"James, I have no idea how you arrived at this conclusion, but I swear to you, never in my
life did I-"
"You have no idea? Really? What about all the private conferences you had with Mr. Hickey
that you refuse to explain? The way you talked about him hurting you? Mr. Hickey grinning
like a cat who got the cream every time he leaves your presence?"
Francis could see how that might be somewhat damning, but still he couldn't contain his
surprise and dismay that James had thought... that of him.
"James, I wanted to see Mr. Hickey because I got intelligence that he might be planning a
mutiny, not because I desired to-" Francis lowered his voice still further "-sodomise him in
any way."
James looked at him, sceptical. "Really?"
"Really. Christ, that would be the worst kind of abuse I could commit as Captain, making
such use of a subordinate who can't say no-"
"Exactly."
"And you think so low of me?", Francis asked, unable to keep the hurt out of his voice.

"Part of me didn't believe it.", James said. "But what the hell was I supposed to think? And
now you want to have him hanged, for God's sake- none of this makes sense, none of it! Why
even bring up sodomy, if he was planning a mutiny? Surely that's the greater offense-"
"I don't have any proof, but please believe me that Hickey is dangerous. He needs to be
stopped."
James chewed the inside of his cheek. "But not at the cost of your integrity. And also, what
do you think it will do to the men if you hang one of them at the beginning of a long winter in

James was right, damn it all to hell. Francis knew he was right.
"I'm sorry, James.", Francis said, reaching for his hand. "For everything, especially the things
I just said. I didn't mean to confuse you, or make you think ill of me. Good Lord, I certainly
don't think sodomy is a hangable offense- I just needed to think of a way to rid us of Mr.
Hickey before he becomes even more dangerous."
James looked greatly relieved, though he didn't return the press of Francis's hand.
"I take you're not going to explain to me how you know that Hickey is going to be dangerous
in the future.", James said dryly.
"I wish I could, but I need to keep this from you."
There was hurt in James's expression, and it made Francis ache to see it.
"I'm sorry too for suspecting you of having an affair with Mr. Hickey.", James murmured.
Had this been a less serious situation, Francis would've laughed at the sheer absurdity of it.
"Let's just not mention it.", he said.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Chapter 13: James
James had never felt so many conflicting emotions at once as during this conversation with
Francis.
Something in him felt like it was breaking when Francis had said that he would hang Hickey
for sodomy, and he was still recovering from it.
He had clung to Francis's apology, his words 'I certainly don't think sodomy is a hangable
offense' with the desperation of someone drowning grabbing the life line.
At the same time, there was definitely something Francis wasn't telling him, something vital
to the wellbeing of this expedition, he was sure.
He doubted that it actually had anything to do with sodomy, that was just smoke and mirrors
that happened to distract him rather effectively, he had to admit.
Maybe Francis was clairvoyant?
James had never believed in such things, thinking himself a child of an enlightened, scientific
age, but all the facts he had gathered up to this juncture certainly seemed to point toward
something beyond the scope of natural science.
Francis just knew things he shouldn't rightly be able to know, from Hickey's sexual
preference to the poisoned tins.
And it would explain much- James certainly would've become a hopeless misanthrope who
sought refuge in drink if he were assaulted with visions of a horrifying future every day.
It even made sense that Francis had chosen to go on this expedition despite him knowing it
would end in disaster - he had been depressed and suicidal, and that was certainly one way to
end one's life...
But somewhere along the way, Francis had become determined to use his abilities to stop the
disaster, and now he was trying to save them all.
Was this sudden onset epilepsy another symptom of that, James wondered.
He had been almost beside himself with worry over Francis when he'd dropped off yet again.
There was always a tiny part of him that believed Francis would never wake up, that he
would stay lost to them.
"It appears I'm Calpurnia yet again.", he murmured.
"Pardon?", Francis asked.
They were still in his cabin, Francis had just said that they shouldn't mention what James had
thought about him and Mr. Hickey.

James was glad for that, he didn't want Francis to closely examine why James had believed
what he did. At the same time, many other men would've been so mortally offended by what
James had accused Francis of that they would've never spoken to James again.
It made treacherous hope flare up in James's heart, and James knew he had to be careful
about that.
Wanting Francis was dangerous, more so than everything he had done with Dundy. He
couldn't know for sure if Francis was inclined towards him, save by making a pass at him,
and that would be foolish indeed.
James had almost forgotten the nail biting uncertainty of knowing if another wanted him, he
had gotten comfortable in the arms of Le Vesconte.
Yet James knew he was already acting reckless. Climbing into Francis's berth and taking him
into his arms was a very clear indicator of that.
He couldn't forget the way Francis had clung to him so desperately, but perhaps he had been
only plagued by his visions.
James wondered if he should just ask Francis if he was clairvoyant, though he sensed there
was a great resistance in Francis to talk about that sort of thing.
"Calpurnia, worrying about Caesar.", James said softly. "Me, worrying about you."
Francis eyed him carefully. James imagined him asking: "Would you like to be my wife,
James?" and a hot shiver went down his spine.
"Well, I certainly don't plan to have myself killed by a bunch of assassins I work with.", was
what Francis really said.
James raised an eyebrow. "Glad to hear it."
They were silent for a moment, and James knew he should probably leave now, but he hadn't
forgotten what brought him here in the first place.
Jopson had been smart, to get him, knowing he himself couldn't disobey Francis. For some
reason, Francis had been able to stop drinking without going into withdrawal- that seemed to
be one of the few things James couldn't explain at all, even with clairvoyance.
It still stood to reason that it should be avoided at all costs that Francis started to drink again.
Not too long ago, James wouldn't have thought himself the right person to help Francis stay
sober, but obviously things had changed.
Meanwhile, around them, the ship was starting to wake up; the usual sounds of footsteps and
voices reached them.
"We should get dressed.", Francis said. "Where is Jopson?"

James looked gravely at Francis. "I will let you call him only if you promise me that you
won't order him to get you whiskey."
"If I do, he's just going to get you again anyway.", Francis grumbled.
"Francis.", James said, putting two fingers under his chin to make him raise his eyes.
"Promise me."
Francis's gaze was so intense that James wanted to back away, but he stood his ground.
"I promise.", Francis said.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
James had promised to take care of Francis -Sir John seemed delighted to see how well they
were getting along, all thoughts of them disobeying his orders forgotten-, yet he wanted to
visit Sir John parse out his mood.
Maybe inspiration would strike and he would have an idea on how to sway their leader.
Still, he wanted make sure Francis was looked after, after the bad night he'd had, and so he
went to Thomas Blanky and asked him to keep an eye on their mutual friend.
"Sure I will!", the Ice Master promised. "Consider it done, Commander."
James turned to go, but hesitated. "Mr. Blanky", he began. "You've known Francis for a long
time..."
"Aye."
"In that time, has he ever- shown an ability to... see things that others would only know with
hindsight?"
"I'm not sure what you mean.", Blanky said. "He's always looked somewhat bleakly into the
future. He told me himself that he's been this way since he was young."
"What way?", James asked.
"Possessed of a melancholic temperament."
James wondered if this was a euphemism, or really what Blanky meant.
"Would you say that this... melancholic temperament has been more pronounced as of late?"
Blanky, who had been in the process of stuffing his pipe, stopped and looked at him archly.
"Why?"
"Oh, I don't mean for you to betray Francis's confidence, Mr. Blanky.", James assured him.
"I'm merely worried about him as a friend. His drinking, these seizures... It's all... worrying."

Blanky's gaze softened. "Aye. I'm sorry, Commander, it's just that I feel protective of Frank. I
know he likes you quite a lot, and I very much hope that affection is reciprocated...?"
"It is."
"Wonderful. It is good that Frank is making new friends, even amidst this crisis."
"You mean the crisis of his health?", James asked. Or do you mean the expedition?, he didn't
say out loud.
"Whatever you want to call it. I know something is going on with him that he won't say,
which you probably also noticed."
James nodded. "Are you worried about him?"
"I'm not sure.", Blanky said, cocking his head. "He gave up the drinking and that is definitely
good for him. He doesn't fly into rages half as often, and actually seems to give a damn about

definitely happened to him, and part of me thinks that it wasn't anything good."
"He told me not too long ago that he finally let go of his feelings for Miss Carcroft.", James
said.
"Aye.", Thomas replied with a sudden grin. "But that might be because his heart belongs to
someone else now."
James stopped short. Blanky's knowing look was hardly difficult to interpret.
"Mr. Blanky.", James said, trying to sound stern but missing the mark by a long shot. "You
don't mean to imply that Francis is in love with someone on this ship! That would be
inappropriate, illegal, not to mention-"
"Oh, I don't imply anything.", Blanky grinned. "I merely observe, poor Ice Master that I am."
Blanky clapped James on the shoulder and said: "I like you two together."
James could've demanded to know what he meant by that, and also write him up for these
inappropriate insinuations he kept making, but James felt his heart warm at Blanky's easy
approval.
He couldn't help but think that besides Neptune and Francis, he had another friend on Terror.
"You need to make sure he doesn't drink.", James told Blanky. "Jopson hid all his whiskey,
and I don't know how long he can withstand Francis should he order him again to give him
some."
"Consider it done.", Blanky said again. "Someone needs to catch ol' Frank up on all the ship's
gossip anyway."

James wrapped himself in his slops, judged the meager daylight they had, and decided that
the wind wasn't howling so much as to not attempt a crossing to Erebus.
He was asked if he needed an escort, but James was fairly confident he could manage the
small distance between the ships.
At the last minute, Harry Peglar joined him, apparently being done with Seneca's letters.
"It really is a mystery to me how much time you find to read between everything that needed
doing in the last days.", James said to him as they climbed down the railing.
"I don't need much sleep.", Peglar explained. "I'm fine with four hours at most."
James hummed. "We share a habit then.", he said, remembering fondly how he would stay up
at night to write to his sister-in-law.
Elizabeth had asked him to keep a journal for her for the family's perusal.
He had already thought that Elizabeth, for one, would be delighted to read his changing over
to Terror, because then she would get descriptions of the men aboard her as well.
Walking on the ice was much different than stepping on a frozen pond back home. It wasn't
slippery, or flat, which suited them fine walking like this, but would be a nightmare when
hauling a boat, James knew.
The wind was too loud to converse above a shout, so he and Mr. Peglar stayed mostly silent
during their walk over. Snow was falling in thick floks, clouding their vision white.
When they reached Erebus, James put a mittened hand on her hull and looked up. They were
in the process of taking her masts and excess rigging down, as well.
James suddenly had to think of his dreams, and how they never featured any of the ships, not
his Erebus, nor even Terror.
That was strange in of itself; when he was at sea, the ship tended to insert himself as a
backdrop to every single on of his dreams.
He dreamed of having tea with William and Elizabeth, but it wasn't in their garden in
Brighton, but on the deck of the Cornwallis; Minney took his hand to show him a rabbit hole
in the garden, but for an inexplicable reason they were moving around Erebus's orlop.
But these new nightmares, sensual and terrifying, took place away from the ships.
James hadn't considered if maybe, these dreams had something to do with Francis and his
probable ability to see the future; Perhaps it was the place they were in. He had heard of
people who believed that magnetic readings had the ability to impact the human mind; such
people were generally considered mad, but that was back in good old England, a place where
everything made sense and no dipping circle picked up anything unusual.

Maybe it was the place they were in, messing with their minds. James decided to find out if
there were others who were similarly affected.
Sir John was busy, supervising the work on deck to make Erebus winter ready. He greeted
James briefly and told him to wait at his leisure.
Before James gave into his longing and visited Dundy -he would so dearly like to confide in
him, though he didn't think it was wise- he went by sickbay to see Mr. Goodsir.
"Commander Fitzjames!", Dr. Stanley greeted him, one of his rare smiles on his face.
"Stephen.", James replied, shaking his hand. "No need to stand on ceremony, you saved my
life after all."
"It was my job.", Dr. Stanley said. "I could hardly let you bleed to death."
"As long as I don't give you cause to regret that action, I am a happy man."
"Never.", Stanley assured him.
James knew that Stephen Stanley was an authoritative man, but whenever he and James were
talking, there was submissive, almost meek quality to him, and James wondered at it.
It wasn't simply their difference in rank, he thought, but something else.
"Are you well, Commander? Do you have some sort of medical problem?", Dr. Stanley
asked.
"Just visiting an old friend.", James murmured, not quite managing a smile.
"I'm glad. Though you do seem... troubled."
"How could I not be after the meeting yesterday?"
Even though they were alone in sickbay, James lowered his voice.
"I understand. Though Mr. Goodsir blew it all entirely out of proportion, in my opinion. I'm
sure all will be well as long as we listen to Sir John."
James stared at him in disbelief. "Stephen, I'm not sure how one can blow news like that 'out
of proportion', as you say. It's horrifying."
"We have enough provisions to get through the winter. And in summer, we will hunt! But
let's not talk about such disagreeable subjects, shall we?" Stanley's look was almost pleading.
James shook his head. If everyone that had heard the truth denied it like Stephen did, they
would get nowhere.
He opened his mouth to retort something when Goodsir came in.
"Ah, Mr. Goodsir. I wanted to talk to you, too.", James said.

"Oh?"
"In private.", James added, knowing Stephen wouldn't forgive him for this, but he couldn't
very well bring up what he wanted to say in front of him.
"We can go to my cabin.", Goodsir told him, awkwardly avoiding Stephen's burning stare.
"I'm sorry.", James said to his friend. "It's Captain Crozier's concern, not mine."
Stephen nodded curtly and let them go, though James could see the hurt in his eyes he
quickly covered up with his stoic demeanor.
Goodsir's cabin was barely large enough for two men to stand in, especially when James
ordered the door closed.
"It was Captain Crozier who told you about the lead in the tins, wasn't it?", James asked.
Goodsir looked torn. "I can't-"
"-betray his confidence, I know. Yet it seems fairly obvious that I'm right."
Goodsir sighed. "The truth is, I'm worried about him. He shouldn't have known this. And I'm
beginning to think that he knows a great deal more, and it's all bad."
"We are in agreement, then.", James said, surprised.
"Will you perhaps talk to Sir John?", Goodsir asked hopefully. "He might listen to you- I
know he only wants the best for us and the expedition, but he doesn't believe Captain Crozier,
and if I may say so, I think that is dangerous."
James nodded. "I will do my best."
"Thank you. I am sorry for killing Jacko. I know Sir John is cross with me for that, but I
could think of no other way..."
James tried a reassuring smile. "You will be forgiven, Mr. Goodsir. Oh, and one more
thing..."
"Yes?"
"Do you have any idea why Captain Crozier came to you with this matter? Have you earned
his trust in some way since the beginning of our voyage?"
Thankfully, Goodsir wasn't offended, but looked thoughtful. "I had asked myself that same
thing, yet I can think of no incident."
Perhaps Francis saw Goodsir's trustworthyness in the future too, James thought.
He thanked Goodsir and made for Dundy's cabin, where Le Vesconte was drawing in his own
sketchbook this time.

When he saw James he stood up wordlessly and pulled him into a tight embrace. James
returned it, closing his eyes briefly.
"I missed you.", Dundy murmured into his shoulder. "That conference was dreadful, I wish I
could've talked to you after."
James felt himself flush. After Francis'd had his seizure, he had been entirely occupied with
worrying over him, and somewhat lost sight of Dundy.
"I'm sorry.", he said sincerely, drawing back. "But we can talk now."
"I was really worried when Goodsir first told us.", Le Vesconte admitted. "But Sir John
displayed great qualities of leadership in bolstering our spirits, as it were. I can only imagine
how it was on Terror, with Crozier being so dreadful."
James winced internally, knowing that he had talked just like his friend not too long ago.
"Crozier isn't dreadful, Dundy. He is rightly worried about the expedition."
"Well, that's an entirely new tune from you.", Le Vesconte said, crossing his arms. "Whatever
did Crozier do to you to get you on his side?"
"Nothing.", James replied.
He realised too late that that sounded somewhat incriminating, denying a clear answer like
that, especially to Dundy.
And yes, a tell tale frown appeared between his friend's brows.
"Is it a secret then?"
"Of course not. We simply... talked, that's all."
"And apparently you read Shakespeare together.", Dundy said.
James felt irritated. "Now who told you that?"
"Everyone on Terror knows it. Now, please don't tell me it's Julius Caesar you're reading, or
else I would need to doubt your sanity."
Unfortunately, Dundy was very aware of the special significance Julius Caesar had to James,
and not just the part where James had played Calpurnia on the St Vincent, but the entire
dynamic between Brutus and Cassius that had so caught him.
"And what if it is Julius Caesar?", James said defensively. "What would be so bad about
that?"
Dundy shook his head. "James, do you... you know... like Captain Crozier?"
"I don't know what you mean.", James muttered.

"Oh dear.", Le Vesconte said, staring at him in disbelief. "You do! Really? Him? What is it
about him that is so irresistible, then? His drinking? His Irishness? His rages?"
"Oh, be quiet!", James told him.
"You know, I was joking when said that I don't want some handsome lad on Terror to snatch
you away, but you just couldn't help yourself, could you? And of course, no one but the
Captain would do for the beautiful, dashing, James Fitzjames, yes no one but a lonely,
brooding drunk of a man-"
"Dundy!", James exclaimed. "Stop it!"
"-has he some hidden talents, perhaps? He can't have, or else Miss Cracroft surely wouldn't
have turned him down-"
Fed up, James shoved Dundy away from him. "I'm warning you!"
Le Vesconte shoved James right back, and suddenly they were having a bit of a tussle. Such
was definitely beneath the dignity of a Lieutenant and a Commander, but they were both
touch starved and perhaps still shocked from the truth about the tins, and so they shoved and
kicked each other until Dundy had James pinned at the door momentarily. Le Vesconte took
the opportunity to kiss James thoroughly, and James only put up a token resistance before
sinking into him.
Dundy was safe, and familiar, and James did care for him like he did for few others.
James looped his arms around the other's shoulders while Dundy pried his lips open with his
tongue, and James felt a sigh escape him.
Perhaps they could just enjoy each other for a few moments...
Sir John's voice outside broke through his lustful haze, and they both jumped apart, and none
too soon, for next Sir John knocked on Le Vesconte's door.
In record time -they had practice with this, after all- Dundy sat back at his table and got his
sketchbook open, meanwhile James smoothed out his hair and leaned casually against the
wall.
Dundy called and admission to enter and Sir John opened the door.
"I thought I might find you here.", their leader said to James. "I hope I didn't interrupt
anything."
Only Sir John Franklin could say a sentence like this without the slightest hint of a double
meaning, James thought.
"Not at all.", James assured him, and Dundy nodded.
"Let's go to my cabin.", Sir John said to James. "Feel free to catch up later, of course."

"Of course."
"Do you want a drink?", Sir John asked, when they were in his cabin. "I hear these things
aren't handled as liberally on Terror as of late."
James shook his head. At the beginning of the voyage, James had always enjoyed relaxing
with Sir John as company; he could be a very entertaining narrator, telling of his exploits in
Van Diemen's land and his previous expeditions -and also Francis's failed suit for his niecebut that had changed, now.
It was simple, James realised; he didn't trust Sir John as he had; he wasn't at ease. He felt a
flash of anger at Francis, even unjustified as it was, for making everything so goddamn
complicated!
But he might as well be angry at the Arctic, for being cold, and dangerous, and inhospitable.
James could admit it to himself now: he had underestimated this place, was perhaps still
underestimating it.
What puzzled him was that Sir John had no such excuse - he had been to the Artic, had nearly
starved here, for God's sake! But perhaps that was the very thing that made him reckless, he
had survived it all once, and now thought himself immortal, maybe.
"How is Francis?", Sir John asked. "Did you leave him well looked after?"
"I did. He's doing alright, for the most part. But we all worry, of course."
Sir John nodded. "To be honest, I had not thought that anything was strong enough to fell
Francis Crozier, but apparently I was wrong."
James considered carefully what to say next. "And what he said to you about the tins...?"
"I understand his point, James, I do. Francis is a pessimist, he sees everything as a
catastrophe waiting to happen. The problem is, that as soon as things actually start going
wrong, men like Francis think that everything else will go wrong as well; even if there's
actually no indicator for that. It looks bleak now; it's winter and everything seems cold and
dead. But do you remember the abundance of hunting we were able to do last summer? It is
responsible for the good state of our stores now, and it will be so again."
James nodded. Sir John's view did make sense, but deep down he still believed Francis was
right. Why? Perhaps it was the dreams...
"But you're sure we'll get through? We don't need to contend with lead poisoning?"
"James, I would never put a the finding of the passage over the wellbeing of a single man on
Erebus or Terror. Surely you know that."
"I do.", James said.
And he did. Sir John loved his crew and cared for them, that James had never doubted.

More than God loves them, he thought.
"The news is shocking to us all.", Sir John continued. "As is the death of Jacko. I already told
Mr. Goodsir that I'm deeply dismayed about that, at least he seems penitent- but we knew
when starting this voyage that achieving our goals wouldn't be easy. This is simply another
difficulty to deal with, and God will ensure us passing it safely, I'm sure."
It would've been so criminally easy to let himself be lulled by Sir John's dulcet tones. And
part of James was. There was another part, however, which remembered Sir John assuring
him that they wouldn't get stuck in the ice with the same confidence.
Fretting about who was right wouldn't help right now anyway, James was here to get
information, not let himself be swayed!
"Captain.", he began carefully. "I couldn't help but notice- well, it appears to me that there is
some strife between you and Francis. Personally as well as professionally."
Sir John sighed, looking at James keenly. "I wish it were not so, James, truly, though you're
wrong in part. Professionally I think there is no better Second than Francis. He has the
experience and the vigor to see this expedition through, and though we disagree on many
points, I always invite his honest opinion."
James doubted the truth of that, but he let it stand, little choice as he had.
"Personally, on the other hand...", Sir John said, letting it hang in the air.
"You needn't tell me, though I suspect it has something to do with Miss Cracroft?"
Sir John rubbed his forehead. "Yes, of course. You see James, I don't mean to be harsh, but
Francis had ideas above his station. Maybe they could be initially excused by his being in
love, but he persisted, even when it had been made clear to him that there would be no hope.
The sheer obstinancy of it was baffling! Not to mention that his suit caused great unrest
within the family."
And what about the unrest it caused Francis, James thought, indignant.
He couldn't help but sympathise with Francis in this, and even admired him for his courage,
his "obstinancy", as Sir John called it.
James himself would certainly never have done as Francis had, in fact, the mere thought of it
made his stomach lurch unpleasantly.
"How was Francis, when he courted her?", James asked.
Maybe Francis had been particularly obnoxious, but that James very much doubted.
"Not much changed, I suppose, especially in front of me and my wife. He was more softspoken, though. And the way he looked at Sophia... As if she might drop from the earth at
any moment and he would be utterly bereft without her."

James stopped short. That was exactly how Francis tended to look at him, now.
"And when she talked, told stories of her day and such, he listened with the rapt attention of a
man captured...."
James remembered that evening on Terror a while back, when Francis had started his strange
behavior. James had told a story, then. And Francis had listened, oh how he had listened...
"Whenever she touched him -all within the realm of politeness, of course- he flushed the
most brilliant shade of red.", Sir John continued. "It would've been quite charming, I suppose,
had I not worried every minute that Sophia might be stupid enough to accept his suit."
James was barely listening.
Oh, what an idiot I've been, he thought.
He had known that Francis regarded him with love, yes, but he had never made the
connection this blatantly.
He'd told himself that at best, Francis was holding some newfound avuncular affection for
him.
But this... this meant...
Sir John looked at him with a sad smile. "I know why you're asking about this. You wonder if
I let my continuing dismay of Francis cloud my judgment."
That did bring James successfully back to the present.
He nodded, abashed. "I couldn't help but ask myself that, yes."
"I understand.", Sir John said. "I do. But rest assured, I do manage to maintain an objective
view of our situation. And Francis and I disagreeing is not an indication of any sort of crisis
between us, it's simply the nature of command."
"I'm relieved to hear it.", James said.
"Good. Why don't we talk of something more agreeable, then?", Sir John suggested. "I've
been giving some thought to your idea of a Carnivale."
"You have?"
James was surprised. He had believed that he would need to use every method of persuasion
known to man to get Sir John to even consider it, and the same went for Francis.
Sir John hummed. "I had thought... perhaps we could organise one for the end of this winter.
It will be a hard time for all of us, and perhaps it will bring some much needed good cheer."

Chapter 14: Francis
Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Francis was working on his sermon when James came back. He had mostly spent the day
exercising with the crutches and smoking with Thomas.
He had wanted to leave the Great Cabin once in a while to give his officers some time to
spend there without his constant presence, and so he had braved the way to Thomas's
quarters.
Thomas himself was busy with all the winter preparations, and so he had left Francis some
time later and let him write at his desk.
Thankfully, Francis had an idea now what to hold the sermon on, but he knew he wasn't Sir
John when it came to pontificating.
Still, a better way to build a rapport with the crew than the Ship's Articles, Francis thought.
At least I hope so.
As it was, he was grateful for the distraction from his thoughts. He was aware that he
shouldn't have brought up the thing with Hickey before James, even though he was grateful
to James for talking him out of executing the caulker's mate.
Heaven knew what James thought of him now. That he was insane, probably.
Too late did it occur to him that James was maybe right now telling Sir John everything,
which doubtlessly would lead to Sir John removing him from command or worse.
But no, somehow he didn't believe that James would betray his confidence. He wished to
believe it, of course, yet he also knew he had given James no reason to trust him.
And James had freely said that he didn't trust him, also...
Francis had to think of the other James then, the James who died. He was the James Francis
had fallen in love with, that Francis could now plainly see.
Were these two men really the same person?
Of course, the answer was yes, but if one were to consider it more, it wasn't so easy.
They had different memories, for one. There was less pain in the James here now than in the
other reality, though Francis fervently hoped it would stay that way.
Still, a bond had been forged in the other time between them that didn't yet exist in this one.
Francis was in the process of rectifying that, but he realised it could never be the same thing,
not really.

Perhaps that was good. As established, he didn't want this James to go through the same pain
as the other one.
But it also meant that he perhaps should stop treating this James as if he were the other one.
I can't, though, Francis thought. That I can't do. It would mean that the other James is utterly
lost to me, that he really is dead.
And so, Francis tried to distract himself with the sermon. His burning need for a drink had
already abated after the conversation with James, but he still felt weak about it, so he avoided
Jopson.
When James returned to Terror, Francis already suspected he had, for he heard Neptune
happily barking on deck.
It took some more time for James to actually seek him out; a good half hour later he poked
his head into the cabin.
"Mr. Blanky told me you were here.", he said, flushed and out of breath. "How are you?"
"Well, for the most part.", Francis replied. "It's good to see you.", he added cautiously.
James smiled, just as cautiously, it seemed. "Likewise. I hope you're not angry that I went to
Erebus, as it was, I needed to speak to Sir John."
"About?"
"The tins, mostly. I'm serious about finding a way to change his mind, as I said...", James
trailed off, chewing the inside of his cheek.
"James, allow me to apologise again for everything I said this morning.", Francis said in a
rush. "It was unprofessional, bad form, and-"
"-very confusing.", James finished his sentence. He held up a hand. "No need to apologise,
Francis. Once was enough. I know you didn't speak from malice."
Francis let out a breath. "Good."
There was a pause, before James said: "And Sir John agreed that we can throw a Carnivale to
celebrate the end of winter!"
Francis's heart sank. "Really?"
"Yes! And mind you, Francis, your leg will be healed by then so you have no excuse not to
go!"
"Well first, we have to make it through this winter.", Francis grumbled. "And for the record, I
think this is a terrible idea."

"Of course you do... But-", James stopped short. "Francis, do you see that something bad will
happen? At the Carnivale?"
"See?", Francis repeated. "What's that supposed to mean?"
"Um, nothing... Just if you have... any sense of foreboding or anything..."
James looked slightly embarrassed, and now Francis was confused.
"I suppose I do, yes.", Francis said, though he quickly regretted it at James's horrified
expression. "But I'm sure it doesn't mean anything. Let the men have their fun..."
"Hm." James seemed thoughtful. "Are you up for Julius Caesar again this evening?"
"I thought we could eat with the officers first, and then read it together.", Francis said.
James's frown broke into a smile. "Francis! Are you finally letting go of your antisocial
tendencies?"
"Nothing of the sort. I just don't want them to think we're conspiring against them with all the
solitary dinners we've had."
Francis lifted himself upright and reached for the crutches.
"Do you want me to carry your papers for you?", James asked eagerly.
Taken by momentary panic, Francis slapped James's reaching hand away. "Do not go near my
sermon."
A devilish grin spread on James's face. "Your sermon, you say?"
Francis raised an admonishing finger. "Hands off, Fitzjames!"
"Alright!", James said, laughing. "I prefer to be surprised by your tender words anyway."
"Trust me, none of this will be tender.", Francis growled.
James just laughed harder, and even though it was at his expense, Francis couldn't help
cracking a smile either.
Finally, Francis folded the paper and put it into his pocket, before he made the journey back
to the Great Cabin.
Jopson was already setting the table.
"No alcohol today, Jopson.", James told him. "We'll all drink water tonight."
Francis started: "That's not necess-"
"After last night, it absolutely is.", James said sternly.

"I concurr.", Jopson said with a nod.

They made a sad faced lot, so even Francis thought, when Irving, Little and Dr. McDonald
joined them.
Francis knew it was his task to bolster their spirits as Captain, but at the same time, he didn't
want to lie to them and make out the truth about the tins any less devastating than it was.
Didn't he want them on his side?
On the other hand, if he were to kill Sir John, he would only be making himself suspicious if
he disagreed to openly with him.
He had already arrived at the conclusion that Sir John's death had to look like an accident,
nothing else would do.
As he had already thought before, there couldn't the slightest suspicion of murder, and with it,
mutiny when they returned to England, or else they would all be hanged.
But how to do it, that was the question.
Francis had also spent and inordinate amount of time thinking about that, of course.
It seemed a foregone conclusion that he wouldn't be able to do anything as long as his leg
was broken.
Unless he wanted 'outsource the work', as it were, and Francis was determined that he would
drag no one else into this.
Especially not James.
He had thought of poison, then. Would he able to find the same vial of the stuff with which
he had helped James into death in Terror's stores?
He wasn't certain, and even then he would need to make sure that only Sir John ingested it,
and would keep it down.
No, too much could go wrong with poisoning. Unless he could enlist Dr. Goodsir as help, but
that he wouldn't do. Goodsir already had the unfortunate monkey on his conscience because
of Francis, he certainly wouldn't add more lives to that one.
Because it had to appear as an accident, Francis quickly eliminated most other possibilities,
such as shooting Sir John with his pistol - though maybe the whole thing could be
camouflaged as a hunting accident?
But for that, Sir John would need to be persuaded to go hunting in the first place, and take
Francis with him...

"I talked to Sir John today...", James said into the established silence.
Francis found himself hoping that James might start to tell one of his abominable stories to
spread some good cheer.
As it was, Francis loved every part of James, even his stories.
Especially his stories, for they were a sign that he was well.
"And?", Dr. McDonald asked.
James told them about the Carnivale, and that did spread a better mood, as it started a
discussion on what would be the best costume.
Even Francis couldn't fall into brooding about the other Carnivale he remembered, because
James was so excited about it all.
However, then Francis wondered if the James in the other time had been this excited, and
Francis had only not seen it because he'd been going through withdrawal, and he did feel his
countenance turn melancholy.
"Now, you must tell us, Francis,", said James, after Edward had repeatedly declined Irving's
proposal that all the Lieutenants went in a group as angels. "What would your costume be?"
"Why not let it be a surprise?", Francis grumbled.
"Oh, no, you're not getting out of this the same way as with the sermon, Francis.", James
insisted. "If you don't know as who to go, we will help you."
Francis certainly wouldn't make some elaborate costume, sooner he'd go out on the ice naked.
"How about Neptune?", Dr. McDonald asked, which caused Neptune under the table to perk
up briefly.
Everyone laughed, except Francis.
"I mean the god of the sea, not the dog.", Dr. McDonald clarified, but it was too late.
"That's a hard no from me.", Francis said as they were finally done laughing at him.
"Too bad.", James said, his eyes glittering with merriment.
And just like that, Francis felt elated again. He was helpless to withstand a single smile from
James, it was truly horrifying.
"How about an old crone?", Irving suggested. "You know, a wise woman who can tell the
future?"
"Don't you think those people are in league with the devil?", Francis asked his religious third
Lieutenant.

Irving shrugged. "It would only be a costume."
"How about you just let me think of something on my own.", Francis said.
"I dare say it will be Jopson thinking of something on his own.", James stated dryly, which
caused the others to laugh again. "Isn't that true, Jopson?"
Jopson, who had been refilling everyone's water, loyally said: "I couldn't say."
Blast it, James already knew him far too well. Was he really that transparent? Or was James
just so observant?
"Well, then James, as who would you go to the Carnivale?", Francis asked. "Something
showy and alltogether ridiculous, I should think."
James grinned. "I have a few ideas."
"Do share them with the group.", Francis pressed him.
He didn't see why he should be the only one feeling uncomfortable.
James cleared his throat then leaned over to Francis and whispered in his ear, which was in of
itself enough to make Francis almost drop his fork.
What caused him to turn a no doubt telling shade of scarlet though were James's words,
delivered in a husky tone: "Would you like to see me don women's skirts again, just for you?"
Francis tried to assure himself that James was only teasing, and that he didn't know about
Francis's feelings towards him, which had turned so very... physical as of late.
As it was, he could hardly breathe when James drew back and looked at him with that
positively wicked grin on his face.
"What did he say?", everyone demanded to know.
Francis just shook his head weakly.
"Whatever it was, it must've been very indecent.", Irving opined.
James gave a fake gasp. "I'm never indecent!", he exclaimed.
"What did he say, then?", Edward asked.
"I'm not repeating this in polite company.", Francis said, finally having regained some of his
composure.
James shrugged, still grinning. "It's just going to have to be a surprise, then."

Francis had experience by now with making mistakes. Any man his age would have.
He knew, of course, that some mistakes cost more than others; and that was doubly true in the
Arctic or Antarctic.
His mistakes there had served to make him a careful man, at least when it came to these

And so he had made another mistake, and he could already see that it would cost him dearly

Chapter 17: James

Yes, he did want to bring the hunting party home safely, and a part of him liked to think he
would've volunteered to search for them even without everything that happened with Francis.
Perhaps he would have.
On the other hand, he probably wouldn't have been on Erebus when Sir John wanted to send

They set out, him, Pilkington (the only marine who had stayed back) and John Morfin, who

surrounding area and then return, lest they get into trouble themselves.
Despite the worrying circumstances, James felt excited to walk for a while again, even if it

They would have to use the stars as their guide, useless as compasses were in this part of the

They were head in the direction of King William Land, since that was the course the hunting

James watched the landscape in the light of his lantern. Even though it wasn't flat, and one
mostly had to look at the ground as not to trip over ice, he felt exposed and didn't like it.
He also noted the huge berg that had formed a good way west of the ships.
Dundy had not liked him volunteering for the search party, same as Sir John, but in the latter

With the rifle slung over his shoulder, he would certainly be able to handle a goddamn polar

"They're supposed to be very intelligent, and they like to play with their prey."

"It's a fucking bear. What else would it be?", Des Voeux said from somewhere behind.

There was a movement on the ridge. James immediately pulled the trigger, and after the

James, who had torn off his mitten with his teeth to reload, took aim again, but it was hardly

The bear -James still called it that in his head, even though this massive beast resembled no

It wanted to attack him, of course.
James stumbled and fell to the ground, - everything was happening very fast. He heard it

The monster was enormous, and it most definitely wasn't a bear. It had grabbed someone Lieutenant Gore, as it turned out- and it was looking at him with an intelligence that James
had never seen in any kind of animal.
Then it used its claws to break him apart.
