best out of all of us, I think."
"She doesn't want to talk, though. Not that I blame her.", Thomas said.
"Alright that's it. Everyone out!", Francis thundered. "Let the poor woman rest!"
After everyone had squeezed themselves past Francis and left, including the doctors, leaving
just the sleeping Mr. Collins on one cot, Francis approached Lady Silence. She was lying on
her cot with her eyes half closed, her father holding her hand.
"I will leave you to rest soon.", Francis said in the Netsilisk tongue. "I just need to ask you a
few questions."
Lady Silence opened her eyes fully to regard him, and said nothing. Francis hadn't forgotten
the piercing intensity of her stare, how it seemed to judge them all and find them wanting,
entirely justifiably.
"It's about Tuunbaq."
Obvious surprise on both faces. The man made a gesture, and Lady Silence asked: "Who are
you?"
"I'm known among your people as Aglooka.", Francis said. "This is my ship, my men, and I
would like to lead them back to safety."
"Why are you here, then? This is not your land. You are..." Lady Silence stopped and looked
at her father. "You are not safe here."
A chill went down Francis's spine. However, that was a good question. Francis could try to
explain about finding the Northwest Passage, but that would be lying, at least in his case.
He hadn't cared a whit about the Passage when he'd signed up for this expedition, well, he
hadn't cared a whit about anything, except Sophia.
"We know that.", Francis said. "Some of us do. And we mean you no harm. Hurting you was
an accident."
Lady Silence was, characteristically, silent.
"I know Tuunbaq is out there.", Francis continued. "I've met him before. Will you please tell
us how we can make him not hurt us?"
"You've met Tuunbaq and survived.", Lady Silence said. "How did you do that?"
Francis searched for the right words. "It wasn't... it wasn't the right way. I had angered
Tuunbaq."
The door opened in that moment. Francis was ready to yell at however had deigned to disturb
him against his expressed order, when he saw who it was.

"James! What's wrong?", Francis exclaimed.
James looked terrible, even more exhausted than before, and Francis, always wary to see
James unwell, felt his heart clench. Of course it was no wonder, James had seen the violent
deaths of not just one, but two crewmates, and Graham Gore had probably been a personal
friend.
"I- I came for a bit of laudanum.", James mumbled. "Can't sleep."
"Nightmares?", Francis asked.
James nodded. He looked so unguarded and small in that moment, that Francis wanted to
race to him and gather him in his arms.
As it was, Francis took his crutches and walked over to James, taking his limp hand. James
looked down at their intertwined fingers as if they could tell him the secrets of the universe.
"I'm sure Dr. McDonald is in his quarters. Go ask him for the laudanum.", Francis said gently.
"If you like, I can check in with you after I've talked to our guests."
Francis bit his tongue for being so forward, but he wanted to help James as best he could.
James's gaze fell on the Netsilisk. "Hello again.", he said awkwardly. "Will you tell the
woman I'm sorry for us shooting her?", he added with an earnest gaze at Francis.
"My friend apologizes for your injury.", Francis told Lady Silence. "As do I."
Both of the Netsilisk absorbed this, looking at James rather than Francis.
After a moment, James turned back to him. "I will seek out the doctor.", he murmured, then
left.
Francis cleared his throat and went on his crutches back to Lady Silence and her father.
"I had angered Tuunbaq.", he repeated. "I would know how I can appease him."
"Leave.", Lady Silence said. "Take your ships and leave."
Francis could've screamed in frustration, but he forced himself to remain calm.
"We can't leave right now. The ships are stuck, and it's winter."
The man made another gesture at Lady Silence. "Do all your men want to appease
Tuunbaq?", she asked.
Francis could lie and say yes. However, he was sure that he wouldn't be believed. And that
was the problem: he was the leader of his men, which automatically meant he was
responsible for everything they did. He had been responsible for Hickey killing the Netsilisk
family in the other reality, just as much as he was responsible for Des Voeux shooting Lady
Silence in this.

Well, technically it is still Sir John who is in charge of Des Voeux, a tiny voice inside him
said.
But it didn't matter. If they wanted mercy from Tuunbaq, they needed all to be worthy of it.
And Francis had no idea how to ensure that.
With another sermon, perhaps?
"My men don't know the ways of Tuunbaq.", Francis said. "It is only I who met him before.
They still think they can kill Tuunbaq."
"Then Tuunbaq will kill them."
~~~~~~~~~~~~
After her dire pronouncement, Lady Silence declined to talk further, and finally Francis left
her to rest. He had the faint hope that their hospitality would perhaps convince her and her
father that they weren't a threat, but he knew it was unlikely.
He then agonized over going to see James or not.
The offer to check up on him had left his lips quite without permission, because James had
been looking so miserable.
But maybe he was sleeping now, and Francis would only wake him if he came clambering in
with his crutches.
On the other hand, what if James was waiting for him?
He is likely still angry with me, Francis thought. It's only the shock that made him forget it
temporarily.
In the end, Francis went to Lieutenant Hodgson's room and pressed his ear to the door like
mischievous school boy.
He heard nothing. Much to his chargin, it was at this moment that Thomas came walking likely on his way to the wardroom.
"Ah, Francis!", Thomas boomed. "What are you doing here this fine evening?"
Francis shushed him, but it was already too late. He heard shuffling around behind the door.
Thomas winked at him and squeezed past, and Francis only had a moment to right himself
before James opened the door and peeked his head out.
"Errm... I hope you weren't sleeping.", Francis said.
James shook his head. "I didn't take the laudanum. It reminds me too much of being ill."
"Do you want me to sit with you a while?", Francis asked carefully.

James wordlessly pulled back his head and left the door open, so Francis took it as the
cautious invitation it was.
He sat down on the only chair in the room, relieved to be off his feet. James, in his
nightclothes, stood to the side of him.
"None of that.", Francis said. "You're not on parade, man. Get in the bed."
Obediently, James climbed into his bunk. He looked deathly pale and tired, and Francis tried
to remind himself that he had already seen him in a much worse state. Oddly, this had the
opposite effect as intended, and Francis had surpress the urge to ask James if he wanted tea,
or bisquits, or another blanket perhaps.
"How can I help you?", Francis asked instead.
James sighed. "I don't know what's going on with me. I did sleep, but Graham is dead andand-"
"Yes?"
James said nothing and chewed his lip.
"You can tell anything you want, James, I won't betray your confidence.", Francis assured
him.
He realised his mistake just as the anger flashed across James's face.
"Well, I have to believe that, don't I?", he snapped. "As it is, I have nothing to say. You
already know everything."
"I do not.", Francis said. He was overcome with the urge to stand up in a hurry, but his
blasted leg wouldn't let him.
"Yes, you do! Everything that matters-"
"James, it doesn't matter! Not to me, not for a single second!"
James stared at him, his eyes wide. "I want to believe you, Francis, I do.", he said in a rush.
"But you need to tell me how you know. Please, tell me how you know."
Francis shook his head desperately.
But maybe, maybe he could tell James the truth, if only part of it. It would be a risk, yet he
needed to earn James's trust.
And he didn't want to keep this from him anymore.
"James,", Francis began. "It was you who told me about your birth. Or rather, you will tell me
about your birth. I don't know what motivated you, why you thought me worthy of knowing
it, but you will. And so I know."

James sat upright in his bunk, shock written all over his face.
"I didn't- I wouldn't-", he stuttered, then cleared his throat. "So it is true. You can see the
future."
"An approximation of it, yes.", Francis said. "But I'll tell you right now that I will not share
any more of what I know. It's not that I don't trust you, because I do-"
"Why?", James asked.
"Pardon?"
"I've given you no reason to trust me.", James said.
Francis looked at him helplessly. "You will."
"Francis, I-", James began. "I have these dreams. They started when I came over to Terror.
They're about you and me, and... I'm dying in them. I'm always dying. I lose my teeth, and
my bullet wound reopens, and I go blind... and then I'm begging you, begging you for death
and I-"
Francis felt tears prick at his eyes, and he saw that James was already crying silently. He
reached for his crutches and made the few steps to the bed. He touched James's wet cheek as
if to ensure he was real.
"Is that the future you see for me?", James asked. "Is that why you won't tell me?"
"James.", Francis breathed.
James stifled a sob with his arm. "Please, Francis, I'm terrified. Tell me-"
Francis took James's face in both hands, standing in precarious balance because of his leg. "It
will not happen, James. I promise you, it will not happen. I'd sooner die myself."
James tipped his face forward and leaned against Francis's stomach. Francis wrapped his
arms around him and pulled him close.
He stood there on one leg, trying not to cry himself, thinking he would truly do anything to
save this man, even if it meant tearing Sir John limb from limb.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Chapter 19: James
James clung to Francis, crying like a child, but he didn't care.
It will not happen, James. I promise you, it will not happen. I'd sooner die myself.
James clung to the words as well, spoken with such passion. He wanted to believe them more
than anything, he wanted to trust Francis.
He had tried to sleep before, but once again the nightmare had been so near, so real that he
was afraid to fall asleep again.
He had seen Graham, being torn apart by the beast, yet when he tried to lift his rifle to shoot
it he found his arms wasted, his wrist broken again from that time he had fallen off rigging as
a boy.
He had then watched, helpless, as the beast turned its eye on Francis...
As a child, he had always been given laudanum to sleep when he had a fever, and it had
caused James to hate the stuff pretty early on.
Dr. Stanley knew of it, for he had refused laudanum to help ease his pain after the surgery on
his bullet wound in China, only giving in when he was near delirious with the ache in his
chest and arm.
But he'd been absolutely exhausted, unable to sleep for terror, and so he had decided to try
laudanum once more.
After dressing halfway decent and finding no doctor in sickbay, however, James's desperation
had eased and he had gone to his cabin again, where Francis had found him.
"James.", Francis said gently, after his sobbing had eased. "James, I need to sit down."
James lifted his head from where it had been buried in Francis's waistcoat. "Of course. I'm
sorry, I didn't think-", he muttered in a gravelly voice. "Sit down."
Without considering the intimacy of such an invitation, James moved to the side so Francis
could sit on the edge of the bunk.
Francis sat down with a sigh and discreetly wiped his eyes.
"Will you stay with me a while?", James asked. "Of course, if you have other duties I won't
keep you-"
"Of course I'll stay. If you'll have me.", Francis said gravely.
James tried to smile, didn't quite manage it, and so took Francis's hand instead. "I'll have
you."

Francis started to move back to the chair, and James felt a twinge of disappointment. A part
of him had hoped that Francis would climb into bed with him.
It's better for your heart if he doesn't, he told himself.
"I must've thought I was dying.", James murmured.
"Hm?"
"To tell you the story of my origins, I mean.", he clarified. "You see, I've never told anyone
that. Never. People either knew or they didn't, but it wasn't talked about. But if I thought I
wouldn't have another chance to ever tell it..."
"James.", Francis said again, softly chiding. "This is hardly a subject that will help you fall
asleep."
"Well, now that we've started talking about it, I can't just put it out of my mind.", James
defended himself.
Francis approached the bunk with his chair and took James's hand. "Lie down under the
blankets. Close your eyes."
"Aye, aye, sir.", James said with irony, but he did as he was bidden.
Francis squeezed his hand, and to James's joy didn't let go.
"And now?", James asked after a moment, his eyes closed.
"Now you try to sleep."
"That's not how it works!", James protested. "You're supposed to tell me a story, at the very
least."
To his credit, Francis didn't call him childish. As it was, James was only trying to provoke
Francis a little, as he was wont to. Get some semblance of normalcy back.
"You're the one with all the stories, James.", Francis said. "I don't have any."
"I don't believe that for a second. You've had an eventful life. You've been to faraway places,
your heart has been broken..."
"So it's details about Miss Cracroft you're after?", Francis said, though he sounded amused.
"I'm surprised that Sir John didn't already tell you everything there is to know about that."
"Please, I know you're a gentleman. I would never force you to divulge details of such a
delicate matter.", James replied in mock offense. "No, tell me something else. About you and
Ross in Antarctica, perhaps. It'd be nice to hear about an expedition that was successful."
Francis sighed, but James suspected his reluctance was half for show at this point.

"Alright then.", Francis said. "But don't get any ideas when I tell you of the New Year's ball
we held."
"New Year's ball?", James repeated, his eyes glowing.
He felt about ten pounds lighter already, even though at the back of his mind, the terror still
lurked.
"All in good time.", Francis said with a smile. "So, we set out from Van Diemen's land on the
21st of November..."
As Francis talked, James found himself more and more calm. He wasn't surprised to find
Francis a gifted narrator, despite his protestations. He had a steadier, less excited cadence
than James himself, which did well.
The story was engaging, one might say too much even, but James was so tired that he soon
felt himself drift off.
The last thing he remembered was McCormick shooting some interesting bird they then ate,
and then he was fast asleep.
He still heard Francis's voice, distant and steady, carrying him through his dreams. He longed
for Francis again, to feel his body against his, and so he reached for him.
But Francis was always drifting away, fading into the distance.
When James woke, he was alone in his cabin. Of course, he hadn't expected Francis to stay,
but it he still felt a pang. He stood and dressed himself, then went to Sickbay.
The Netsilisk woman was sleeping, but her father was awake. Goodsir was talking to him in
English, having just brought them and Mr. Collins food.
He straightened and stood when James came in.
"Ah, Commander, I didn't get the chance to personally tell you yesterday how glad I am that
you returned to us unharmed!", Goodsir said to him. "I'm just attempting to get to know our
guests..."
"If you don't mind me asking, why are you on Terror in the first place?", James inquired.
Goodsir looked grim. "I was hoping to recruit Dr. McDonald so we could speak to Sir John
about the tins, and maybe convince Dr. Stanley of the direness of the situation. I was all for
starting to do all that yesterday, but Dr. McDonald said it would be strategic to wait until our
dead are buried." He sighed. "I am awfully sorry for Lieutenant Gore. He was always very
kind to me, and helped me with drawing my specimens. Bryant I know less well, but it's still
terrible."
James nodded. He too, had had nothing but kind feelings for Graham Gore. There had been
one time where the Lieutenant had nearly caught him and and Dundy going at it in James's
cabin, and to this day James didn't know if Graham had kept quiet for them.

He had treated neither James nor Dundy any differently, after, though there was something
more thoughtful about his countenance.
For James this incident had led him to end his association with Dundy, though.
Still, he thought had thought even more highly of Gore afterwards.
James had been too distracted by his own shock to truly process Graham's death, and now
suddenly a wave of grief hit him like a bludger.
He had sat there, crying about his own fate, meanwhile Graham was dead, and they couldn't
even bury him...
This was worse than war, he thought. There was a cruelty in Graham's death that no human
enemy could've replicated.
"The burial will be today, I expect.", Goodsir continued. "During the meager daylight we
have left."
James nodded. He longed for Sir John's calming words, this time. His sermon over the dead,
making something right again. In Sir John's imagination, there was no room for monsters
beyond human comprehension. They simply didn't exist, as didn't all the other threats to their
existence here.
"One more thing.", Goodsir said, lowering his voice, even though Mr. Collins was sleeping as
well and the Netsilisk couldn't understand him.
Still, James leaned closer in confidence. "Yes?"
"Sir John made the suggestion that we feed the Esquimaux from the poisoned tins.", Goodsir
whispered.
James felt cold suddenly. It had occurred to him too, of course, that the presence of the
Netsilisk was hardly good for their weakened stores.
He had never thought particularly highly of them, uncivilized as they were, but he was
beginning to realise that they knew something that he, for one, did not: how to survive in the
Arctic without the stores they brought.
Still, he felt guilty about shooting the woman, and he certainly wouldn't add to these people's
woes by giving them lead poisoning.
"He said he was sorry to do it, but they wouldn't stay long enough to feel any ill effects, he
said. And he only has the well-being of the crew in mind, he said."
James looked at Goodsir. "Was it a suggestion, or an order, Harry?"
Goodsir wrung his hands in discomfort. "It's difficult to interpret, sir."
So it had been an order.

James considered a moment, then said: "Let's treat it as a suggestion then. One we don't listen
to."
Goodsir looked immensely relieved. "Yes, sir. Thank you, sir. I, ah, had already disgarded it
for this meal, because I- I thought exactly as you did."
James clapped him on the shoulder, just as Mr. Collins woke from what seemed like a
nightmare.
Goodsir went to him and took his hand, fussing over him, and James felt oddly touched,
watching them.
He turned to the Netsilisk man and greeted him. He received a tilt of the head in return.
Dr. McDonald came in and wished him good morrow, then said something in the Netsilisk
language to the man.
"He has no tongue.", Dr. McDonald explained at length. "It was removed with a sharp cutting
instrument. That's why he doesn't talk."
"Is he some kind of outcast then, among his people?", James asked.
"I don't know. It doesn't seem like it. Both he and his daughter have been eating well, and are
in good condition."
After talking some more with the doctor, James went to the great cabin, where Francis was
bent over paperwork. Breakfast was laid out on the table, a cautious invitation James took.
Still, Francis barely looked up when James entered, but James saw that his cheeks were red.
"It seems to me that I have more cause to be embarrassed than you.", James said as he sat
down, trying for charming, but ending up more awkward.
"James, I shouldn't have-"
"You absolutely did, and we both know it. I could never trust you if you didn't tell me the
truth."
Francis looked up at him at last, his gaze full of desperation. "I'm sorry to burden you with
this."
"I was already burdened. And I do want to survive this expedition, so I'm going to talk to Sir
John again."
Francis opened his mouth, but James was faster: "I won't tell him anything about your
clairvoyance, never fear. It will not convince him, anyway."
"Good.", Francis said, fiddling with his papers.

James also had the impulse to talk, but he didn't know what to say. Apparently this was the
man he trusted above everyone else, whom he would tell his greatest shame.
What was there to say, after that?
Part of James still couldn't believe that Francis knew it all, yet didn't despise him for it.
He felt vulnerable, clumsy in front of him, as if he had just leaned how to talk.
"Have you always been this way?", James asked. "That you could see the future?"
Francis pursed his lips. "No, not always. Though there was always a certain sense in me if
something was going to go wrong, that's true. But actually knowing what is going to happen
down to the last detail, that is new."
James took a breath to try and fortify himself. "And what is going to happen?"
Francis shook his head. "I will not tell you. Please don't ask me again. It's for your own
protection that I keep my counsel."
It was clear as day that even now, there was something that Francis was keeping from him.
Should James try and find out what it was? Or should he just trust Francis?
Both were options that James didn't like for various reasons, and he decided to make up his
mind later.
He ate his breakfast of biscuits and coffee, which made him feel better already. He really
needed to stop this... dependance on Francis, crying in his arms and such.
It was ill-advised, to say the least.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The funeral of Lieutenant Gore and Sergeant Bryant was as grand an affair as they could
make it. During the rapidly shortening hours of daylight, James led the Terrors, save for
Francis and Mr. Collins, over the ice to Erebus, where there were two coffins, one empty.
James didn't get a chance to speak to Sir John before the service, and so he just stood next to
their leader while he eulogised Graham and the Sergeant.
Sir John spoke of both, and James especially felt his grief well up when he told of the good
times they had with Graham at the beginning of their expedition.
It wasn't fair, that he should have suffered a death like that.
James looked at all the other's faces, the Lieutenants, Stanley and Goodsir, Des Voeux,
McDonald. Somewhere at the back of the crowd, the countenance of Mr. Hickey.
James had forgotten to ask Francis about him, but it now seemed fairly obvious that Francis
had seen him plan a mutiny in the future.

What desperate portend would drive him to do so?
Would they simply run out of rum or was there something different afoot, something too
terrible to contemplate?

TWO MONTHS LATER
James was deep into Erebus's stores, opening crate after crate, each seemingly holding more
useless items than the last.
Francis wanted to walk out of here, that James knew by now. Because thaw wouldn't come.
They would have to leave all of this behind, if they went. The napkins and the glasses and the
books...
The books made James think of the Complete Works of Shakespeare, still lying in his cabin
on Terror. He had read a lot in them in the last days, as he had lost interest in the tales of
other Arctic expeditions.
In the time immediately after Francis's revelation, James had read them obsessively, trying to
find the component that defined their success or failure.
He also tried to find comfort in the fact that all of these expeditions had in the end returned,
some with significantly less men, but they had returned.
In the end, rather like now, he didn't discover what he was looking for.
The reassurance that they would make it.
Sir John was full of such reassurances every time they talked.
"I do wonder where all your good cheer has gone. I'm worried about you, James. You insist
that Francis isn't to blame for your turn of mind, but to be honest, I see no other
possibilities.", he had said recently.
"It's not Francis who changed my mind, but this place. And the... bear that attacked us."
James had stopped himself from saying the word "monster", knowing Sir John had
expressedly forbidden it. He couldn't do much to stop the rumors from going around the
crews of both ships - though they were louder on Erebus than on Terror - except remind the
men in his sermons that monsters didn't exist in the Arctic, no matter what Captain Crozier
said about the leviathan.
It was for another such talk with Sir John that James had walked over, that and an errant
Francis had send him on.
James had almost forgotten it in his frustration with their esteemed leader. Sir John didn't
want to admit that his expedition was a failure, no matter what James argued.

Goodsir and McDonald hadn't been able to convince him, either -there he'd had Dr. Stanley
like a devil on his shoulder, arguing against them, and James had an inkling that Goodsir
liked to stay on Terror not just to communicate with the Netsilisk.
The woman and her father would leave soon, now that her shoulder was better. Francis
wanted them to stay, for reasons he didn't make clear to James, but he wouldn't force them.
James was nearly as frustrated with Francis as with Sir John, though for different reasons.
It was obvious that Francis was keeping something monumental from him, and all that
stopped James from outright confronting Francis was his own fear of what Francis would say.
He was afraid it would have to do with his dreams, his own slow and agonising death.
Still, James was right now stuck between Francis and Sir John in a way he was coming to
despise. Sir John had made mention of him returning to Erebus soon now that Francis's leg
had improved, and the only reason James stalled was that he feared that would make it worse.
There had been no repeat of their physical intimacy, another thing that caused tension
between them.
James could by now not deny that he desired Francis, desired him more than he had ever had
anything in his life it felt like. They would sometimes look at each other, both knowing what
the other was thinking, and it had recently been enough to get James hard, which was
inconvenient for many reasons.
James felt like he was stuck, and of course he was stuck, like they all were, in the ice.
Something had to happen.
With determination, James opened another crate, and found none other than a bunch of
Carnivale costumes. Sir John had hidden them well, but not well enough for James.
He should just note what they were and move on, but the twinkling fabrics and elaborate
masks beckoned seductively. James rummaged around in the crate, pulling stuff out rather
like someone dying of hunger would look for food.
He found multiple dresses, each more beautiful than the last.
He held up one made out of red velvet and nervously licked his lips. Did he dare...?
The last time he had worn a dress had been as Calpurnia on the St Vincent. The men had
bought him the dress in port -someone, James would never find out who, had provided
money. They wanted him and his friend David who played Portia to look the part, like
"proper ladies".
James knew he had enjoyed the whole thing more than a real man ought to.
It had taken a while to get used to the petticoats flowing around him, and of course, he had
needed help with the corset.

The men had cheered for him when he'd appeared on stage, and then had cheered a great deal
more at the end when he bowed.
James hadn't been drunk, but he decidedly felt that way after everything. For the first time in
his life, he didn't have to hide.
It was paradoxical, since he had outwardly been wearing a disguise, but he felt like himself in
that dress, like someone he wanted to be and was.
He had kept the dress on the rest of the evening, let them call him "Lady Fitzjames" and bow
to him.
He knew that some of them had looked at him with lust in their eyes, yes, some had even
downright flirted with him.
It was all a mere game, of course. But for James, it had been reality.
Now, he looked at this dress, and the impulse to wear it was almost overwhelming. He took it
in both hands, the velvet whispering seductively.
He could wear it at the Carnivale, of course.
But that was still a long time away, they were in the midst of deep winter, now.
James sighed, and just as he made up his mind he heard footsteps behind him. Not, now, then,
the mask needed to come back on.
His traitorous hands though bundled up the dress and stowed it in his pouch to take with him
to Terror.
"I had been told I might find you here, sir.", Dr. Stanley said as he appeared in the door.
James straightened. "Hello, Stephen. You were looking for me?"
Stanley nodded. "I came to ask you if there is anything you require, Sir John said that you
were not the best in health."
James regarded his friend, wondering what Stanley was really thinking. James had not
forgiven him for taking Sir John's side against Goodsir, even though he puzzled over
Stephen's motives for doing so.
Stanley was smart, a doctor with experience and he knew what danger lead poisoning
represented.
"I don't think Sir John meant my bodily well-being, Stephen.", James said. "I don't need your
expertise as a doctor."
"As a friend, then?", Stephen asked carefully.

James knew by now that there were certain things one didn't talk about with Stephen Stanley,
for these subjects made him deeply uncomfortable.
"You must be feeling very guilty, then, to offer me a shoulder to cry on.", James said dryly.
Stephen drew himself up. "I don't feel guilty. I'm simply worried about you, sir."
"You would do better to be worried about this expedition as a whole."
That said, James turned back to his inventory.
"I trust Sir John. He is our leader. He knows the Arctic best out of all of us. Why would you
cause yourself needless grief by disagreeing with him?"
James looked at Stephen, who seemed almost desperate in that tightly controlled way of his.
"Because even Sir John Franklin can be wrong.", James murmured.
"But he isn't. He can't be."
I dream of death, every night., James wanted to say. I know that we're doomed, or more
importantly, I can feel it.
This wouldn't convince Stephen, James was aware.
"There is one thing you could do for me.", he said out loud, changing the subject.
"Sir?"
"You could give me a list of all the medical remedies you have. Dr McDonald is looking to
match our combined stores."

you told me. He is certainly closer to you than he ever was to Sir John, besides, he would be

"I still want him to stay out of it.", Francis said. "I won't involve him until I absolutely have
to."
"That's foolish, Frank. If he finds out some other way, you can't control what he might do."
Francis didn't reply and stared angrily at his hands.
"It's because you love him, isn't it?", Thomas said.
Francis sighed. "I promised him to get him out alive, Thomas. I couldn't keep that promise in
the other time, but I'll be damned if I don't keep it here.", he murmured. "It might be foolish,
it might be selfish, but I have to do it this way."
Blanky sighed. "You're fighting a losing battle there. But I won't quarrel with you. Just be
aware that as long as he doesn't know, you have to treat him as if he is on Sir John's side, an
obstacle for us to overcome. Which means, you have to send him back to Erebus."
Francis felt pain in his heart, as he knew that James would see such a request as rejection, but
Thomas was right.
If he wanted James safe, he needed to commit to it.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
So Thomas had been recruited. Next on the list was Dr. McDonald, and Francis already knew
that he needed to find a different strategy with him.
Thankfully, Dr. McDonald was acquainted with the realities of the Arctic, and he knew how
serious their situation was.

Before he could look for the doctor however, James appeared in the great cabin, just as he
and Thomas stepped out of Francis's cabin.
He was clad in just his socks, so he hadn't found the boot Neptune had stolen yesterday.
"Francis, I need to speak with you. In private.", James said urgently.
"It couldn't wait until you were dressed?", Thomas asked in an amused tone.
"Neptune stole my boot.", James explained.
"I know. He brought it to me.", Thomas said. "Very odd, because it didn't look like Neptune

Francis shot the Ice Master a warning look.
James huffed. "And why, pray tell, haven't you returned the boot to me?"
"I brought it to your cabin as soon as the hour was decent.", Blanky said. "You weren't there,

"I was searching the entire ship!"
Before anyone could say something more, Goodsir knocked on the door and came in.
"There is a matter, Captain, I wish to talk to you about. It concerns the Netsilisk."
Technically, James was of higher rank and should be heard first, but the Netsilisk were for

When Blanky made to leave as well, Goodsir stopped him. "You should hear it too, as you

Goodsir swallowed and nodded as well. "So I thought, that perhaps- perhaps we could make

It was an ingenious idea, of course. One Francis himself should've had, really.

Thomas and Francis exchanged a look. They were both aware of the glaring obstacle to this

James stopped them on their way to Sickbay, boots on this time.

"Can't it wait?", Francis asked. "Dr. Goodsir has actually formulated a plan to-"
"I'm sure it's riveting, but I need to talk to you.", James said urgently. "Just us two. Right

Thomas gave him a meaningful look over James's shoulder. Francis already felt horrible

"What happened?"

with Mr. Hickey?"
Of all the things Francis had expected, this hadn't been it.
"I do.", he said. "Why-"
"And you said you knew Mr. Hickey was committing sodomy on this very ship-"
Francis was alarmed. "I only knew it because of my... second sight, not because-"
"I'm aware.", James interrupted him. "Well. I caught Hickey. Committing sodomy on this
ship."
"Ah."
Francis cursed inwardly. Why couldn't these people at least be smart enough not to get caught
when breaking the law?
"I don't know what to do.", James continued in a panicked voice.
It took Francis a moment to understand James's problem. Of course, James wouldn't want
anyone to get punished for sodomy, lashed or even worse, hanged. But if he said nothing, he
was making himself culpable. Hickey might wonder, when there were no consequences for
his actions, why exactly the Commander hadn't told on him.
It would be another matter if Hickey were a kind-hearted man, but Francis had told James
about the mutiny in the future, thinking that in regards to Hickey, James not only deserved an
explanation, it also wouldn't do any harm.

It might even distract James from Francis's plans for Sir John, Francis had thought.
"It's best you do nothing.", Francis said, in what he hoped was a reassuring tone. "Let me
worry about it."
"Francis, I-", James stuttered, then gathered himself. "I've always had to hide part of myself. I
don't know which was worse, the fact of my illegitimate birth or that I'm an invert, but both

"He won't." Francis put both hands on James shoulders, leaning his cane against the table.
"Listen to me, James. He won't. I will make sure of it."
James's eyes searched Francis's face, afraid. "How?"
"Well, first of all, you did report Hickey, didn't you? You did your duty. I know now. Any
actions that are or are not taken are my responsibility. Feel free to tell Hickey that, should he
have the nerve to approach you."
James cradled Francis's jaw, caressing his cheek with his thumb. "I don't want you in danger,

Francis felt a lump in his throat at the earnestness of James's gaze, the love it held. He
couldn't help himself and pressed a small kiss to the other's lips.
"I won't be. I have an idea how to deal with him. Trust me."
"I hope you know what you're doing.", James said in a rush. "I don't want to see you hanged,
Francis, or even lashed. I couldn't bear it."
Francis was utterly taken aback at this worry about his person. He realised, while he may
have given up on suicide, he still didn't rate his life particularly highly in the grand scheme of
things.
It touched him deeply that James worried about him the same way Francis did for James.
"It won't happen.", Francis promised him. "As I said, I have a plan."
Francis wasn't lying. Slowly, a picture began to form inside his head. It was risky, foolish,
perhaps, but if he was successful he could rid himself of two problems in one stroke.
James pressed his forehead against Francis, breathing a kiss to his cheek. Francis closed his
eyes and pulled James closer, unable to help himself.
"I take it you won't tell me your plan.", James murmured.
"It's not exactly conventional.", Francis whispered back. "The less you know, the better."
"Hm." James drew back, eyeing Francis. "You don't want to kill him anymore, do you?
Especially not for-"

"No, James. I won't be unjust.", Francis said.
Francis wasn't lying. There were still moments -few and far between- when he hated Hickey
so much that he wanted kill him with his bare hands. Not so much for the mutiny, he had to
admit, but for robbing James's corpse, which was the lesser crime, he knew. Still, he couldn't
help feeling this way.
But it had been a while since he had stayed in the other time, and in this one Hickey had as of
yet done nothing wrong.
Francis could still hear James telling him that it would be unjust to punish Hickey for crimes
he hadn't committed yet, and knew he was right.
And the sodomy didn't and shouldn't bother him, as in that department he wasn't any better
than Hickey himself.
"I must confess, it amazes me that you have lived so well in the navy with such a great risk
hanging over your head.", Francis said to James.
"I could say the same to you. I know I wasn't the first man in your bed."
Francis cleared his throat. "That may be true, but I was very young when I last... indulged. I
thought women were safer after that, on the whole."
"Well, I've never had any interest in women.", James admitted. "And in a way, the navy helps
with that. Few people ask why I'm not married. The ones that do are satisfied with the usual
explanations."
Since the beginning, Francis had been wondering why James didn't seem to have a
sweetheart. When James had told him, in the other time, he really should've put two and two
together.
"How did you know? About me?", Francis asked.
James gave a gentle scoff. "You weren't exactly subtle in your affections, Francis. Especially
not for someone like me."
"Someone like you?"
"Trained to read gazes and gestures like a book. Studying actions and reactions, most of all it
is someone I care for as well."
Francis stole another kiss, heedless of what he should do instead. James kissed back, opening
his lips, and suddenly Francis was holding on for dear life as they devoured each other's
mouths.
"I missed you tonight.", James said between kisses.
"Me too, my darling." The words were out of Francis's mouth before he could call them back.

Really, Francis mused, he was bad at being honest with James, but equally bad at staying
away from him.
James backed away a little. "It was Billy Gibson, by the way. The one with Hickey."
"I'd figured.", Francis said.
"How? Did you have a vision of them having sex or something?", James asked, a curious
mixture of fascinated and repulsed.
"Nothing so crass. It's just that Gibson was involved in the mutiny, and consequently there
were... will be rumors about them."
James nodded, thoughtful.
Francis knew he had to get James out of here before he went back on his plan to send him
back to Erebus for good.
"James, why don't you go and send me Mr. Hickey? I'd like to have a talk with him."

Chapter 23: Confessions of a Caulker's Mate
Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Someone who the men will listen to, someone who will tell you what is going on with them,
and who has no moral qualms about your plan, but nevertheless will stay loyal...
Francis heard Thomas's words in his head as Cornelius Hickey took a stance before him. He
didn't look particularly afraid, or penitent, not that Francis had expected such a thing.
Francis stayed sitting down, and he was reminded of when Hickey had stood before him after
abducting Lady Silence back to the ship in the other time.
By God, he had deserved the lash, but Francis also knew with hindsight that the harsh
punishment had been a mistake.
It certainly hadn't made Hickey more obedient, just apparently awakened his thirst for
revenge.
"You know why you're here, Mr. Hickey?", Francis asked.
"I haven't the slightest idea, sir.", Hickey replied. "I had thought that you had tired of talking
to me, Captain."
Francis made sure his face betrayed nothing. "I simply found that I didn't need your expertise
anymore."
Hickey smiled, perhaps aiming for cocky, but it looked more like a nervous gesture. "And
you need it again now?"
"In a manner of speaking.", Francis said.
He paused, wondering at the last part of Thomas's words. Of course, loyalty was something
that didn't come easy to Hickey. And Francis doubted that he had reached the caulker's mate
with any of his sermons. Hickey was neither God-fearing nor respected authority.
"How badly do you want to go home, Mr. Hickey?"
Hickey looked taken aback by the question, since he had probably expected to be called out
for committing sodomy.
"Well, sir, I mostly signed up for this voyage because I wanted to get away from home, to be
honest."
Not surprising.
"How badly do you want to live, then?", Francis asked.

Hickey raised his eyebrows in surprise. "Are things that dire?"
"Things are always that dire in the Arctic. But there are a few matters that the crew is not
aware of, which considerably lower our chances."
"What matters, sir?", Hickey said.
Francis gave a scoff. "You expect me to tell you that?"
This was a mistake. Francis could see the anger flashing across Hickey's face right before he
hid it.
"I have a problem, Mr. Hickey.", Francis continued in a kinder tone. "I don't know if I can
trust you. I would like to, but I don't know."
Francis watched as Hickey obviously tried to puzzle out the meaning behind this meeting.
"Well.", Hickey said. "You could just blackmail me, Captain Crozier."
"What you would do, no doubt?"
This time, Hickey smiled again. "What anyone would do."
"I want your trust and your loyalty, Mr. Hickey. I can hardly earn it by blackmailing you."
Francis wondered, though, if perhaps that was precisely the way to earn it, or at least
Hickey's respect.
"I thought you expect our trust and loyalty to be a given.", Hickey said.
"As Captain, I should be entitled to it. But we both know that things aren't always as they
should be."
Hickey frowned. "I suppose you want me to prove my loyalty to you, sir?"
"I'm going to tell you something in the strictest confidence. And I'll tell you right now, I will
know if you even so much as breathe a word of this to someone else."
"Why?", Hickey asked immediately.
"Because I need your help. That's all I can reveal for now."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Cornelius Hickey would've laughed in the Captain's face if he didn't have a better handle on
himself than that.
The Captain needed his help. His help.
This had to be some kind of joke.

When Fitzjames had sought him out in the mess and told him to report to the Captain, Hickey
had thought that his good luck had finally run out, and he would have to answer to charges of
sodomy.
They were serious about that sort of thing in the Navy, that much Hickey knew from Billy,
who had been freaking out in that quiet way of his ever since Fitzjames had caught them.
Hickey had honestly thought that Fitzjames wouldn't report them. At least he told Billy that.
Hickey still remembered the conversation he'd had with the Commander, months ago now,
where Fitzjames had honestly all but asked him if the Captain was sleeping with him.
What had been so confounding about that was that Fitzjames seemed to have asked out of
genuine concern for his wellbeing, not to punish him or any other ulterior motive.
Hickey should've known that it was too good to be true. No one ever cared about the likes of
him, especially not someone who was high up in that stupid, arbitrary system of rank ships
had.
Hickey had thought going to sea would make him free; instead, he was toiling at the bottom
of the same empty system of authority that existed on land.
More so, even, because if there was one thing these Navy people were obsessed with it was
rank; as if they all didn't shit through the same hole on deck; and now didn't freeze their
bollocks off at the same rate of they stayed outside for too long.
Well, it was Hickey's own mistake for not doing enough research beforehand. He hadn't had
the time, honestly. He had needed to get out of a bad situation and so he had done what he'd
always done: take the next available route that ensured his survival.
He had heard people talk about going out to sea before. It had seemed like last ditch, but
downright romantic option for someone who didn't make it on land.
It turned out that the people he'd heard talking were either all liars or they had been in for as
badly a surprise as he; out at sea, not everyone was equal, and free, and having great
adventures all the time.
Hickey did what he had done since he was thirteen years old and working in a canning
factory; working for the rich, the lucky ones, the better off.
He didn't understand how someone like Billy could actually be hired just to dress them up
like peacocks and shave them and carry off their shit, when Hickey himself was feeling
mutinous just caulking leaks that would cause everyone to drown if he didn't do it.
And there weren't even out on the open sea anymore, but frozen in ice for the second time in
a row. Which wouldn't be so bad (Hickey had been surprised at the bad case of seasickness
fate had dealt him when they'd set off, partly because he had thought seasickness was a myth,
partly because even if it wasn't, he thought he would be strong enough to resist it), had
Hickey not hated it on this ship in general.

He got along reasonably well with the crew, the ones low enough to associate with him, at
least, but their sheep-like acceptance of the Captain's authority irked him greatly.
Hickey wondered what made the Captain such a special man, that he deserved people's
loyalty like that.
At the canning factory, at least all the workers had been in agreement that their overseer was
an arsehole.
But the venerated Captain Crozier was apparently some kind of God, hardly present though
he had been until his decision to stop reading the Ship's Articles at Sunday Service and
instead grace the crew with his own words.
He was a good speaker, that much even Hickey would admit, though he had little room in his
head for all that Bible shit, as his brother used to call it.
And one couldn't even mention anything amiss about Sir John Franklin, their glorious leader
who apparently shat silver nuggets, or else Hickey couldn't think of an explanation why that
man was so loved.
Anyway, Hickey had told Billy, who was already seeing the lash rain down on him, that
Fitzjames was far too soft-hearted to ever report them -and there could perhaps be some kind
of opening that he could later use for his own purposes- and even so, there were worse things
than being lashed.
Of course, Hickey had never been lashed, but he had endured pain before, pain from getting
beaten, pain from hunger, pain from broken bones...
He hadn't told Billy that, of course, and even if he had Billy would've hardly heard him, lost
as he was in his personal world of anguish.
When Fitzjames had come to get him, his eyes steel and his lips pressed together, Hickey had
just felt a sort of resigned urge to laugh.
Hickey knew that Fitzjames and the Captain were close, and that it had not always been this
way.
Apparently now, they were reading books together when before, they had barely tolerated
each other's presence. There was still room for misunderstandings, apparently, as evidenced
by the time Fitzjames had asked Hickey if he was being abused.
Hickey could only sneer at it now, but that had been the first time in his life anyone had cared
about such a thing. Of course it would turn out to be false, no, far more interesting were the

Could it be that Crozier had some kind of reputation, in elite circles? Was he known for
seducing his subordinates?
Hickey had seen such things before, though so far had escaped that particular kind of
attention. It happened to women more often, of course, women who couldn't afford to be

decent.
Decency was another thing that belonged to Hickey's betters, to be doled out as they saw fit.

Naturally, Hickey had lapped up the Captain's attention like a starved dog and later hated

Billy had been relieved. He had said that only bad things could come from an arrangement

"Don't get yourself into such trouble, Cornelius."
Well, now they were both in trouble. Hickey didn't fear the lash, if he was honest, but he

Hickey had been surprised when Billy hadn't been in the Great Cabin, standing before the

He had then scolded himself for his surprise; Billy might be soft, but he was also crafty. He

Really, one couldn't imagine his surprise when Crozier turned the whole exchange into a

What new game is this?, Hickey thought. Am I about to be used in some intrigue among the

If so, he had to find some kind of way to turn it around on them, so that he wasn't the one

He still was sure that Crozier would blackmail him. It was obvious that he knew about the

But instead of doing that, Crozier told him that their provisions were, to a large extent,

Part of this joke Crozier couldn't be in on, however.

"Someone should stay with him to hold him down if he convulses.", Goodsir said. "I'm going

Blanky and Fitzjames looked at each other, while Hickey looked at the Captain, fascinated.
His eyes were open, staring into nothing. Hickey wondered what he was seeing.
"Well, I'm going to pack my things.", Fitzjames said coldly, very at odds with his emotional
reaction from before. "I trust you have it well in hand, Mr. Blanky?"
"Aye."
It seemed like Blanky wanted to say more, but he stopped himself.
Fitzjames nodded curtly and left.
Hickey made himself scarce as well. He really hoped that the Captain wasn't dying, after
everything that happened.
Hickey wanted to know what Crozier's mysterious plan was, and he also now had some very
real dirt on him.
Hickey was sure that Sir John wouldn't exactly be delighted to find out that his Second and
Third were fucking each other.
And really, who did Fitzjames think he was, to tell on Hickey for crime he himself
committed, with the Captain himself, no less?
It had all been plain and simple jealousy, Fitzjames's whole show of concern for him.
More fool you are for falling for it, Hickey thought.
He indulged himself for a moment with the image of Crozier and Fitzjames, lashed for their
disobedience.
But no, Hickey was sure that Sir John wouldn't do that. It would hurt the command structure
more than help it, and after all, these people protected their own.
Hickey decided to search for Billy, to at least calm him down a bit, now that Hickey knew
that probably no punishment was forthcoming.
In the passageway, he almost collided with Dr. McDonald, on his way to the Captain.
Hickey mumbled an apology and a greeting, but the doctor barely seemed to hear him in his
hurry.
He was just looking after the doctor with a shake of his head, when he literally ran into Billy,
who apparently had been loitering here a while.
Wordlessly, Billy grabbed Hickey by the arm and dragged him into his room.
"And? Will we be lashed?", Billy asked urgently. "I heard you saw the Captain-"
"Yes.", Hickey said, grinning. "I saw the Captain."

"Please don't drag this out, Cornelius, I can barely-"
Hickey had been planning to drag this out, but now he decided not to be cruel. "We won't be
punished.", he said. "At least I don't think so."
"But Fitzjames told the Captain?"
"Yes, but the Captain isn't interested in lashing us."
Billy looked suspicious. "Why?"
Hickey knew that he couldn't tell Billy the truth, he wouldn't risk the secrecy of his
knowledge like that.
"Well, the Captain thinks it's not good for the overall discipline of the crew to have men
lashed at this time. The winter is already hard enough, he said. Let us go with a warning."
Billy still didn't seem convinced. "And why wasn't I present for this?"
"I don't know. Maybe Fitzjames only got me because he thinks I seduced you with my many
wiles, not the other way around."
Billy scoffed, then smiled for the briefest moment. Hickey was reminded that he did owe
Billy a lot, for making this entire voyage more bearable, for making at least part of it fun.
However, Billy wouldn't be able to collect on the debt if he didn't know it was there.
"We have to stop, you know.", Billy said.
"Why that?"
"Seriously, Cornelius? Getting caught by a Commander isn't enough for you?"
Hickey was about to say that said Commander knew quite a bit about sodomy himself, but he
stopped himself. As much as he wanted to tell Billy, and thought it would be hilarious if it
was all over the ship by noon, he could hardly blackmail the two lovebirds later with
something that was common knowledge.
"We'll just have to be more careful.", Hickey said with a shrug.
"Yes, and most careful of all is if we don't do it all."
Hickey smiled and crossed his arms. "You really want to give this up? After being such a
good wife to me?"
Billy pressed his lips together. "Stop it, Cornelius."
Hickey took Billy's hand, opened it, and pressed a kiss to his palm. Billy snatched his hand
back.
"It's too dangerous.", he insisted.

"Alright, alright.", Hickey said, thinking that Billy probably needed a little time to recover
from the shock. Then he would come crawling back for sure. "By the way, did you know that
the Captain had some kind of fit just now?"
Billy frowned. "So that's why Dr. McDonald came running... No, I didn't. Is it very serious?"
"Serious enough that he probably doesn't give a shit who Fitzjames caught doing what.",
Hickey said with a meaningful eyebrow-raise.
"Be that as it may, he will remember once he's recovered."
"If he recovers.", Hickey said.
Billy looked at him, shocked. "You don't believe the Captain is in mortal danger, do you?"
"Well, it was unnerving to be sure. He just lay there with his eyes open, unseeing, like a
corpse. Do you know of a disease that does that?"
Billy shook his head. "That sounds serious indeed. Maybe he's having some kind of vision?"
"If he does, I hope it's of a worse place than this one.", Hickey said.

Chapter End Notes

Actually, it's not advised to hold epileptic patients down when they have a seizure, but
I'm sure that was seen differently in Victorian times.

Chapter 24: Francis
Francis opened his eyes to see Goodsir looking down on him. Not the studious, optimistic
Goodsir of the past, but, as his beard showed, a much more sober Goodsir of the future.
Still, Francis smiled, even as he felt like crying.
"It's good to see you, doctor.", he murmured.
Goodsir shook his head slightly, deeply sad. "It seems you fainted, Captain. Do you know
where you are?"
Francis looked around. He was in a tent, away from the ships, obviously. Goodsir was at him
with a wet cloth.
"Hickey's camp?", Francis asked.
Goodsir nodded and continued to clean his wounds.
"I thought- I didn't dare hope- that I was done with this.", Francis murmured.
James was dead again, of course, the men scattered. Francis thought of how he had sent
James away in the other time. It seemed cruel, towards James and also towards himself, when
thought about from this perspective.
No, I'm done! I will leave for Erebus, gladly! Do whatever you want, but don't believe for a
second that I still care about you!
Francis closed his eyes briefly. He could still hear James's voice so clearly, how could it be
that he was dead for days here, his corpse robbed and desecrated...
"Done with what?", Goodsir asked.
Francis shook his head to clear it. He tried to stay in the present, if only to reassure Goodsir.
"I know Lieutenant Little's nature. He will be here by day's end with a dozen armed men. We
need to be ready." Francis looked earnestly at Goodsir, but the doctor didn't meet his eyes. "I
counted eleven men total.", he continued. "What about arms? Who carries them?"
Goodsir was silent a moment, then he said: "Tozer. Benson. Armitage. Pilkington. Gibson-"
He stopped, considering. "No, no. Gibson is gone as well. I think Des Voeux has his gun
now."
A terrible feeling of foreboding gripped Francis. Still, he asked: "Gone? Do you mean he ran
off?"
"Dead, sir... and consumed.", Goodsir said.

Ah. Francis absorbed this, stone-faced. He wondered if he had heard such a thing at the
beginning of the expedition, he would've recoiled in horror. Now, it only seemed the
chillingly logical conclusion when there was no food left.
Had he not suspected? Was that not the reason he had been so angry at Hickey, because deep
down he knew what else he and the others had done to James's body, besides stealing his
boots?
"I'm sorry, sir, however unpleasant it is to hear, I must put what is going on here into words.",
Goodsir said.
Francis swallowed. "Five guns, then. You're certain?"
"We thought the creature was at the ridge to our north three days ago. Hickey ordered every
man out to face it... and I counted five."
Did Hickey think they could kill Tuunbaq with a mere five guns? Francis didn't like the idea
that Hickey should have such a plan, and he was aware that Hickey was planning something,
and it had to do with him, too.
"Well done.", Francis told Goodsir, patting his arm. "Well done."
Goodsir merely nodded, the dejected expression not leaving his face. Then he stood and
fumbled with his pouch.
"If the chance to run comes and we're not together... go southeast, yes?"
Goodsir turned back to him and held his hand up, showing Francis a golden ring. He asked
Francis to deliver it to a girl in London, and it was at that point that Francis knew that
Goodsir had given up on getting out of any of this alive.
"You will deliver it yourself-"
"I will not leave this camp, Captain. I know that."
Francis was aware that Goodsir's pessimism was more than justified, but he still tried to rouse
him: "You mustn't lose heart. I need your help, doctor."
"If ever I was a doctor, I am one no longer.", Goodsir said.
Francis felt his heart break for this man, as it did for all the men still alive, even the
mutineers. What did this place turn them into by the end of it?
"Even if God sees every last thing we do here, you have nothing to fear. You're clean,
Goodsir. Even as your hand is forced by swine."
Goodsir again shook his head slightly. "Is God here, Captain? Any God?"
Francis didn't know. Previously, he had seen the beauty of the Arctic as proof of God's
existence, as well as his cruelty.

But in this time, even God's cruelty seemed to have abandoned them. There was no biblical
justice in this, slow dying, being forced to break every rule of decency and civilisation.
"It doesn't matter.", Goodsir answered his own question. "You know, this place is beautiful to
me even now. To see it with eyes as a child's... There is wonder here, Captain."
Then Goodsir asked after Lady Silence, and at least there Francis could reassure the man.
Francis was certain that she had made it back to her people by now, the people they had so
wronged.
Francis and Goodsir looked at each other, and Francis had the sudden, eerie feeling that they
were saying goodbye.
"I'll deliver it if I can.", he said, indicating the ring. "To whom did it belong?"
But Goodsir had evidently forgotten the name. Before they could talk more of it, or Francis
could search his own memory -so many dead men... - Magnus Manson appeared in the
entrance to the tent.
"Your color is better now.", he said with a shy smile.
Francis supposed that out of the many ways one could meet the Captain one had mutinied
against, this was one of the better ones.
"Thank you, Manson."
After Manson had disappeared again, Goodsir entreated him to only eat of his feet, should he
be forced to.
Francis wanted to protest, he didn't want to make it end like this, but there was no time.
Pilkington came to take him away, and he had one last glimpse of Goodsir, turning away.
The ring burned and imprint into his fist.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Hickey sat in the middle of his tent, waiting for him. Francis looked at him and wondered.
His bout of impotent rage at Hickey had abated, and now all he thought of was how he could
prevent Hickey from getting this far in the other time.
"We'll be settling down for sick nap, soon. But come and sit for a moment, Mr. Crozier.",
Hickey said. "I've been looking forward to this."
Francis was loathe to lower himself to Hickey's level, literally, but he did as he was bidden.
"Why not let Lieutenant Hodgson go back?", Francis asked. "Here's some men that could use
his leadership. Mr. Diggle, Manson, Dr. Goodsir..."
Francis trailed off, because he felt the treacherous rushing in his ears again. Goddammit, not
now! He couldn't faint away now, in front of Mr. Hickey! This was too important, and he was

loathe to think of what Hickey would do to him if he was deemed "too infirm".
Hickey gave a small smile. "Lieutenant Hodgson was the first of your officers I enlisted.", he
said. "I remember the day..."
Francis struggled to listen for what else Hickey said. He felt dizzy, and the rushing in his ears
increased.
"Well, I forgive him.", Francis forced out. "All of them, but you..."
"Do you include yourself in that forgiveness?", Hickey asked.
"I won't know until-" Francis stopped. The pull of the other time was overwhelming, and he
couldn't resist anymore.
Why did he resist, anyway? He wanted to be back with James so badly. He wanted to see
Thomas again. He needed"Are you alright, Mr. Crozier?" Hickey's voice, as if from very far away.
Francis closed his eyes, just for a moment...
~~~~~~~~~~~~
When he opened them again he was back in his berth on Terror, Thomas and Dr. McDonald
staring down on him.
Francis blinked and sat up, only to be forced back into the pillows by the doctor.
"Easy now, Captain. You experienced another fit."
"James?", Francis asked, looking around frantically. "Where is he?"
Blanky and Dr. McDonald exchanged a look.
"I will see if he is still here.", Thomas said and left before Francis could demand to know
what he was talking about.
Right, Francis thought. I told him to go away. I sent him back to Erebus.
"What a fool I've been!", Francis exclaimed.
"I'm not going to disagree with that.", Dr. McDonald said dryly. "Especially if you try to get
up again in this state."
Francis barely heard him. It all came crashing down on him, the realisiation. He couldn't keep
James out of it. It was a fool's errand. James had to be part of it, or else he could bring them
all into danger.
The stakes were to high for a dangerous variable like that. By God, in the other time his men
were eating each other!

And Goodsir, poor Goodsir...
"Dr. McDonald? Is everything alright?" There was Goodsir, decidedly less unkempt, but
definitely him, peeking his head through the door.
Francis felt tears well up at the sight of him.
"Harry...", he murmured, and Goodsir looked at him, surprised.
"You stay with him.", Dr. McDonald said to Goodsir. "I'm going to get the laudanum."
"I'm not taking any laudanum!", Francis groused, but Dr. McDonald either didn't hear or
chose to ignore him.
"Captain...", Goodsir began. "How can I help you?"
"Just stay, here.", Francis murmured.
Goodsir nodded and took his hand. Francis gave it a firm press that Goodsir returned.
"Did you see anything? While you were out?"
Francis was alarmed. "Why?"
"It's just... what you experience doesn't quite appear like epilepsy, limited though my
experience is.", Goodsir said. "And it always seems that you... witness something, perhaps,
while the fit is occurring."
"I do.", Francis breathed. "God help me, I do."
"Might it help you talk about what it is?", Goodsir asked.
Later, Francis would blame the time jumping for him immediately starting to tell Goodsir the
truth, when James hadn't been able to get it out of him for months.
Goodsir listened as Francis explained as quickly as he could. His reaction, however, was
stopped short by Thomas coming back.
"The Commander already left for Erebus. He took all his things, too."
Francis bolted upright. "I have to get him back."
"You are not going anywhere.", Goodsir said sternly.
"You get him back, then, Thomas.", Francis pleaded. "Thomas, please... I've made such a
huge mistake, but if he hasn't reached Erebus yet there might still be a chance..."
Thomas Blanky gave an almighty sigh. "I could've bloody well told you all that days ago!
And I did, if I remember correctly."
"Thomas, please.", Francis repeated.

He tried to get up again, but Goodsir pushed him firmly back on his bunk.
"And if the beast out on the ice gets me while I'm bringing you back your beloved-"
"Thomas!", Francis hissed.
Goodsir seemed harmless enough, but it was still a risk to have him know that.
"I'm sorry, Thomas, I would go myself- You know what? I am going myself! Where is my
cane?"
This time, Francis didn't let himself be pushed back onto the cot anymore, shoving away
Goodsir's reaching hands.
"Captain, please, you can't-"
"It's alright, Frank, let me go.", Thomas said. "You rest and-"
"No, I need to get him myself!" Francis stood and reached for his cane. "Really, I'm feeling
right as rain!", he told Goodsir.
The problem was, that once James was back on Erebus, it wouldn't be so easy to get him
back, especially if he had no desire to go over himself.
Francis already saw himself in front of James, Sir John in the room of course, desperately
searching for any kind of excuse to be alone with his future Second.
Thankfully, Dr. McDonald seemed to still be scarce on his way to get the laudanum, for
whatever reason.
As Francis grabbed his slops and dressed himself, Goodsir desperately started to ask him
questions. Was he feeling any dizziness? Blackness in front of the eyes? Was he unsteady on
his feet?
Francis grunted a no every time, even though he was partly lying. His stays in the other time
tended to greatly unmoor him, and he didn't feel precisely up for making the crossing
between the two ships, and there was also his leg to consider.
On deck, Thomas rejoined him, likewise wrapped in his slops.
"You don't have to-"
"Someone needs to save you from your own stupidity, Frank, so yes, I absolutely have to.
Also I seem to recall Fitzjames saying something about being the best walker in the service,
so you need someone who can catch up to him."
Since time was of the essence, Francis didn't protest further but carefully started to lower
himself down the side of Terror.

The wind was howling, bringing gales of snow with it, and Francis couldn't even see the part
of Erebus that wasn't obscured by the ice berg.
Thomas carried a lantern, but it was practically useless with all the snow.
Once on the ice, they started walking, and Francis's leg already hurt. He felt as clumsy as
newborn deer on the ice, and hoped that this insecurity would go away if he just kept
walking.
"I'm sorry, Thomas!", he yelled at his friend so he could understand. "I shouldn't have
dragged you into this!"
"That wasn't your mistake. Really, Frank, one of these days I'm going to kick your stupid,
obstinate arse!"
Then, the wind howled too loud for them to talk, and they had to focus all their attention on
walking.
Francis tried not to lose hope at the glacial pace they moved forward. Was James already on
Erebus? Were they too late?
It was barely possible to walk, but Francis refused to consider turning back while the distance
to Terror was still shorter.
The weather was not on their side, however. Francis couldn't see anything, because the wind
was blowing snow into his face, in addition to almost physically pushing him back.
"We need to find shelter!", Thomas yelled into his ear. "We can't have you falling out here in
the shale!"
Thomas was right, unfortunately. Francis was limping badly, and his leg hurt like hell.
"Back to Terror?", Francis called, resigned.
"No, the berg is closer!", Thomas returned.
At least that's what Francis thought he heard, one couldn't really understand the other in this
storm.
Francis put his entire energy into his next step, another, and another.
He couldn't think about James anymore, he only knew that if he fell, he wouldn't be getting
up.
Every time he thought he would fall, he was somehow able to go on another step. And then
Thomas dragged him into the shadow of the berg, and his back hit the solid wall of ice.
Slowly, some of Francis's vision returned, and he made out the shape of the ridge he was
leaning against, and Thomas, next to him.

Their shelter provided a respite from the wind, and now that snow wasn't blowing in his face
constantly, Francis felt a little better.
And he saw...
With a frown, he took Thomas's lantern, which miraculously hadn't gone out, and squinted
into the darkness.
Another figure was huddled against the berg, wearing a familiar pair of slops.
Francis could've wept with relief.
"James!", he called, wanting to approach him, but his leg finally gave out from under him,
and next thing he knew he was sitting arse-first on the ice.
"Francis?" James came over and crouched before him. "Good grief, what are you doing out
here?!"
"Getting you back!"
James stared at Francis in complete surprise, that even Francis could see though most of
James's face was covered.
"Good to see you, Commander.", Blanky called. "We were despairing that you had already
reached Erebus."
"The storm surprised me.", James said. "Francis, you shouldn't- not with your leg- what in the
hell were you thinking?"
"James, I'm sorry.", Francis said desperately. "I made a huge mistake, I shouldn't have lied to
you, shouldn't have sent you away... But I do love you. It's why I wanted to protect you from
the truth-"
"Frank, maybe this isn't the best venue for this.", Thomas gave to consider.
Francis took James by the shoulders and leaned close. He didn't know how much of his
words James had understood, so he said again: "I love you. And I'm going to tell you the
truth."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Before Francis could do that, though, they had to get him back to Terror.
At least James said that he would go back with them, though he seemed more than a little
confused.
After the storm had let up, Francis tried to stand, with the help of his cane. Getting upright
was the most difficult part, even with help from both Thomas and James.
In the end, he leaned on James as he walked, with Thomas carrying James's things.

It got a little brighter, and one could see the stars, distant and reliable. Francis felt bad about
leaning on James, as well as needing any help, but there was no time to complain.
"I have a feeling that Dr. McDonald is going to rip my head off when we return.", Francis
said, looking at Terror's lights coming ever so slowly closer.
"He'll have to get in line.", Thomas replied.
Francis was so overcome with guilt that he couldn't even think of an answer besides another
apology.
Somehow, they made it back to ship without Francis collapsing, though his leg gave out from
under him again after he heaved himself over the railing.
So Francis had to subject himself to the indignity of being carried back to his bunk, where a
very irate Dr. McDonald waited for him, together with a sheepish Dr. Goodsir.
As Jopson got him out of his slops, he listened to Dr. McDonald berating him, knowing he
deserved every word.
James, of course, absolutely refused to leave his side, giving no indication of his own
feelings.
Their parting had been ugly, but there was also the tenderness of all their other moments
together.
"If you don't want to take laudanum, Captain, you have to promise me that you will rest
now.", Dr. McDonald said sternly. "I will place Mr. Jopson as a guard at your side, if I have
to."
"I would do that duty.", James said before Francis could reply.
James was standing next to Francis’s head with his arms crossed, not looking at Francis at all.
Dr. McDonald was more than willing to accept James's offer, and since Francis longed to be
alone with James he didn't protest overly much.
Before he left with everyone else, Thomas clapped Francis on the shoulder and whispered to
him: "Don't muck it up!"

Chapter 25: James
James Fitzjames was once again very confused.
Again, the source of that confusion was Francis.
Francis, who had run over a frozen sea in a storm with a nearly healed broken leg to get him
back, and right after some kind of seizure too.
Their fight before had been vicious, and James had been deeply hurt by Francis sending him
back to Erebus.
Somewhere along the way he had also gotten the suspicion that Francis had only told him he
loved him to distract him, not because it was true.
Then Francis had dropped off again, and James was thrown into a sea of anxiety, at the same
time hating himself for caring.
He couldn't just wait at Francis's bedside, and so he had gone to pack his things with a bitter
taste in his mouth. He had lingered longer than he needed to, waiting for confirmation that
Francis had woken up before starting to make his way over to Erebus with no word of
goodbye.
The storm had surprised him, and at first he had tried to go on regardless, his wounded pride
urging him forward, but he'd had to realise that he couldn't win a battle against nature, against
the full power of the Arctic unleashed.
The berg had been closer than either of the ships, and so he had sought shelter there.
The sight of Francis and Mr. Blanky was like a dream, and James couldn't believe it.
Believed it even less when Francis had said that he loved him, and that he would tell him the
truth. Finally.
James didn't really have a choice but to go back with them, especially with Francis in that
condition.
He decided to give Francis one last chance to explain himself. Just one, that was all he
thought he could manage. He loved Francis, yes, but that was precisely the reason he couldn't
let himself be pushed around or otherwise used by him.
James was already angry at himself for giving up his heart like that, and he almost feared the
connection he had with Francis.
Perhaps it was for the best if they were separated, perhaps that was what was needed for
James to get a handle on himself.

Francis looked absolutely exhausted, but James was done with waiting, as it seemed, was
Francis.
"Sit down, James.", Francis said with a sigh. "But before that, you can perhaps make sure that
no one is in the Great Cabin."
James did, and afterwards settled in Francis's chair.
"So?", he asked, when Francis didn't say anything.
"Give me a moment, James, these words don't come easy to me.", Francis muttered.
He looked so miserable that James longed to reach over and take his hand, but he stopped
himself.
It could be that Francis was just gearing up to lie to him again, and if that was so he didn't
deserve James's forgiveness.
"I should probably start with the fact that I can't see the future.", Francis said.
James was surprised. "But then, how do you-"
"I've lived the future, James. Two years from now, I woke up in the past. The past was here,
this."
"How is that possible?"
"I don't know. I'm just certain that I'm somehow tied to both times. These fits I have... They
aren't epilepsy. Whenever I have one, I fall back into the future. Our future, if we don't stop
it."
James digested this, thinking hard. It explained a lot of the things that had puzzled him, even
though it seemed even more fantastical than mere clairvoyance.
"I got off the whiskey, in the future. I still had my plan to die, but you made me realise that I
needed to be there for the men. You made me realise a whole lot, if I'm honest."
James didn't know what to do with the devotion in Francis's eyes. It wasn't for him, but
another version of him, one that James didn't know.
"Were we... close, in the future?", James asked. "We must have been for me to tell you about
my origins..."
"Not at first." Francis smiled ruefully. "We wasted a whole lot of time antagonizing each
other needlessly. By the time we put that aside, it was almost too late..."
"Too late for what?"
Francis closed his eyes briefly and sighed again. "It's not a future that is good, where I'm
from. I think you already surmised that."

"I did.", James said. "How bad will it be?"
Now, James did reach for Francis's hand, to prepare himself for what was to come.
"Thaw doesn't come. We wait out another winter here... And by that time we're already sick
and mad. Scurvy, lead poisoning, they all eat at us. We try to walk out, but we're too weak.
We starve and we die."
James felt as if he were child, finding out that Father Christmas didn't exist, only a million
times more horrible.
He swallowed. "I see."
"I want to stop it, James. I need to stop it.", Francis said, his eyes wet.
"We need to stop it.", James whispered. "We, Francis."
Francis seemed to overcome to speak.
"Why didn't you tell me this sooner?", James asked. "I would be happy to help you- I would-"
He stopped, considering. "How do you want to do it, precisely? How does the future need to
change?"
"Well, we need to walk out sooner, as I said, to have a fighting chance."
James felt ill suddenly, realising why Francis hadn't told him. He hoped very desperately to
be wrong.
"It's Sir John, isn't it?", James whispered. "He won't agree with your plan..."
Francis nodded, pained.
"But we can still change his mind! There is time, there is-"
"How?", Francis said. He sounded almost gentle, now. "You've been trying, James, and you
have achieved nothing. I've tried. The thing with the lead- I told Goodsir to look for it, in the
hope that Sir John would call off the expedition. He didn't."
James shook his head. "Then perhaps we need to tell him the truth, too. Perhaps then he'll
listen..."
Francis looked at James, deeply sad. "In the other time, after thaw didn't come the second
time, I proposed to Sir John that we sent out a rescue mission. Six men, no more, to get us
rescue for the next year... What followed was not only a personal attack on my person, but a
plain denial that we were in any danger."
"What did he say?", James asked, shifting anxiously in his seat.
"I won't repeat his exact words now, but I do think that you heard them all. In the other time,
as well as now."

James ran a harried hand through his hair. He did know what a low opinion Sir John had of
Francis, no matter how well he cloaked it in politeness. And he also knew how Sir John
refused to see the danger of their situation, of course he did.
"But surely, when things got worse, he realised his mistake?" James's tone was pleading.
"He didn't live to see things get worse. The beast out on the ice killed him in June of this
year. It was too late for all of us to walk out by then, or else I would've attempted it."
James fell back into his chair and closed his eyes, then he abruptly stood up. He wanted to
