Francis had slept, but only because he had given in and used a few drops of laudanum. It was
only the tiredness brought on by the opium that had stopped him from seeking out a glass of
whiskey to wash it all down with.
"You look terrible, Frank.", Thomas said. "I take your reconciliation with your other half
didn't go smoothly?"
"I told him the truth. Everything.", Francis muttered.
Thomas raised his eyebrows. "I see. Do you think he went to Sir John with it?"
"No, I don't think- I don't know. He was very shocked. Kept saying that there had to be
another way."
"You made it clear to him that there isn't?"
"Of course I did!"
Thomas considered for a moment, then said: "I'm sure he'll come around. You need to give
him some time. It isn't ideal, but we'll make do."
"So you don't think I should try to make the crossing again, to talk to him?"

Thomas shook his head. "Not you.", he said. "Let's leave Fitzjames in his corner for a
moment. We need to recruit others besides Hickey."
Francis tore his thoughts away from the subject of James with great difficulty.
"Little, I think will be on our side. Jopson, too."
Thomas nodded. "We need to get to the lads on Erebus, somehow. Perhaps if Fitzjames has
calmed down and joined us, he can be of help there."
Francis didn't want James to recruit people for them. He didn't want James to stain his hands
with blood. Yet he knew he was fighting a losing battle. He had to get over his protectiveness
of James's soul in order to save it and everyone else's.
They decided to call for Jopson and Little together. Francis knew that his stewart and his first
Lieutenant were getting along well, a strange bond existing between them that Francis didn't
quite understand.
He was certainly sure that Edward wouldn't be cross to be recruited with a mere stewart. As
they took their places before him, Francis absently wondered if there would be an
opportunity to give Jopson his promotion in this time as well. No one had ever deserved it
more.
"I won't mince words, not with you.", Francis began. "You know the situation of our stores.
Even you, Jopson?"
Jopson nodded hesitantly.
"Who told you?", Blanky asked.
"Edward- Lieutenant Little did, but it was in the strictest confidence and he knew I would
never repeat it."
Francis told them: "None of you is in trouble for that. It's something else that I want to
discuss, that I want to ask of you. And it won't be pleasant. If you believe that our expedition
isn't in danger, and that we can continue as we are, I advise you to leave this room now. We
will speak no more of it. Should you stay, however, I will be plain."
Edward and Jopson exchanged a look. Neither of them moved.
"Good.", Francis said. "Let's begin, then."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
"We should do it at the Carnivale.", Edward said.
He and Jopson had listened to Francis, with occasional input from Thomas, silently and
without questions.
After a pause, Edward had broken the silence.

"I think so too.", Jopson agreed. "Everyone will be at least a little drunk and wrapped up in
the celebrations. We will wear costumes with some of our faces obscured. We can easily
overwhelm him and make it look like he just slipped on the ice."
"And we have enough time to prepare.", Edward gave to consider.
"So you would... help?", Francis asked, taken aback by their casual loyalty.
Jopson and Little looked at each other again, then both nodded equally curtly.
"The Carnivale is a good idea.", Blanky said. "But of course, the unpredictability of it could
also work to our detriment."
Francis thought of his dream, of dancing with both Jameses and the following violence.
Perhaps it was meant to happen at Carnivale. Another violent end to what was supposed to be
a celebration.
"I think we should try poison first.", Francis said. "It would be good to have a doctor on
Erebus on our side, but that doesn't seem likely."
"I think Dr. Goodsir would help, sir.", Edward said, to Francis's great surprise. "He already
proved what was wrong with the lead. He is very principled, but he has already shown he is
willing to kill when it comes to the greater good of the crew."
"That was a monkey, Edward. I think killing a man is quite a significant step up from that.",
Jopson told him.
"Be that as it may, Dr. Goodsir is back on Erebus, now. We would have to think of a pretext
to visit him.", Blanky said.
"And we will have to do the same with Commander Fitzjames."
Francis winced internally at Edward's words.
"Isn't he already in on it?", Jopson asked.
"Let us worry about the Commander.", Blanky said. "We hope him to be on our side soon."
There was a knock on the door. After they had exchanged significant looks, Francis called an
admission to enter.
It was Lieutenant Hodgson, reporting back from Erebus.
"At the doctor's instructions, I waited until you had rested, Captain.", he said.
"It's alright. We were just done here."
Blanky, Little and Jopson left the cabin, though Jopson said he would be back with tea
momentarily.

It was really remarkable how they acted as if nothing happened, Francis thought.
He then regarded Lieutenant Hodgson. He still remembered Hickey saying: He was the first
of your officers I enlisted.
While it was true that Francis forgave him for that, as he was sure Hodgson had acted out of
desperation and not malice, he was still more wary of him on the whole.
Francis didn't know Hodgson half as well as he did Irving and Little, and he thought it would
be too risky to enlist him now.
Francis was also aware that Hodgson had served on the Cornwallis together with James and
Le Vesconte over on Erebus, so perhaps James would be able to discern Hodgson's loyalties
better than him.
"How was your time on Erebus?", Francis asked Hodgson, who smiled.
"It went very well, sir. The men over there are no less kind than the ones here, and it was
good to see Dundy- that is, Lieutenant Le Vesconte again. He, in turn, missed Commander
Fitzjames, so I hoped to distract him a little."
Francis nodded. He knew Le Vesconte even less than Hodgson, and he supposed he needed
James's assistance in that area as well.
"How was Sir John?"
"Very well, sir. His sermons were wonderful, though I'm told there have been some changes
on Terror in that regard?"
"I do my best to hold sermons as well, now.", Francis said.
"Wonderful. I look forward to your next one!"
After Hodgson had told Francis more about the mood on Erebus -unfortunately Sir John was
as much adored there as ever- Francis dismissed him.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Cornelius Hickey was standing before him, and he was in a good mood. Francis felt alarmed
about that, which wasn't surprising, given their history.
In the last days, Francis had waited for the story of the tins to spread like wildfire throughout
Terror, but it hadn't. Francis honestly didn't know whether to be relieved or dismayed at this
development.
It was obvious that Hickey wanted to advance to the second round in this game they played,
and Francis only hoped he could maintain the upper hand.
"You have your ear on the ground when it comes to the men, have you not?", he asked
Hickey.

"I share the every day toils with most of them.", the caulker's mate replied. "I don't think I'm
more influential than the average Able Seaman."
"I think you're too modest, Mr. Hickey. I know that should you want a certain opinion of, for
example, me to prevail, you would have the means to make it so."
Hickey blinked, the beginnings of a smile forming on his face. "I thank you for thinking so
much of me, Captain."
"I didn't mean it as a compliment."
Hickey wasn't stung by this, in fact, he seemed even more proud.
"I am satisfied with your conduct, though.", Francis allowed. "You did as I asked, and kept
the terrible knowledge to yourself."
"Well, the last thing we need is a panic.", Hickey said.
Unless you could use the panic to your advantage, Francis thought.
"And I have to admit, I'm curious of what you could possibly need my help for.", Hickey
continued.
"You haven't figured it out by now?"
Hickey smiled again. "I thought it best not to speculate."
"I made a vow, Mr. Hickey, to bring you and every other man home safely. There are other
vows, but none are more important than this one. And to keep it, I have to do something
reprehensible..."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Of course Sir John noticed that something was wrong, because even James wasn't that
consummate an actor.
"I wish I could somehow ease your worries, James.", Sir John said at dinner after James's
embarrassing entanglement with Dundy. "I'm quite certain that God will see us through this
unscathed. Or at least, as unscathed as it is possible in these latitudes. I'm sure you're still
grieving Graham's death, as we all do."
"I am.", James replied.
It wasn't even a lie. James grieved for the cheerful friend Graham had been, the senselessness
of that death.
But that wasn't why James sat rigid, conscious of every single one of his movements, and
them all feeling somehow wrong. It wasn't why James didn't take the opportunity to tell some
kind of story of his exploits, even though Sir John's silence clearly invited him to.

Sir John leaned forward in confidence. "My dear James, you can tell me honestly if you miss
Terror. I won't think any less of you, in fact, this means I can pat myself on the back for a job
well done, as well as you."
James decided to pull himself together. "I do miss Terror.", he said with a self-deprecating
smile.
"And I dare say Francis in particular, hm?"
It took all of James's self-control not to flinch bodily at this.
"I'm glad you get along better now, truly.", Sir John said. "Dear Francis can make an effort, as
one could see with the whole sorry business with Sophia. I knew that all you needed was a
little time to get to know one another, hm?"
This time, James did flinch, though he covered it up by shifting in his chair.
Dear Francis is planning to kill you, and he wants me to help him, James almost said.
James knew he was the worst kind of fraud, that he already made himself culpable by staying
silent. He should tell Sir John, tell him right now and let justice take its course.
Justice, he thought with an internal scoff. As if such a thing existed out here.
"Francis and I became fast friends.", James said, aiming for an easy, careless tone. "He
doesn't drink anymore, you know."
"I had heard." Sir John dabbed his mouth with his napkin. "Now, James, tell me of your time
on Terror. I'm greatly curious how you spend it, outside of visiting me."
Somehow, James managed to tell a halfway engaging story of his exploits, though he left out
so many details, as well as straight up invented some others, that he felt as if he was
recounting a dream rather than reality.
There was no mention of sodomy, neither Hickey's nor his own, or Francis seeing the future,
or the crushing doubts about the expedition that James experienced along with his
nightmares.
Over time, James fell into a familiar rhythm with his story, like he had with countless other
pretty lies.
Sir John was none the wiser, but then he would never see me for what I am and still respect
me, James thought.
Francis, on the other hand...
James stopped that thought before it could come to its painful conclusion.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

James spent the next days sleep walking through his duties. It was for him as if he observed
himself from a great distance. He was laughing and talking and going about his business, and
nobody noticed anything wrong, meanwhile the real him was in a corner somewhere losing
his mind.
James knew these states, they always happened to him when he was under some sort of strain
to keep up his false identity. Well, more strain than usual.
He could've kept this up for weeks, never really thinking about the underlying problem, every
part of him busy keeping up appearances, and none the wiser.
Almost none. Harry Goodsir was a very observant man, and he had also heard part of the
truth from Francis.
Whenever James saw the young assistant surgeon, Goodsir looked worriedly at him, asking
him privately if everything was alright.
James replied what he replied to everyone else: "All is well."
That Goodsir didn't believe him was rather obvious, and so James took pains to avoid him.
He avoided Dundy, as well, which consequently meant he was spending almost all of his time
at Sir John's side, the prized pet poodle once more.
Often they sat together, James with a book he wasn't really reading, while Sir John worked on
his next sermon.
James didn't know what his endgame was, only that he needed to survive the next day, and
keep away from Francis. Perhaps he had the childish notion that pretending the mutiny didn't
exist would make it go away, put everything back to rights.
At night, he dreamt of dying. Not the actual death itself, but the pain and suffering leading up
to it. James had never had scurvy at this point, yet it hardly mattered when he dreamed he had
it every night.
He was begging Francis for death, bleeding out of his wounds and losing his teeth.
And Francis, who never left his side in these dreams, refused to end his suffering.
"It's not real.", he would say over and over again. "It's not real..."
James didn't know what was real anymore. His nightmares felt more real than what he did in
his waking hours. And he knew that they had happened, or would happen, or rather a
combination of the two.
He tried not to think of Francis. In fact, he tried to forget Francis entirely, something he had
never been particularly good at. Still, during the day he somehow managed it.
His sleeping mind, however had no compuctions imagining Francis. His desperate words,
replaying over and over.

He sentenced us to death...
It's the only way. Believe me, I tried to think of alternatives, I've debated with myself. I may
not like him, but God help me I don't want to see him dead. Yet it has to be done.
It took an enormous amount of effort for James to keep functioning, but he also lacked the
strength to break the pattern. He knew Francis was waiting for him on Terror, waiting for him
to come around. He would wait forever at this rate, and part of James hoped Francis would
attempt to see him instead. He also feared it, though.
One evening, there was a visitor from Terror, but it wasn't Francis.
James was sitting in the wardroom with Sir John, pretending to read as usual, when
Lieutenant John Irving knocked on the door.
"Come to visit a friend or make a report, Lieutenant Irving?", Sir John asked him.
Irving had a deep frown on his face that deepened further when he looked at James.
"Could we perhaps discuss this in private, Captain?", he said.
Behind his mask, James felt a prick of unease. Out loud, he said: "Now, now, Irving, haven't
we become capital friends during my time on Terror? You can share anything you want with
me as well."
Irving visibly squirmed. "Of course, Commander, it's just-" Irving stopped, lost for words.
"Does the matter concern you privately, perhaps?", Sir John asked gently.
"N- No, not me, exactly."
"Well, then feel free to say whatever you want in front of Commander Fitzjames, as well! I
trust him with my life, and indeed, anything concerning the expedition concerns him, too."
James nodded and smiled encouragingly at the blushing and stuttering Lieutenant Irving.
"Well, there is- there is a matter, sir.", Irving said, straightening. "I don't mean to- to accuse
anyone of misconduct, but I've become aware of a certain... story, circulating among Terror's
crew."
Had Francis been careless? Were there already rumors about the mutiny on Terror?
James knew he ought to panic, but through his daze he watched himself calmly urging Irving
to continue.
"What story?", Sir John, too asked.
Irving looked at James again, then stared at the floor.
Further, did Francis implicate me in some kind of way?, James thought.

Even the notion of that didn't alarm him as it should, so numb did he feel from the last days.
"A crew member came to me, concern on his mind.", Irving continued with effort. "And so I
was told that... that apparently Captain Crozier has been engaging in sodomy, together with
Commander Fitzjames."
This was a different kind of nightmare, made reality before James's eyes. He felt like the
floor had been swiped out from under him, and he was glad that he was sitting down, at least.
For his part, Irving looked like he longed to be swallowed up by the earth right now, and Sir
John... Sir John's eyebrows had climbed to his hairline.
"Do you mean to accuse me of- of-"
James couldn't say the word. Thankfully, Irving spoke again: "No! Of course not, but, after
hearing such a story, I thought it best to inform you..."
"But you believe this story?", Sir John asked mildly.
Irving floundered. "It was... was most convincing.", he said. "Of course, I would never have
thought that my Captain- or even you, Commander-"
"Who told you this story, Lieutenant?", James demanded, barely keeping his voice steady.
Irving was red as a cherry, and at least James could've taken some comfort in his discomfort,
had he not been too busy trying not to have a panic attack.
"It was Cornelius Hickey, the caulker's mate."
James took a deep breath. Time to make a scene to save his own - and Francis's- hide.
"You mean you're condemning me and Captain Crozier on the word of a mere caulker's mate,
someone who already has a past of insubordination, not to mention-"
No, not wise. James would've loved to mention Hickey's own sodomy, but something stayed
him. He wouldn't stoop so low, besides, Hickey was capable of much in the manner of
revenge, as Francis had told James.
"Apparently, he overheard a conversation between you.", Irving pressed out. "Where you,
Commander, made a comment of the past sodomy between you and the Captain."
"What kind of comment?", Sir John asked.
He looked angry, but James couldn't know if it was on his behalf or because he believed
Irving.
"I-I couldn't repeat it in this company, sir."
James remembered the fight he'd had with Francis when he had sent him away, and he also
remembered saying something about Francis sucking his prick far too loudly.

Technically not sodomy, but who cared at this point?
It stood to reason that Hickey had been listening at the door for that one.
"I see.", Sir John said.
"There was no malice in Hickey's reporting, sir.", Irving hurried to assure them. "Or else I
wouldn't have credited it. He was merely concerned, and disturbed by what he heard. As
anyone would be."
James opened his mouth to say something, but snapped it shut when Sir John held up a hand.
"Well, I thank you for coming to me with this, though it appears you have been the victim of
a most gross miscommunication.", Sir John said. "I don't doubt that Mr. Hickey thought he
heard something damning, but that doesn't mean that Captain Crozier and Commander
Fitzjames did any of the things you would charge them with."
James didn't dare feel relieved yet.
"But how-", Irving began.
"What Hickey heard was merely a misunderstanding, I'm sure. Crude sailor's talk,
misconstrued to such a serious accusation. I dare say it surprised the caulker's mate that a
Captain and a Commander sometimes talk as if they were simple ABs in private. And really,
James, I know you went to sea at age twelve, but do try to remain civilised in your
conversation, even if Francis inspires you to vulgarities."
There was a pause, where James waited for relief to hit him, but it didn't come.
"Of course, sir.", he said, ever the eager pet poodle.
Irving, however, looked greatly relieved. "I hadn't thought of that explanation, Captain.", he
said. "But of course that is what must've happened! Commander Fitzjames, I'm greatly sorry
to have inconvenienced you with this, I hope you're not angry with me, I was acting out of
Christian concern for everyone's wellbeing."
"You're forgiven.", James told him. "Though I don't appreciate being accused of such filth by
any man."
The word, "filth", slipped from his lips so naturally, more easily than "sodomy" would have.
"No one would, sir.", Irving agreed tremulously.
"I do believe that no one is at fault for this,", Sir John interjected. "But please make sure that
Mr. Hickey doesn't spread this story around the ship. Should he do so, he must be punished."
"Naturally."
Sir John looked at James with a benevolent expression, and the affection in it made James
want to vomit.

"Now that that's settled, Mr. Irving, why don't you tell us what other news there are on
Terror? Is the ice temperate?"
"No danger of crushing us yet.", Irving replied.
"Would you excuse me for a moment? I have to use the privy.", James said, willing his legs
be steady as he rose.
He only dimly registered Sir John's nod, then he was fleeing to his cabin. The door slammed
shut behind him and he sank to his knees, the fear crashing down on him.
It was a moment of blind panic before he could convince himself to focus on his breathing,
heavy and fast, and try to slow it.
He hadn't been feeling his emotions properly for days, and now it all came to bear down upon
him, the terror and the guilt, so strong that he could hardly think.
James leaned back against the door, attempting to focus on the wood at his back, solid
underneath him.
His ship, his beautiful ship. It would never sail again.
James closed his eyes and finally, he wasn't just gasping in air, but actually breathing.
He sat there as long as he dared, afterwards he rose, practiced his smile in the mirror, and
went back to Sir John, feeling hollow, like a Russian nesting doll.

The next day, there was another visitor from Terror. James wasn't with Sir John when he
found out, but on deck, comiserating with John Morfin on watch.
They had been part of the fateful hunting party together, after all.
James was still putting on his act, playing the assured Commander in total control of himself.
The ice, the dark and the cold were pressing down on his senses, but at the same time he
liked to go out on deck and watch the storms, the Northern lights, the never changing ice.
It got him away from Sir John, which was the main thing.
"Man approaching the ship!", Morfin's partner on watch called.
"From Terror?", James called back, now ever aware of the presence of the Netsilisk people in
this region.
Though he doubted that in this cold, any of them would be stupid enough to venture out on
the ice.
It must be one of ours, James thought.

Minutes later, Thomas Blanky heaved himself over the railing.
"Ah, Mr. Blanky!", James greeted him amicably. "Here to confer with Mr. Reid?"
"Here to see you, actually.", the Ice Master replied.
James immediately felt his stomach drop. Thomas had to know the truth as well as he, and

"Why?", he demanded, aware of the curious Morfin next to him.
Thomas threw an arm around his shoulder, causing James to jerk. "Surely you're joking,

James couldn't do anything but let himself be pushed below decks by the ebullient Blanky.
"Your cabin?", the Ice Master asked.
James was silent a moment, then relented. "Just through there. I'll ring Bridgens for tea-"
"No need, Commander.", Blanky said. "Come on."
James drew his undressing out as long as he could, but he knew he was fighting a losing

Thomas, for his part, undressed himself and waited patiently until James was sitting across

James felt very tired, all of a sudden.
He sighed. "What do you want from me, Mr. Blanky?"
"For you to get over yourself.", Thomas replied. "We haven't the time for whatever moping

James stared at the other, dumbfounded. "Excuse me?"
"Look, I know it's difficult for you.", Thomas continued in a gentler tone. "You're close to the

James, gasping his last breath.
Give my body to the men. Feed them.
James shook his head to clear it. "I know. Believe me, Francis made that abundantly clear."
"Then what keeps you here, Commander?", Thomas asked. "You know the reality of our
situation, what's at stake. Why do you hesitate?"

"Because it's monstrous!", James hissed. "It's monstrous and it's wrong, and frankly I-" He

"You thought right.", James grit out.
"You know what I think your problem is?"
"I'm sure you're about to tell me."
Blanky patted his arm. "You're thinking too much with your feelings instead of yer mind. It's

James was stunned. "Are you saying... that I'm hysterical?"
"I'm saying that yer need to look at the cold, hard facts instead of what they morally mean.",

Each time Blanky said "fact", James flinched a little.
"But Francis-"
"Francis is doing this because of those facts, whatever other reasons he may have. You

Chapter 27: Francis
It was true that Thomas had been the one keeping Francis from visiting James, as well as
been the one to keep him halfway sane over the last days.
Not trips to the other time, at least.
In their place, nightmares about James telling Sir John everything, of Edward and Jopson and
Thomas hanged before his very eyes.
He tried to project an outward front of confidence, even more necessary now that he was not
only the Captain of the Terror, but leader of a mutiny against Sir John Franklin.
Wonder of all wonders, Hickey had agreed to help him. He hadn't seemed greatly shocked at
Francis's plan, and a little confused at the flowery language Francis had cloaked his
intentions in.
Francis wasn't a fool; he still wanted plausible deniability, especially in front of Hickey.
When he had asked Hickey why he agreed to help him, feeling like Cassius asking every
potential assassin of their grievance against Caesar, Hickey had simply said: "I don't want to
die."
That was as good a reason as any, Francis supposed.
"I have to ask you to keep all this to yourself for now. Test the mood among the crew, but
don't take anyone into your confidence.", Francis had said. "Even Mr. Gibson."
Hickey raised an eyebrow. "Billy would make an excellent mutineer, sir.", he replied in an
infuriatingly smug way.
"Be that as it may. No telling him yet."
"I don't want to hang for this back in England, either.", Hickey said. "And I certainly won't
take the fall for you."
"I'm not asking you to. We will make it look like an accident, and no one will be the wiser.
Should anything go wrong, I will protect you."
Hickwy eyed him. "Why?"
Always so suspicious!
"Because it's my responsibility, as your Captain and the leader of this... affair."
"You mean mutiny, sir."

Francis sighed. "Be careful with that word, Mr. Hickey. I don't want to hear it from you again,
no matter what the truth is."
"As you wish."
"If everything goes according to plan, you won't have to do anything at all.", Francis
continued. "Should anyone ever ask you, you can claim complete ignorance. Is that enough
for you?"
Hickey thought for a moment. "It is, Captain. Though it seems a waste not to use me for
anything, now that you've recruited me."
Francis thought with a shiver of Lieutenant Irving's mutilated corpse. Should push come to
shove, Hickey would come in handy...
"Keep yourself ready, Mr. Hickey."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
After careful consideration, Francis had decided to speak to Dr. McDonald alone. He was
familiar by now with the nervousness and the unease that accompanied these talks of
recruitment, for he could never know for sure if he was not making a dreadful mistake.
He found the doctor not in Sickbay, but in his quarters, reading.
"What can I do for you, Captain?", McDonald asked, putting his book down.
"I need your help.", Francis said. "In a very delicate matter."
The doctor nodded, probably used to hearing openings like that.
"You must know the direness of our situation.", Francis continued in a hushed tone, despite
the closed door.
McDonald nodded again. "It's imperative that Sir John changes his mind... I do worry what
we'll do if he doesn't, but the Commander assured me that his efforts wouldn't be in vain."
Francis winced internally. Poor James.
"When did he say that to you?"
"A number of weeks ago, now.", Dr. McDonald said. "I must admit, my unease is growing."
"Then I will be plain with you.", Francis replied. "You already know my position in this. You
know my plans to get us out of this. And I'm telling you now that I will carry out that plan,
and I will let nothing and no one stop me."
McDonald was silent a moment, and Francis was sure he had understood the meaning behind
his words.

"I see.", the doctor murmured. "Do you have... ideas already, on how we could overcome the
obstacles?"
"A great many. And for one of them, I need your help."
"You want to commit murder.", Dr. McDonald said. "Don't you?"
Francis didn't shrink from his gaze. "One life, to save all of us. And there is no other way,
believe me."
The doctor's next objection surprised Francis. "I do worry about you on a long walk, with
your epilepsy. I don't mean to be harsh, but you have to make sure that a good command
structure is in place, should you die."
Francis hadn't thought about that at all, but he could reassure the other: "Lieutenant Little will
replace me should anything happen to me, and he has my complete trust."
"And what about Commander Fitzjames? Does he know of your plan?"
"He does.", Francis said curtly.
Why did it always come down to James? Francis wished he had gone and seen him,
regardless of what Thomas said. He hated himself for it, but it didn't sit well with him that
James was alone with only his doubts and Sir John.
What if he decided to stand by their leader, no matter what?
Over the next minutes, Dr. McDonald laid out his idea, should they go with poisoning.
"We need to know his eating habits above all. Especially the, as I have heard, rare occasions
he drinks alcohol."
"Why?"
"Because most poisons taste terrible, and he is sure to notice them in his food. Alcohol will
mask most substances better." McDonald considered. "We have to go over to Erebus and
speak to Dr. Stanley. Perhaps Sir John takes laudanum or mandragora to sleep, and we can
somehow give him an overdose."
Of course, Dr. McDonald didn't suggest recruiting Stanley, but he did say that perhaps it
would suffice to speak to Goodsir about what he knew, back as he was on Erebus.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Francis was getting ready to cross over to Erebus. He still needed the cane, but was overall
more sure on his feet now. Dr. McDonald would go with him this time, as opposed to
Thomas.
As it was, Thomas was nowhere to be found.

He should've put two and two together at that point, for all Thomas had said that Francis
wasn't to visit James, Thomas had made no such rules for himself.
Just as Francis was about to go out the door, Thomas arrived, still wrapped in his slops and
with a lantern.
"I brought Fitzjames.", he said before Francis could ask him what was going on.
Francis felt all the air punched out of his lungs. "James...", he murmured.
"Now, now, none of that.", Thomas admonished him. "It's touch and go, with him, and you
getting emotional will not entice him to our side. Keep yerself together, Frank, for the sake of
everyone."
Francis nodded, and Thomas opened the door.
The first one to enter the room was Neptune, not James, the dog cheerfully plodding ahead of
the Commander of Erebus.
When Neptune jumped up Francis's leg, Francis mechanically petted him, his face trained on
the man behind the dog.
James looked radiant as ever, his cheeks red from cold, a few errant snowflakes rapidly
melting in his hair.
For some reason, Francis was reminded of the time he a struck James in the other reality.
That meeting had begun in a similar way.
"James.", he said, trying for a sober tone.
"Francis.", James returned, voice betraying nothing.
Francis stepped closer, causing James to make an abrupt step back.
"Why do you shrink from me?" Francis didn't disguise the hurt in his voice.
It was as if he really had struck him, in this time as well.
James pressed his lips together. "I'm sorry.", he said. "I'm just not- there is a great deal to
consider."
Francis nodded, making another attempt to step closer to James. This time, he didn't recoil.
Carefully, as if approaching a skittish horse, Francis put both hands on James's shoulders. He
was already wearing his gloves, and he could only divine James's shoulders underneath all
his layers, yet the intimacy of the touch still unfloored him.
He thought about how he had cried in James's arms again, how James had said: "I'm here."

Francis was beginning to think that James's death in the other reality had hurt him somehow
permanently beyond the obvious, had put a wound in him that no one could see.
He couldn't talk about the whole thing without crying, without fearing that it would happen
again it he put it into words.
James's presence healed him, but only in the moment; once he was alone, the fear came back.
"I've missed you, James.", he choked out.
Surprise of surprises, James smiled. It was sad, regretful, but still a smile.
"Oh, Francis.", he said. "Whatever is happening to us?"
Francis tried to project confidence, though his answer was: "I wish I knew."
James leaned forward a fraction. "I will help you. God will damn me, but I will help you."
Francis stared at him, speechless. "James-"
"And you will need me, I reckon. You need someone he trusts, don't you? Someone who can
lure him into death."
Francis had no idea what to say. A "thank you" didn't seem appropriate, same as another love
confession.
"I'm sorry.", was what he settled on. "I'm so sorry, James."
For a moment, James looked angry, like he was going to lash out at Francis, but then his
expression softened.
"I know.", he said.
Francis wished to say more, wished to apologise again, but the other's expression stayed him.
So instead, Francis told him of their plan.
"I will accompany you.", James said simply, and they went, meeting Dr. McDonald on deck.
It was James who carried the bottle whiskey Jopson had picked out, wrapped in several cloths
to keep it from breaking.
This time, there was no storm, though the crossing was still hard on his leg. He was
hopelessly dependant on the lantern James was holding -Dr. McDonald was carrying a few
medical supplies.
Poisons, to use another word.
They had just made it past the berg, when Francis became conscious of a sound he had until
then attributed to to the howling winds.

"Do you hear that?", he asked James.
James stopped and listened. "Yes. It's not the wind, isn't it?"
"It sounds... like an animal.", Dr. McDonald said.
There was a pause as they all realised the reality of their situation.
Francis remembered Lady Silence, telling him that no one controlled Tuunbaq.
"We need to hurry.", James said as he started to walk. "Erebus is our best bet."
Francis looked ahead at Erebus's lights. They still seemed horribly far away, and his leg
already hurt.
"Go ahead.", he told the doctor and James. "I'll follow..."
"No, we're staying together.", James said, and McDonald nodded. "We go as fast as you can,
Francis."
It wasn't fast enough, that much Francis knew. The howling sounds of the beast got closer
and closer, and still Erebus was only seen in the distance.
They would hardly be safe on deck, as well, as Francis remembered.
He was leaning heavily on his cane and was in danger of stumbling for all he needed to drag
his leg.
Then the ice was moving under his feet, vibrating from the beast's footfalls, and Francis did
fall.
James was at his side in a flash, helping him up.
"We'll not make it.", Francis gasped.
"Shut up and run!", was James's reply.
Francis tried, he did, but even the most lenient of people would be able to describe the
hobbling he was doing as "running."
He also worried about the strain he put on Mr. Honey's cane, fearing it might break -the thing
had withstood so much already, really Mr. Honey was an excellent carpenter.
There was howling directly behind them, now.
Francis was caught by the urge to turn around, meet his end head on, but James pushed him
farther forward and he had to make sure not to fall again.
Dr. McDonald screamed, and there was a horrible tearing noise.
The next moment, both Francis and James stumbled and crashed onto the ice.

None of them had brought any weapons, not that they were at all useful against the creature.
Dr. McDonald was still screaming, and Francis made a move to get up and turn around, help
the man who would've helped him without question, but before he could do anything, the was
a bone splitting crack and the doctor fell silent.
On his way to scramble to his feet, Francis slipped again and fell to the ground. James was
standing again, that Francis could discern even though the lantern had gone out.
"Run!", Francis gave back the command. "For God's sake, James, run!"
James didn't run. He bent down and shielded Francis's body with his own.
They were going to die here, out on the ice. Everything was going too fast for Francis to feel
any real fear. He wanted James to run, but his future Second clearly had no intention of doing
so.
"James!", he yelled, trying to push the other away. "James-"
At this point, Tuunbaq ought to have gotten to them. Why wasn't it attacking? Francis could
hear the sounds the creature made, so it was still there, but it wasn't roaring anymore.
Francis closed his eyes and waited, until he sensed James detaching himself from him.
"Francis, look.", he said.
Francis turned around at last. In the beginning, he saw nothing but darkness because James
was blocking him, but then the stars allowed him to make out another figure standing before
them.
It was the father of Lady Silence, directly between them and the beast.
Tuunbaq himself was just a shadow gleaming white. He was silent compared to before,
though Francis could hear his exhalations.
He didn't know what the Netsilisk man and the creature communicated among each other, but
it still took quite a while for Tuunbaq to stand down.
James helped Francis to his feet in the mean time, and when he made to detach himself from
Francis, Francis held on, grabbing his mittened hand.
Finally, finally, Tuunbaq gave a mighty roar, before turning around and disappearing in the
darkness.
"Thank you.", Francis said to the Netsilisk man.
He couldn't make his face out, but believed he saw him nod.
Lady Silence, who had been standing to the side, came closer. On her approach, she went
carefully around the bleeding corpse of Dr. McDonald.

In the Arctic night, one could only see a twisted dark shape on the ice, but it was enough for
Francis to feel grief like a punch in the gut.
Another good man, gone.
Lady Silence was yelling at her father. Even if Francis had not understood her, her tone was
one of universal worry and reproach.
"Do not put yourself in danger for these people!", he heard her say, among other such
pronouncements.
"Ask her what they are doing here.", James said to him.
"Saving us, obviously.", Francis replied.
"But how did they know we were in danger? And couldn't they have come sooner, before it
killed Dr. McDonald?"
James sounded lost and confused, which blunted the anger in his tone.
Francis shook his head, sensing that it was better give Lady Silence her space, for now.
Instead, he approached the body of Dr. McDonald. His old friend, to whom he owed so
much.
"We can't carry him back, with your leg and everything.", James said, having followed him.
"We need to send someone back-"
Carefully, Francis lowered himself onto his knees next to McDonald's head. The doctor's eyes
were open, his mouth gaping in one perpetual scream. James was silent as Francis closed his
eyes and murmured a prayer.
"I'm sorry for him.", Lady Silence said behind them. "He was a good man. We were too late."
Francis looked up at her, the fur of her hood shining in the starlight. "Thank you, still.", he
replied.
"What is she saying?", James asked.
Lady Silence gestured to James. "Your tall one ought to learn our tongue. He is very
curious."
"That he is."
"Francis, what is she-"
Lady Silence's father stepped up beside her and held out his hand towards them. When James
stayed frozen to the spot, Francis laboriously got to his feet.
He reached for the shaman's hand, thinking he wanted to shake it, perhaps, but instead the
man pressed something hard into Francis's mittened palm.

Francis closed his fingers around it as best he could. "Thank you.", he said again, puzzled.
"We will leave now.", Lady Silence said.
"I wish you the best.", Francis replied, because it was the least he could do.
The Netsilisk man took his daughter's hand, and they turned away. Despite the cold, despite
the body at his feet, Francis stood still, watching them vanish into the darkness.
He turned to James, wishing once more that he could see his face clearly.
"Are you unhurt?"
"I'm fine.", James said. "Even the whiskey stayed intact, you'll be pleased to know."
Francis had no words for what he really wanted to say, and he suspected James didn't either.
It was clear that it was useless to gather Dr. McDonald's medical supplies; there were a bunch
of broken bottles, strewn all over the shale.
"We continue in our plan.", Francis said, though it made him feel sick. "And we'll tell Sir
John nothing of the Netsilisk saving us. We escaped due to luck, nothing else."
"Francis-"
Francis didn't know if James was beginning to make an objection or an entreaty, as it was, he
interrupted him: "We can't have his death be for nothing, James. We can't turn back."
James was silent a moment. There was nothing but the Arctic night, surrounding them.
"Alright.", James said at last. "But how are we going to poison him without the medical
supplies?"

Chapter 28: A Doctor's Lament
Harry Goodsir had not thought that this journey would be like this.
Over the last years, he had had an uncomfortable number of realisiations about his situation,
as well as that of the entire crew.
Worst out of all of these was doubtlessly the truth about their canned provisions, but there
had been other examples.
It had started all so promisingly when they left Greenhithe. His only worry back then had
been his tempestuous relationship with Dr. Stanley, a problem that had persisted all the way
to where they found themselves now.
Harry made it his business in general to get along with the people he met, and he absolutely
hated strife of any kind. Yet even he had shrunk under the force of Dr. Stanley's sneer, and his
arrogance, his approach to the world that in Harry's opinion wasn't at all scientific and proper
-to use a Stanley word- for a man of medicine.
They had learned to keep out of each other's way well enough, Stanley letting Goodsir
engage in his "little hobbies" which Harry saw as his duty - he had initially wanted to join the
expedition as a naturalist, not an assistant surgeon, and in his head he still wanted to live up
to that title.
However, keeping out of each other's way was infinitely easier when they weren't stuck in the
ice and there were still diversions to distract them apart from the books.
Now, Harry remembered with great nostalgia the time when Commander Fitzjames had
dragged him on deck to show him a catch the men had made, or Lieutenant Le Vesconte had
peered at the life flourishing under his microscope so he could help him draw it.
There was no life here, except for the monster out on the ice.
Captain Sir John called it a bear, but other members of the crew who had actually seen it had
different words for it.
Harry hadn't known what to believe, until he talked to the Netsilisk, with the aid of Dr.
McDonald. They called the being "Tuunbaq" and to them it was no bear.
In other circumstances, Harry might've been glad at the mystery the whole case represented,
but he had little reason to feel glad, these days.
Ever since he had found out about the tins, Harry had battled feelings of complete
hopelessness on the regular. It wasn't so much the fact of the lead, but Sir John's refusal to
break off the expedition, his insistence that everything was fine.

To Harry, this attitude bordered on the delusional. How could Sir John still claim to care for
his crew when he would consign them all to a horrible death?
But then, Sir John honestly seemed to believe that they could go on as they had been without
losing lives.
And of course Dr. Stanley had taken his side. To be honest, Harry had feared going insane if
he stayed on Erebus a day longer, so he had gladly left to confer with the Netsilisk guests on
Terror.
He had been greatly fascinated with the Netsilisk culture ever since he had met these people
in Greenland, and he regretted that there was no way to learn their language back in England.
Hence, his idea to create a Netsilisk dictionary for such instances.
Only after he had stayed on Terror a while though, had he realised what a tremendous
opportunity their two guests represented. The Netsilisk knew how to survive where
Englishmen couldn't, and perhaps they could be persuaded to teach their ways to Harry and
the others...
Harry had felt hope, then, for the first time in weeks.
Even better, Captain Crozier approved of his plan, and would help him make it fact. The
Netsilisk too, were open to conversation.
Of course, Harry reflected, it had been too good to be true.
As soon as he had been back on Erebus, he had seen that while Captain Crozier might've
agreed with him, there was no way that Sir John ever would.
Harry had broached the subject cautiously several times, and he had been brushed off every
single one of them. Sir John seemed to think that the Netsilisk were nothing but pitiful
savages, and of course Dr. Stanley shared that opinion.
Harry shouldn't have been surprised. Sir John had, after all, ordered him to feed their guests
poisoned food.
Never in his wildest dreams had Harry imagined that he would ever go against the express
orders of his Captain, but his conscience hadn't let him pursue another way.
Right now, what felt above all was a great frustration, mixed with dread about their future. He
didn't know what to do anymore.
Should he go back to Captain Crozier and entreat him for help?
Yes, that seemed like the most sensible option.
It turned out that Stanley had requested him back because something was wrong with Mr.
Collins.

Well, according to Stanley, nothing was wrong with Mr. Collins, he was simply having a bit
of a bad time, but his behavior was starting to affect the rest of the crew, and Harry had
apparently always been the one to concern himself with "such trifles".
Every disease that didn't affect the body was a trifle in Dr. Stanley's eyes, Harry was well
aware.
Harry had taken it upon himself to visit Mr. Collins daily and talk with him, and while Harry
wouldn't say that he was well, he was at least improved.
"It's the nightmares.", he had told Harry. "They used to be of Billy Orrin, you know, the man
we lost when the propeller broke, but now they've... changed."
"Changed how?", Harry had asked.
"I dream of the creature we saw, out on the ice. How it killed Lieutenant Gore, how it will kill
me..."
Harry had put a hand on Collins's shoulder. "It won't kill you, Henry. Dreams are images of
our deepest feelings, such as our fears. That doesn't mean that they will happen in reality."
Collins had looked anguished. "Are sure?"
"Most certainly.", Harry had replied.
It turned out that Mr. Collins had been out of sorts ever since the outing on the ice. He felt
guilty because he had been the one to spot what he thought was a bear, and he blamed
himself for Lieutenant Gore's death.
Harry hadn't precisely known what to do, but he had known instinctually that Mr. Collins was
suffering, and that he needed help, help Harry tried to give.
He couldn't believe the kind of cruel, thoughtless responses Stanley had been giving to the
man, insisting that he wasn't a doctor for these kinds of "pretensions".
How could someone be so cold when confronted with the pain in another human being?
Besides his worries over Mr. Collins, there was Commander Fitzjames. Harry had been glad
when he had returned to Erebus with him, hoping that he perhaps had another ally for his
cause.
It had soon turned out, however, that Fitzjames was preoccupied with something else.
It had something to do with Captain Crozier and his trips to the future, Harry suspected.
Harry had learned in his studies that a true scientist used the unshakable facts of the world
around him to draw his conclusions about said world.
In Crozier's case, the facts did allow for an outlandish explanations like that, and so Harry
had believed him.

He wished he could've talked more about it with Crozier, another reason for his plan to go
over to Terror one of these days.
What had stayed him until now was a curious conversation he'd had with Fitzjames a few
days ago.
Harry had had the distinct impression that Fitzjames was avoiding him. He sought Sir John's
company instead, which worried him.
When asked, Fitzjames always insisted that he was fine, that everything was "capital,
capital", and only Harry seemed to be able to see this for the lie that it was.
One evening, Fitzjames had appeared in sickbay. Harry was drawing and Dr. Stanley had
gone to bed, which Harry promptly told Fitzjames when he inquired.
"What do you need, Commander?", Harry asked.
"Something to help me sleep.", Fitzjames said, very reluctantly.
Harry nodded. "Do you have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep?"
"Both." Fitzjames pursed his lips, frowned. "I have nightmares... they keep me awake."
Like Mr. Collins, then. Though at this point Harry wondered if there was a single person who
knew about the tins who didn't have nightmares, except for Sir John.
"I can recommend several things, though I had heard you're not very fond of laudanum, sir?"
"That's true.", Fitzjames said.
"Mandragora, then. A few drops will do you well."
"Thank you.", Fitzjames murmured, the frown not leaving his face.
Harry stopped on his way to the cabinet and turned around. "Commander, if there's anything
else I can do for you, you can talk to me. I will keep your confidence."
Fitzjames looked at him as if he was seeing him from a great distance.
"Has it do with Captain Crozier, perhaps? His..." Harry lowered his voice, though they were
alone. "... unusual trips through time?"
For a long moment, Fitzjames said nothing, and Harry waited patiently. "In a manner of
speaking, yes.", he finally returned.
"Did he tell you more about the kind of future he saw?", Harry asked. "Was it very bad?"
Fitzjames chewed the inside of his cheek, then nodded curtly.
Harry wasn't surprised, but it was shocking to have the confirmation. "But surely, we can still
change it, somehow? It isn't fixed?"

"We can change it.", Fitzjames said, and Harry breathed a sigh of desperate relief.
"Then why are you so troubled, sir?"
Fitzjames sighed and closed his eyes. "There's a price, Harry. There is always a price."
Fitzjames had refused to say more and taken the mandragora. Harry had let him go, not
wanting to press him, for fear what he might reveal.
His every instinct told him that there was something reprehensible going on, and that perhaps
he was better off not knowing.
Harry wondered if he was acting cowardly, but on the other hand, did it matter? His influence
was small, as mere assistant surgeon, as he had repeatedly felt in the last weeks.
Even when he had found out something vital to the wellbeing of the expedition (with
Crozier's help, but still) he had been dismissed by nearly everyone who mattered.
He decided to focus on his tasks for now, though he still watched the Commander, and so
noticed when he went over to Terror a few days later, together with Ice Master Blanky.
Harry was just present for Dr. Stanley's examination of Lieutenant Le Vesconte, how he was
faring without his toes, when Mr. Collins burst into Sickbay. He had been on watch.
"Is someone dying, Mr. Collins?", Dr. Stanley asked archly. "Otherwise, I'm with a patient
right now."
Collins, shrunk back a little, but he returned promptly: "Already dead, sir. It's the creature. It
killed Dr. McDonald from Terror. Captain Crozier and Commander Fitzjames barely
escaped, and are here right now."
Even Dr. Stanley seemed momentarily thrown at that. "I see.", he said. "Do they need
medical attention?"
"They went to report to Sir John, and he told me to get you."
Dr. Stanley nodded and turned to the door. "Mr. Goodsir, finish up here."
"Yes, sir.", Harry said, but Stanley was already out the door.
Harry was greatly curious as to why Captain Crozier had crossed the ice, something he had
never done - hadn't been able to do- up to this point.
He also wondered at another attack of the strange beast.
Mr. Collins looked greatly distressed, and so did Lieutenant Le Vesconte, though he hid it
better.
As Collins had to go back to his watch, Harry went to him first and told him to seek him out
after he was finished.

Collins nodded, a little relieved. "Thank you, Harry."
Collins left, and Harry turned around to find Le Vesconte pulling his socks back on. "I trust
you've finished staring at my non existent toes, because I need to make sure that James is
alright."
Stanley hadn't said anything about Harry or Le Vesconte joining him, but then, he hadn't said
anything against it, either. And Harry had finished up here, like he had been told to do.
"We'll make sure together.", Harry said.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
When Sir John admitted them upon knocking, the Commander and the Captain were just
making their report.
Evidently, Sir John had allowed Crozier to sit down on account of his leg, while Fitzjames
stood there with his hands crossed behind his back.
Dr. Stanley was examining Crozier's leg, and apparently, they were in the middle of a
discussion if Crozier should be moved to sickbay.
"Ah, Mr. Goodsir.", Stanley said. "You can help Captain Crozier to sickbay right away."
"Of course, sir.", Harry replied.
He expected Crozier to insist that he was fine, but the Captain of the Terror merely nodded.
"I would still like to talk to you later. In private.", he said to Sir John.
"Of course, Francis.", Sir John answered. "I'll send James and Dr. Stanley after you when he
made his report. Lieutenant Le Vesconte, you may stay."
With the help of Harry and his cane, they got Crozier to sickbay fairly quickly, even though
he was carrying a pouch he refused to let go of. Harry tried not to show his excitement. Here
it was at last, the opportunity to speak to Captain Crozier.
Even though Harry also had reservations, he wasn't going to let it slip away.
"Is Dr. McDonald really dead?", Harry asked.
"Unfortunately, yes.", Crozier replied as he sat down. "Really, you don't need to examine me.
My leg just needs rest, that is all."
Why are we here then, Harry thought. Could it be? Did Crozier want to speak to him as well?
"It's a terrible loss.", Crozier continued sincerely. "He was not only Terror's doctor, but my
friend. I so very much wanted to bring him home."

Harry could only concur. Two days after his sujourn on Terror, Dr. McDonald asked him to
call him Alexander, and after months of Stanley's vitriol this had been a balm upon Harry's
heart.
They had discussed many things in Harry's research and of course, Dr. McDonald had helped
Harry with his communications with the Netsilisk, having greatly approved of the idea of a
dictionary, not to mention Harry's plan to work with the Netsilisk for their survival.
Harry had missed him greatly over the last days, and now he would never see him again.
"If I may ask, how did he die, sir?"
Crozier gave a deep sigh of sadness. "He was torn apart by Tuunbaq. At least it was over very
quickly. He didn't suffer."
Neither of them even made the pretense of calling the creature a bear. It was greatly ironic
now that Harry had tried, together with Dr. McDonald to get the Netsilisk to talk about the
strange animal, so they might know more about it.
But Tuunbaq was a deeply personal subject to them, Harry sensed, and even when he had
gotten to know them better, they were tight lipped about it.
"Will someone go and get the body?", Harry asked.
"Of course."
"If they do, it is my professional opinion that Mr. Collins shouldn't be part of the party to
retrieve him. He is still much disturbed by his previous encounter with Tuunbaq, and sending
him will put him, as well as others, in danger."
"Sir John said nothing about sending Mr. Collins.", Crozier calmed him. "As he is on watch,
it wouldn't be proper for him to leave the ship anyway."
"That's good.", Harry said, relieved.
"Dr. Goodsir.", Crozier began. "I'm sorry to do this, but we don't have much time. I need to
ask a favor of you."
Harry felt an uncomfortable shiver down his spine. Still, he sat down next to Crozier and
nodded for him to go on.
"I haven't told you, what I experienced in our future. I'd like to do so now." Crozier reached
out and took his hand. "I'm sorry, doctor. But this won't be pleasant."
"I need to hear it.", Harry said, his heart beating wildly in his chest. "I've been thinking it,
anyway, over the last days, and I'm beginning to believe that uncertainty is worse than the
truth."
"In this case, I dare not agree.", the Captain replied. "I'll begin then."

As he sat there and listened, Harry was struck by his sheer and utter helplessness at the
situation. He had not ever thought of himself as someone who would chafe at his low rank,
but the lack of power he had to change anything was maddening.
He also thought all the men he knew, and how they would die.
It was good that Crozier spoke, for Harry didn't have any words for what he was hearing. Just
despair, endless despair...
Crozier told him last of their final conversation in the other time, how Harry had been still
alive perhaps, but hopeless and beaten.
Harry turned away from Crozier at that, so he would not see him cry. He cried for the
expedition, for all their souls, for their youthful enthusiasm at the beginning.
"Dr. Goodsir.", Crozier said urgently. "I need you to listen to me. It's not fixed. We can still
change it. We can still save the men, those who didn't die in this time yet."
Had he not been sitting down, Harry would've sunk to his knees at the words.
"Truly?", he asked, looking at Crozier again.
The Captain nodded. "And this is what I need your help with."
It suddenly occurred to Harry, as he was about to enthusiastically agree, what Fitzjames had
said in sickbay only days ago.
There's a price. There is always a price.
Fitzjames's entire behavior, and now Crozier taking him aside like this, seemed to suggest
that something nefarious was going on.
"What do you want to do, Captain?", Harry asked.
Crozier sighed again. "Truly you must know by now that Sir John refuses to be swayed in his
plan."
"I do.", Harry said. An ill sense of foreboding gripped him.
"We tried all the other ways, tried to persuade him. It doesn't work. And now, I regret to say,
there is only one road left to us."
Harry felt as if the ground had been swept out from under him.
He stared at Crozier like a trapped rabbit, seeing coming the fatal blow.
When Crozier said nothing, Harry heard himself ask: "How?"
A single word, full of dangerous portent.

"We thought poison.", Crozier replied. He was still holding on to Harry's hand, which had
gone limp in his grasp.
"We?", Harry repeated, head swimming.
"Me and James. Dr. McDonald approved of it."
So Tuunbaq had interrupted them in the midst of an assassination plot, and had taken out the
crucial element, furthermore. A doctor who would know how to poison Sir John.
"You want me... to take over Alexander's role, don't you? You want me to help you... commit
murder.", Harry said.
Some part of him expected Crozier to deny it, but his jaw was set. "Yes."
Harry rose to his feet and turned away from Crozier again.
"I don't know how much time we have left.", Crozier said behind him. "James is keeping Dr.
Stanley away right now, but even he can't do that forever. I need your help, Dr. Goodsir, now
more than ever.. Think of yourself. Think of the men. They have to be saved."

Chapter 33: The Carnivale I
The nights leading up to the Carnivale had been surprisingly clear, and so the men could
work on erecting the tents for their celebration into the first sunrise of the year.
Sir John wouldn't be joining them. He was still much weakened, and he had never been
personally fond of this sort of thing, especially the disguising part.

"Most of them will be too drunk to notice anything amiss, also.", Francis said.
Sir John chuckled. "Well, it's you I have to fear then, sober as you are!"
"Please, we both share the burden of command.", Francis replied gravely. "I would never
pressure you into an indignity."
How dignified will his death be at this rate?, James wondered.
Sir John eyed Francis, the mirth dying on his face. "If that is so, be so kind as to get my dress
uniform. I will venture out, if only to prove to myself that I am better.", he said. "Yes, I think
today is the day I rejoin the world."
James helped Sir John dress, noticing with dismay that his hands were shaking.
"Is everything alright, James?", Sir John asked when James had dropped his epaulette for the
second time.
"I'm just... excited for the Carnivale.", James said weakly.
"That's right, I forgot that the whole venture was your idea..." Sir John sighed. "I think I
would like to eat something before we go, because I feel a little unsteady on my legs."
James heart sank. He didn't know how much delay he could take, but who am I to refuse him
a last supper?, James thought.
This was a bad association, for James was reminded of the actual last supper -which he had
read to Sir John a few days ago- and how Jesus knew that Judas was going to betray him all
along.

It wouldn't do to get paranoid right now, so James got the dinner Mr. Wall prepared for Sir
John.
Salted meat and biscuits, together with lemon juice, the usual fare since they had sworn off
the tins.
James doubted that anyone was much enjoying eating anymore, when it was always some
variation of this that was served.
The men had started to grumble, and there were multiple rumors as to why the tinned food
was banned, many close to the truth.
Both James and Francis didn't want to eat, but as they watched Sir John consume his portion,
James longed for something to do with his hands, and regretted saying no to food.
"How are things on Terror, Francis?", Sir John asked. "Have you made any new magnetic
observations?"
"A few, yes. But the last days have been utterly preoccupied with the Carnivale, I'm afraid."
It wasn't even a lie. James knew that Little had followed Francis here and waited out on the
ice should they need his assistance (which was the most dangerous position to be in, on
account of the beast). Jopson, Hickey and Blanky were at the Carnivale, keeping the crowd
under control, and Goodsir was set to distract Dr. Stanley.
Dr. Stanley was also the reason they didn't want to kill Sir John on the ship, because they
feared Stanley wouldn't accept the death of his recovering patient without fuss, suspicious as
he was already.
Hickey had suggested, as James had heard via Mr. Blanky, that they should just kill Stephen
as well -"You can simply hit him over the head with your cane, Captain, and say he fell on
the ice" - but Francis had, of course, refused to even consider it.
"Well, I suppose it is fitting to usher in this next period of our lives in with a celebration.", Sir
John said, chewing. "It is my firm belief that we will have found the Passage by this time

"Hear, hear.", James said, raising his glass - water of course, on account of both Francis and
Sir John.
Francis frowned. "Sir John-"
"We all know of your pessimism, Francis.", Sir John remarked. "Might we not at least be free
of it this night?"
"As you wish.", Francis replied.
Sir John stopped chewing, looking at Francis for a moment. "I know what you're doing, over
on Terror."

There had been thousands of these moments in the last weeks, moments where James had
been paralyzed with fear, because someone had something alarming like this.
One almost got used to the unpleasantness of it, though the fear never eased.
"Pardon?", Francis said.
"These sermons you hold, about the great untameable leviathan. How we will need to respect
it to survive, how it may eat us whole if we don't - all quite interesting, Francis, if a little
dreary."
"I never meant to criticize you with these sermons.", Francis hurried to assure Sir John.
James watched as Sir John put another morsel on his fork and brought it to his mouth.
There was still food left on the plate.
"Maybe not me.", Sir John said mildly. "But my decisions, certainly. And it is your right...
Yet surely you know that I cannot maintain a good command if my own Second keeps
second-guessing every choice I make?"
Francis didn't seem to know what to say to that, so James jumped in: "I'm sure everything
will be right as rain once this winter is over. Thaw will come, and you, Francis will realise
that you are wrong."
Francis looked at James, his gaze cold. "Or we may all be dead, and they can dig our
sceletons out of the ice."
"That is exactly what I mean.", Sir John said. Then, suddenly: "James, will you leave us for a
moment? You can get your slops, we will follow shortly."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Francis had barely time to register the sound of James's chair scraping across the floor, of

Francis's eyes in a desperate understanding, before he was alone with Sir John, his gaze
benevolent no longer.
Francis knew how this would go. It had happened in the other time, too, after all, when he
had suggested sending out the rescue party.
"Francis, I do wonder sometimes if I have ever done anything to make you despise me so

belying his words.
"I only have the wellbeing of the men in mind-"
"You are not the leader of this expedition, Francis, and that for good reason!", Sir John
exploded. "You have always had this tendency to nag at your betters, forcing your way into
closed doors, with no regard for how command works! You're the worst kind of Second, and

I will bear it no longer. That is, for now I must bear it, but be sure that you will have none of
my kindness when this is over, undeserving as you are of it."
Francis stared at Sir John, close to dumbstruck. Those weren't his words from before, this
was worse. And he didn't dare make a guess as to what had prompted this.
At least it will make it easier for me to kill him, came the detached thought.
Francis shuddered inwardly.
"Everything I did was for the benefit of the expedition.", he forced out between clenched
teeth. "It was never my aim to attack you personally-"
Sir John scoffed. "You dare say that after what you've done? You dare?"
"My sermons were never meant to-"
Sir John's fist on the table interrupted him. The glasses jumped. "I'm not talking about your
sermons, Francis. I'm talking about James."
Francis felt fear clench around his heart in an iron fist. "James?", he croaked.
"You will not make me defile my mouth with the filth that you did to him, but be assured that
I know of it. I know. Is it not enough for you to question my command at every turn? Must
you also ruin my best officer out of petty revenge?"
Goodsir had told him, Francis remembered, that the poison had made Sir John paranoid. It
could be a bodily reaction, a symptom of too much mandragora, or perhaps some
subconscious part of Sir John realising that he had been done wrong.
Still, never had Francis imagined that it all could manifest this way.
"I have no idea what you're talking abou-"
"Feigning ignorance now won't save you, Francis. God sees all sins, and He has seen yours.
And you will stand before Him on Judgement Day, naked and chastised, and He will damn

Francis desperately wished for something, anything to say to this. He knew James was
listening at the door, though he hoped he didn't. James shouldn't have to hear this.
"I don't have to sit here and listen to baseless accusations-"
"Baseless accusations! I've seen you! I've seen how you look at him, how you talk. This
display just now confirmed it. How he came over and tried again and again to change my
mind, see it your way, for the men, he said. For the men." Sir John threw his fork on the plate
with a clatter. "Well, it is for them that I don't strip you of your command right now. I'll also

James come to harm. But believe me, you deserve to hang for this."

Silence. Francis felt like someone had hit him on the head, and he was sitting here, stunned

And what the hell was Sir John talking about? What display had proved it to him?
He had always suspected that Sir John despised him, but for him to say that he deserved to
hang had been near unthinkable until now.
Francis watched Sir John, who appeared winded after his outburst, sink back into his chair.
He had been struck with how ill their leader looked from first seeing him. James looked tired
and worn, but Sir John looked wasted, sickly.
Perhaps a few more drops of mandragora would do it. But they were past the mandragora
now.
They were past anything, but the cold out in the shale.
"I will not let you accuse me of a crime I didn't commit.", Francis heard himself say.
Has it ever occurred to you that it shouldn't be a crime, that the law is unjust?, Francis
thought.
He hadn't always believed it this way. His first time with another man had been when he was
a Mate, the other of the same rank. They hadn't talked about it, just sought solace in each
other's touches.
He had thought he would burn in hell for this, and still he hadn't stopped, because it was too
good. Francis, always with his melancholic temperament, had felt adrift and lonely, and the
other's touch eased that loneliness.
But the guilt had still found its way into the safe cocoon of their couplings, and once Francis
had started to cry in the middle of it. He hadn't been quiet. Great, heaving sobs had wracked
him, and the other Mate had been so unnerved by the whole event that he hadn't sought him
out again for the rest of the voyage.
Then came the North, and Parry. It had been one of his Lieutenants, on the Fury. Francis had
thought himself safe, in a way, because it was someone above him in rank, someone older,
leading him into sin. He could pretend to himself that he'd had no choice, at least for a time,
though the Lieutenant had always asked him for his consent.
His most potent fear had been James Ross finding out about everything, who had been with
him as a Midshipman.
Francis had never examined this fear too closely, but with hindsight it was clear that his own
love for James had made him irrational, fearing for his judgment over the Captain's.
James would never have gotten himself into such a situation, he thought. And surely, if he
was so inclined, the Lieutenant would've chosen him over Francis, who had never had any
illusions of his own attractiveness.

What had been different with this affair was simple, really. The Lieutenant had talked. He had
talked a great deal, even in company, though he had never let anything suspicious pass his
lips, of course.
"We are all God's creatures, and God has given us the ability to love. And not just to love
women, but to love anyone; men, too. How could it be wrong then?", he had told Francis
once, as he had lain in his bunk with his head bowed in shame.
Young Francis had felt these words as soothing balm, but still he protested: "But lust is a sin,
so we hear all the time."
The Lieutenant stroked down his naked back. "You know, I think that was just made up by
some hateful old man who never had sex in his life."
This forced a surprised chuckle out of Francis. "Blasphemy!", he cried, as quietly as he could.
The Lieutenant's opinions about these things had made Francis change his mind about a lot of
it. They presented a different way of looking at the world.
Still, the next time they had been in a port and not in the ice, he had tried it with a woman and
liked it a lot, and immense relief had washed over him. He had put an end to all affairs with
men, thinking that he wasn't "one of those" after all.
As he sat before Sir John now, he didn't feel ashamed, mostly because he was so angry on
James's behalf, as well as his own.
Before Sir John could reply anything to his denial, someone knocked on the door.
It could only be James, and indeed, it was him that poked his head in, his face betraying no
emotion.
"I think we'll need to leave for the tents now, because there may be a storm coming."
"Of course, James.", Sir John said kindly. "Go on deck, Francis and I will follow in a
moment."
James nodded and disappeared.
Sir John turned back to Francis. "We will speak no more of this.", he said. "It has no place on
this expedition. Just know that I am watching you, same as God."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
As he waited on deck, James did his best to compose himself. Of course, he had heard
everything Sir John had accused Francis of, and had at first wondered if had fallen in some
sort of waking nightmare.
The thing with the storm had been a desperate ploy to get Francis out of that conversation.

James had experienced Sir John's fits of paranoia in the last weeks, though they had never
been directed at him.
He had mostly been suspicious at Dr. Stanley, and as it turned out, with good reason, as
Stanley actually did slip sleeping aids into his tea.
Stanley had justified this to James by saying: "He needs to sleep in order to heal. I know he is
afraid to fall into the same delirium that caused his condition, but without sleep, he will only
get worse. And since he refuses all sleeping aids outright, I have to decieve him, may the
Lord forgive me."
James, knowing that making himself complicit in this was downright noble compared to his
other actions, hadn't protested, though he could have.
But still, the change in Sir John had been deeply unnerving. He would be his old self most of
the time, kind and unassuming, but then suddenly he would explode in anger, ranting about
how no one obeyed his orders and how Stanley was trying to poison him.
Never once had he mentioned Francis during these fits, but maybe seeing him now had been
enough to trigger the latent suspicion.
It might've been just an illusion all along, but after this James truly felt that he had no choice
anymore.
Sir John couldn't be allowed to return to England, not if he thought something like that.
James wouldn't be able to stand it, even if he was painted as a victim of Francis's cruel
ambitions, for his own sake as well as Francis's.
Before he could spend more time losing his mind, Sir John and Francis appeared on deck,
wrapped in their slops. Sir John was carrying the lantern, because Francis still had his cane.
James took the lantern from Sir John. "I will go ahead.", he said.
"Of course.", Sir John agreed.
They climbed down the railing in silence. There was no storm, but it was snowing heavily.
James didn't know whether this would aid or block them.
It was difficult to walk in the dress, but he was still the fastest of the group.
Sir John's words were swimming in his head, cutting into his heart.
God sees all sins, and He has seen yours. And you will stand before Him on Judgement Day,
naked and chastised, and He will damn you to hell...
He had known, hadn't he, that Sir John would see it that way when he found out about him.
He had known.
Yet it still hurt, leaving an unpleasant taste in his mouth.

James pursed his lips under his comforter and told himself to focus on where he was going.
This was no easy task, because of the snow. On the other hand, the lights of the Carnivale
were mostly obscured, and so Sir John wouldn't know that he steered them in the wrong
direction.
Now all he had to do was find the berg they had agreed on.
James quickly had to accept that his best guess would have to suffice, and soon all his
concentration was required to keep seeing what was before them.
He glanced back every once in a while and had to lessen his pace, as Francis and Sir John
were slow to follow.
James nearly had a heart attack when he turned back forward and saw a figure with a lantern

"Who's there?", Lieutenant Little called.
James was dizzy with relief.
"It's us, Edward.", he called back.
They waited for Sir John and Francis to catch up, and Sir John asked: "It can't be much
farther, can it? I feel myself a little winded."
"Not far.", Lieutenant Little agreed. "I just stepped outside for a moment to look for the
Captain."
"Good, forward, then.", Sir John panted.
James frevently hoped that Little had a better sense of direction than he had- Little had been
outside before the snowfall, so he probably did.
He followed Little, and had this been any other occasion, James would've been miffed about
himself, the best walker in the Service, to have to rely on someone else.
As it was, he was just grateful for the help, numb with terror as he was.
"Up here, sirs.", Little said, gesturing to where the ice sloped upwards.
"Up?", Sir John asked with dismay. "No, I don't think so."
"We erected the tents on the slope.", James heard himself say. "So we have the majesty over

He had thought Sir John would like the idea of triumphing over nature like this, but he just

There was growl in the distance. Not the wind, that James could discern by now.

Tuunbaq showing up might aid them, but then again, the beast might kill them all. James

"Up we go!", Little said urgently.

Everyone was shocked when Francis grabbed Sir John by his collar and growled: "You will

This was an unconscionable break of the rules of decorum, but it seemed to dawn on Sir John

Sir John was speechless, sputtering. Little remained a threatening shadow to the side.

James could do nothing but obey. Sir John stared at him as he approached and did as Francis

"James...", Sir John began, yet thought better of it.
What followed was that James dragged Sir John up the slope. He wasn't resisting, but clearly

James thought that this was perhaps was a light rehearsal for their hauling later, though he

"You don't have to do as he says.", Sir John said to him. "He's is not your Captain, I am."
"I'm only thinking of your safety, sir.", James replied, because he hoped Sir John would stay

"Indeed?"
James turned to see Francis directly behind him. Little was ahead with the lantern.
At what James assumed was the top - he couldn't see at this angle - , Little abruptly stopped.
"Well? Where's the tent?", Sir John asked, his voice sounding shrill. "Where are the men?"
James stepped back, letting go of Sir John's arm.
They would have to do it now, right now, why was he delaying?
He looked to where Little stood equally frozen, then at the lantern in his hand. He should hit
Sir John over the head with it, like they'd agreed.

Sir John was turning this way and that, demanding to know what was going on.
Then Francis pushed him aside and stepped before Sir John. For some reason, the sight of
him caused Sir John to be silent, even before he raised his cane.
"Why, this is...", Sir John began.
There was a the sound of a crack as the cane broke on impact, and then, frightfully fast, Sir

James heard the dull sound of him hitting the ice before he completely registered what had
happened.
They stood silent in the snow for several moments, Francis with half of his cane still raised.
James knew they had to check now if Sir John was really dead.
Francis turned to James and said: "Goddamn it."
Then he collapsed on the ground. As James was still frozen, it was Little who jumped
forward and kept Francis from rolling after Sir John, and James would forever blame himself

"Captain? Captain?", Little called, shaking Francis. "What is happening?"
James couldn't recall if Francis had told Little the truth about the future, but the first

It shouldn't happen, James thought. If Sir John is dead, it shouldn't happen.
Suddenly, Francis was gasping, his eyes focused again.
"James, something is wrong.", he croaked. "Something is-"
He fell back into the snow, his whole body seizing up, as if he actually experienced a fit.
James had no idea what to do. He was in the middle of panicking, when he heard it.
A voice, down below.
"James... James... Help me..."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
"A man named Cornelius Hickey told me this expedition was a year in the polar sea and then
out the other side..."

Francis dimly registered being back in the other time, the stones underneath his back, the

"He told me that we were going to stop at the Sandwich Islands, and the crew was going to
