"We can just wait.", Little whispered, as if Sir John would be able to hear them from this

God bless our native land...

Or was it rising?
"It's here! It's here!", someone yelled.

Something needed to happen, or he would die here, he realised. Something was happening,

James stumbled down the slope, making sure that the lantern stayed lit.

The snow still fell heavily, and he had to get his bearings again for a moment.

He had to hurry.

Pain. Francis was slipping in and out of it, not sure what was happening.

Francis tasted blood in his mouth and nose.
The light was blinding behind his eyelids.

Smashing the lantern over his head for a killing blow.
Using one of its glass shards to slit his throat.
Undressing him so he would freeze to death faster.

He had an idea.

"Why is the landscape disappearing?"

For the record, almost. These words would help no one. They would vanish into the endless

James was good at tying knots, obviously. He was a sailor. On land, where one could indulge

Hickey and the others had faded into the distance.
He knew they were gone.
He knew he was the only one left, and he was dying.

In the grand scheme of things, it probably didn't take so long for Sir John to choke to death,

Even though the knot was doing its work, James pressed down on the ends of comforter with

Then several things happened at once.

Chapter 34: The Carnivale II
Somehow, the slope was even more work to get up now than before with the still alive Sir
John on his arm.
Halfway through the climb did James realise that he had tears streaming down his cheeks,
and they were frozen there.
He didn't know how long he'd been crying, whether his tears had dripped on Sir John as he
lay dying.
Later, James wouldn't remember loosening his knot and rewarapping the comforter yet

"Commander!", Little exclaimed breathlessly once James came into view. "He stopped

"Is Sir John... dead?", Little asked, his voice low.
James nodded. "Yes.", he said. "It's done."
"Alright.", Little whispered.
James looked at Francis. His eyes were closed, and it almost seemed as if he were sleeping.

"Francis? Francis, can you hear me?"
There was no reaction.

"We need to get away from here.", James said. "Away from the body."

He still hadn't stirred.

Actually, the plan was now to go straight to the Carnivale and make sure that they were seen

"Francis.", James repeated. "Please..."

"Yes, Francis!", James said, laughing with relief.
"Captain!"
"E-Edward?"

woken from a nap.
"I hate to do this to you, but can you stand up?", James asked him. "We need to get away
from here, and fast."
"What happened?", Francis asked, and he sounded so confused that James feared he had

James opened his mouth to explain, but no words came out.
I strangled him to death.
He couldn't say it.
Laboriously, they got Francis into a sitting position, then standing. Little and James stood by

"Where are we going?", Francis asked weakly.
"To the Carnivale."

James stopped. Turned to Francis, and took his face in both of his mittened hands.

Francis blinked at him. He looked so ridiculous, with the fake white hair and lost expression.
"I do.", he said, still. "Stick to the plan, yes."

Francis didn't know what was happening, precisely, as Edward and James pulled him

He didn't really know where he was, or rather, when he was.
He knew something terrible had happened, but he couldn't precisely say what.
He was still trying to pull himself together when the lights of the Carnivale tents became

It was warm inside the tent, warm enough to take off his slops. He was wearing clothes he

He was unshaven, yet happily toasted by a dazzling Jopson in a dress, though there was a

More men spotted him, and raised their voices in cheer, and some whistles as well, yet those

Jopson took Little's arm and led him to the dance floor, crowding close to whisper in his ear.

After a moment, Dr. Stanley turned away and someone yelled: "Merlin will now lead the

Francis needed a moment to realise that the person was talking about him and James.
Christ, his head hurt.
He took James's hand, and suddenly a cup was thrust into his other one. It smelled of alcohol.
He almost took a sip, had not James knocked the cup from his hand.

Francis had no idea how he would manage a dance in this state, and was grateful when James

"James, what happened?", he asked again, feeling desperate, needing to know.
But James pretended not to hear him.

Cornelius Hickey was bored. It was really inappropriate to feel such a thing on the night his

Hickey was bored, and the ecstatic good cheer of the men was beginning to annoy him

He wished he could've been with the party to kill Sir John after all, even though he knew that

Still, murder was something he was more comfortable with than this air of celebration.

drunker, yet even that lost its allure after a while.
Hickey soon arrived at the conclusion that he couldn't relax because he wasn't in control of

Hickey didn't like not being in control.
After looking for Billy but giving up on him when he found him drinking in a group with the

Hickey used to believe that if he only had the clothes of a handsome gentleman, he would

Of course, Hickey could risk himself just fine, worthless as he was, right?

There was a break in the music, and Fitzjames led a stumbling Crozier away, probably hoping

Harry Goodsir was looking for Dr. Stanley. It had only been a moment where he had talked to

Thomas Blanky had been friends with Francis Crozier a long time, and that meant he had
seen his friend in a compromising state from time to time.
Mostly, these states had to do with whiskey. Really, in the early weeks of the expedition,
Francis had been drunk more often than sober.
Whether Francis had grown more adept at hiding it or the crew better at pretending there was
nothing wrong, was up for debate.
In any case, Thomas had quickly noticed the change in his friend when he was suddenly
abstinent, and just a suddenly apparently in love with James Fitzjames.
Of course, Thomas had always watched Francis's regard for the Commander with a raised
eyebrow. Francis had been nothing short of obsessed with him, and had Fitzjames been a
woman, Thomas would've already told Francis to make his interest known, for Christ's sake,
he wasn't getting any younger and this was becoming ridiculous.
All that was to say that Thomas knew a thing or two about Francis, and he would often only
need one look at him to tell what he was thinking.
Which was why he had believed Francis's story instantly, no matter how fantastical it
sounded.
Now, however, Thomas felt deeply alarmed at Francis's state, because he had never seen him
like this before, even on his worst benders.
Francis didn't seem to know precisely what was happening, had the air of a confused child or
a senile old person and he also barely held himself upright.
Thomas had taken his arm from Fitzjames and steered him clear of the crowd. Unfortunately,
there were people everywhere. They had even erected a bathtub of sorts, which Francis
would've balked at had he been in any other state.
Finally, Thomas found a relatively quiet place where all the coats and slops were piled, and
guided Francis to sit down.
"Can you tell me what happened?", Thomas asked him carefully.
Of course, Thomas wanted to know if they had killed Sir John, or if their efforts had been in
vain once again.
In general, Thomas was happy to follow the orders his superiors gave him, but then, in most
cases his superiors were that for a reason, and they were competent and listened to his input.
He didn't know what was wrong with Sir John, and he suspected now they would never
know, but Thomas was convinced of the necessity of killing him.

He had selected to live a life that often carried him far away from good ol' England, but that
didn't mean he didn't love his family and dearly wanted to see them again.
Now, Francis stared at him blankly for a moment before saying: "I don't know."
"What do you know?", Thomas asked.
Francis frowned and put a hand on his forehead. "I think... it's over. The other time. It was
destroyed. Nearly destroyed me with it, had not... something happened."
"Sir John died.", Thomas whispered.
They were alone, but still, it never hurt to be too careful.
Francis blinked. "Where is James?"
"Still inside. You'll just have to get through this night, old man, so no one gets suspicious."

Hickey had the distinct feeling that things were spinning out of control, but as he had never

Hickey let the cigarette fall from his fingers, exchanging a look with Billy, before they

Chapter 35: Francis
Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Francis looked up, into the sunlight. He always felt at peace when seeing the sun again after
so long, but there was none of that, now.
Nine men had burned to death, others were severely injured.
Francis, who remembered another Carnivale like this, couldn't tell the two apart anymore.
Especially since in both cases, it had been Dr. Stanley who had lit the the fuse.
Francis could still see it. The Doctor, going up in flames, along with the tent walls.
The only question was what had prompted this in this time.
James had been holding a speech, rousing the men, because Francis had still been not quite
there yet. To be honest, even now Francis was struggling to stay in the present, or more
accurately, to know what the present was.
His mind felt like it had been beaten and drowned, and he was sure that he would soon
collapse if he didn't go to sleep of his own volition.
But he had to make sure that all the alive men were accounted for.
Goodsir, tattered and dejected, was going around among the injured, one of them Edward
with a cracked rib, whom Jopson refused to leave.
Thomas had received some burns, and Mr. Tozer had been nearly trampled while saving the
life of his fellow Marine, Private Heather.
Lieutenants Le Vesconte and Fairholme seemed alright, though they kept coughing badly,
same as Francis and many of the others.
Henry Peglar, Terror's Captain of the Foretop, had been carried out of the tent by Mr.
Bridgens and was still unconscious. Same as Jopson with Edward, Mr. Bridgens refused to
leave his friend.
Of course, out of all these Francis's main concern was James, but James, hale and whole,
thank God, was very obviously avoiding him under the guise of keeping order to their
tattered remains.
"These men need names yet.", he said, when Francis urged him to go back to the ship.
Francis was deeply worried, because everything they had done before the fire would be a lot
for any man, but then to see a part of their crew burn up in a blaze was too much to bear.

Francis himself only managed to barely hold on to reason.
And he still didn't know how Sir John had died, after everything. Had the fall off the ledge
killed him?
Francis barely remembered that already, only his broken cane somehow leading him to the
conclusion.
He needed to talk to James, but that was impossible at the moment.
They divided the sick between Terror and Erebus in the end, a distraught Mr. Bridgens
agreeing to take up the Doctor's duties in place of Dr. Stanley.
Francis at first tried to help carry everyone who needed to be carried, but his own leg hurt
badly and his mind was still out of sorts, so Goodsir practically ordered him to sleep not soon
after.
Back aboard Terror, Francis breathed a sigh of relief, even though he knew the worst was far
from over.
Jopson was busy, so Francis undressed himself and, exhausted though he was, made himself
wash off the worst of the smoke and soot off his skin.
Redressed in his underclothes, he all but crawled back to his berth and closed his eyes.
Sleep came, but not peace.
Deep in his heart, Francis knew that the other time had been obliterated, though part of him
had hoped that his memories of it would have disappeared as well. But he recalled
everything, down to the last detail.
James's death was still real to him, had still happened.
Perhaps he needed to have experienced that, so he would stay on the right path.
At least that was what he told himself to cope with it.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Francis couldn't even say what he had dreamed of, only that it was painful, because he was
somehow lost between the timelines again.
But it had been a dream, nothing more.
He was woken by Jopson, who still hadn't changed out of his dress. Much time couldn't have
passed, then.
"I'm sorry to wake you, sir, but they found the body.", Jopson said.
So Sir John really was dead. Francis hadn't realised until now that he hadn't known for sure.

Francis had barely dressed when the Lieutenants Irving and Hodgson came into his cabin.
"It seems the fire wasn't the only terrible thing that happened last night.", Irving said.
He looked close to tears, while Hodgson appeared more numb with shock.
"Jopson said something about Sir John?", Francis asked, feigning confusion.
"Sir John is dead, sir.", Hodgson announced. "I'm terribly sorry, but you are now the leader of

and I heard him, how he called out to you. How you ran to him, only to cruelly murder him! I
saw you!"
To his mortification, James realised that he was about to cry.
"Dundy...", he whispered. "Please..."
"Please what, James? Will you still deny it, hm? When we both know the heinous truth?"
James tried desperately to think. "If that is so, why didn't you accuse me in your speech?
Why did you say that I was your Captain?"
Dundy, who had been standing very close but wasn't touching him, suddenly grabbed his
arms. James flinched.
"Because you aren't the mastermind behind this plan. You were just used as its executioner."
James shook his head mutely. Please, someone wake me up from this nightmare, he thought.
"What did he tell you, hm?", Dundy continued, his voice jarringly soft. "That we would all
die if you didn't kill him?"
James could've replied that that was exactly what was going to happen, and that there was
proof, and that, no matter the heinousness of the deed, one life wasn't worth over a hundred.
Instead, he said: "Dundy, stop it. Please, just stop it."
"Whatever his reasoning was, it was still murder. And should things get bad, he can blame it
all on you. That was doubtlessly calculated."
James freed himself from Dundy's hold and turned away. He understood all too well how
Dundy was seeing this, an why. And the rotten, terrible thing was, that it made sense from his
perspective, and wasn't even wholly untrue.
Murder was murder.
James had a talent for dishonesty and obfuscations, but certain things remained true no matter
how well they were coated in lies.
Years and years ago, James had gotten his position as a midshipman through questionable
means, by essentially lying about his service record, counting on the fact that when his
superiors noticed, it was too late to correct the mistake.
He had felt barely any guilt over this, even though that, unlike the circumstances of his birth,
had been his fault entire.
And when his Captain had finally caught on the mistake and confronted him, he had to act
suitably contrite.

"It doesn't matter how guilty you feel.", the Captain had said. "A lie is a lie."
And murder was murder.
James decided to change the subject. "The Carnivale.", he said. "I don't suppose you have any
idea why Stephen decided to have us all go up in flames?"
Dundy sighed. "I told him what I saw. I thought he would help me. And he said he would,
and told me to go and pretend to celebrate, he had a plan. I should've been more suspicious,
but I admit that I my thoughts weren't exactly in order."
So that mystery was solved. And those dead had still been James's fault, the result of James's
actions.
"I'm sorry.", Dundy said. "That horror should've been avoided. Though I suppose Crozier is
just glad that he doesn't have to go up against Stephen anymore."
"Don't be ridiculous.", James whispered.
"What did he tell you?", Dundy asked again.
James took a deep breath and turned around to face him. "I don't think you fully realise how
dire our situation is. I didn't see it as well, only too late, but I wish I could make you realise
that there truly was no other choice. There just wasn't."
"There's always a choice.", Dundy said.
"Not if we want to live."
Dundy shook his head and advanced on James again. James stood his ground this time.
"How do you know that for sure? What makes Crozier's word better than Sir John's? They're
both Arctic veterans. How can Crozier be sure that he didn't just make a false guess, man that
he is, and not God?"
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
As Francis listened to the conversation between James and Le Vesconte, he had to stop
himself multiple times from storming into the room and making a fool of himself.
So Le Vesconte thought he had dragged an unwitting James into this against his will, did he?
And he thought Francis wanted to kill him.
He probably wanted to drive a wedge between him and James, too.
By the time they got to Stanley and the fire, Francis was absolutely seething with rage. One
thing Le Vesconte could be sure of: their dislike and distrust of each other was very much
mutual.

Had he been still on the drink, Francis would've doubtlessly lost himself in that rage, and God
only knew what he would've done next.
Now though, sober as he was, Francis had to realise that regardless of his feelings, he had
problem now. They had a problem, and rage wouldn't help to solve it.
He ought to fear the part of him that would've happily sent Le Vesconte to the gallows, and
he did.
No matter how much Francis hated him, Le Vesconte didn't deserve to die.
Francis was on a mission to preserve life, for God's sake, and he would do well to remember
that!
But doing that didn't make the problem go away, in fact it made it bigger.
Because now he had to decide what the hell he should do with Le Vesconte.
Le Vesconte had witnessed the murder, which meant he could make an effort to have them
hanged for mutiny if he made it back to England.
However, the fact that James had committed the murder, or at least the most important part of
the act, made Francis have to admit that Le Vesconte probably wouldn't talk about what he
had witnessed. He wanted to see Francis hang for this, but not James, so he would have to be
more circumspect.
His strategy was probably to get the crew to question Francis's motives first, then to trust
rumors about him to make it back to the Admiralty in England.
Francis had to say, he had no idea how successful Le Vesconte's instigating had been so far.
He would have to ask Mr. Hickey about the mood among Terror's crew, though he was
generally more worried about Erebus's.
Really, the Admiralty and England were issues for another day, however. First they had to
make it out of here alive.
And Francis would have to drag Le Vesconte with him, kicking and screaming, if need be.
Francis wished dearly that Thomas was here to give him his unfiltered advice, as he would
receive it from no one else, except James.
But while Francis cared too little about Le Vesconte, James went in the opposite direction. He
cared too much. He had miscalculated the threat his friend represented before, and would
perhaps do it again.
"I'm going to leave now.", James said on the other side of the door. "We have to decide what
to do with you."
"I see.", Le Vesconte replied bitterly. "And you will bend your head to Crozier's will, won't
you?"

There was a pause. Footsteps, then James's heated voice: "I swear to you, as long as I live,
that you won't be treated unjustly."
Francis had just stepped away from the door when James opened it.
"I want you to stand guard, Edward.", Francis told Lieutenant Little. "I'll sent Jopson to
relieve you, later."
"Yes, sir. Though it will look queer that the Marines aren't doing it.", Edward pointed out.
"I know. But I don't trust anyone who isn't privy to the... circumstances.", Francis replied in a
low voice.
"Francis, we need to talk.", James said.
"Of course. Follow me."
Francis led the way back to his berth. They passed many men talking amongst themselves,
then characteristically falling silent when they saw Francis. Mr. Hickey was sitting with the
largest group, Francis was halfway relieved to note, though he refrained from pulling Hickey
out in front of the men.
Nobody liked a spy, after all.
He almost told the men to get back to work, until he remembered that he had decided to give
them the day free in light of the funeral. One day, a day that might cost them dearly, but
Francis saw that he had to respect Sir John's legacy at least to some degree or he would have
a mutiny on his hands.
He might have one, still, if Le Vesconte got his way...
Once in the Captain's berth with the door closed, James fell into his arms and pulled him
close, almost knocking the cap he was still wearing from Francis's head with his own.
Francis allowed himself a short moment of comfort, before he said: "James. We need to talk,
as you said."
James nodded against his shoulder and drew back. He began to unbotton his coat and took his
cap off. Francis followed suit.
"We should confine Le Vesconte until we leave, I think. On the walk, I want him to be with
me at all times so I can keep an eye on him.", Francis said.
James looked at him, shaking his head. "Francis, you can't stand each other. If you are with
him 'round the clock, there is no way you wouldn't come to blows before one hour is over."
"How much faith you have in me.", Francis said, irritated.
"I have much faith in you, but Dundy will probably try to provoke you. He wants to bring
you down, that he made abundantly clear."

Francis sighed. "It surprises me that you're willing to believe that of him, I admit."
James glared at him. "Now who's having no faith in whom? I did listen to what he said to me,
as I assume you did."
"I did.", Francis conceded. "Then I'll have Edward watch over him. I think that would work
better. His access to the men needs to be as little as possible, but hopefully it won't matter as
much when we're all focused on surviving."
"That still doesn't take care of the underlying problem, Francis.", James said.
"That being?", Francis snapped.
He immediately felt sorry for his cross tone, as James wasn't at fault for Le Vesconte's
actions. He was just frustrated, with himself mostly, for not having somehow prevented this.
James stayed calm. "He blames you for Sir John's death. He wants you to get punished
accordingly. We obviously have to find a way to get him on your side."
Francis felt vaguely alarmed. "Impossible!", he asserted.
James shook his head again. "Dundy is a reasonable man, and he will listen if we tell him the
truth. If you tell him the truth."
"And what truth is that?"
"The truth of your time travel. How it would all have ended if we hadn't killed Sir John."
Francis scoffed. "As if he would believe that!"
"He will. If you're truly honest with him, if you tell it to him like you told me-"
"If I weep and cry, you mean? Forget it, James. I'm not doing that.", Francis said.
"Francis-"
"I'm not! End of discussion."
James crossed his arms. "Is your pride truly more important to you than your life?", he
demanded.
"This isn't about pride."
"Oh, yes, it is!", James insisted. "You don't want to be vulnerable in front of Dundy!"
"Because 'Dundy' wants me dead!", Francis spat.
"He wouldn't want you dead if you had been civil to him at least once!"
"Are we really having that same bloody argument again?"

James sighed in frustration. "We'll have as often as it takes you to realise that Dundy is not
your enemy, unless you make him your enemy!"
Francis continued in a calmer voice: "You're naive, James, if you think anything can still
change Le Vesconte's opinion of me."
James's mouth curled into a snarl, but before he could reply, there was a knock on the door.
"I was wondering if you're staying for dinner, Captain Fitzjames.", Jopson said after they'd
admitted him.
"I need to get back to my ship.", James replied. He turned back to Francis. "Fairholme is the
only Lieutenant I have left, and Des Voeux has been keeping Dundy company lately. I need
to make sure I don't have a bloody mutiny on my hands until they day is out."
Francis immediately felt contrite. "If there's anything I can do to help-"
"You can talk to Dundy."
"Except that."
James stared angrily at Francis for a moment, then said: "I'm leaving. Have it your way,
Francis, but know that the only thing you're doing is making everything more difficult for all
of us."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Hickey had always been good at gambling. His recipe for success consisted mostly of
knowing when not to play at all.
But if he was forced to, like now, he refused to be pressured. He weighed his chances,
carefully, before placing his bets. He made sure there was no possibility of losing big, even if
that diminished a huge win.
Hickey didn't know Lieutenant Le Vesconte. That was an oversight that had to be rectified
immediately.
Since he couldn't just waltz up to the brig and ask to be admitted, Hickey turned to his trusted
source of gossip and interpersonal relations, Billy Gibson. And sure enough, Billy did know
some stuff, even though Le Vesconte was from Erebus.
"Lieutenant Hodgson knows him. They fought in China together.", Billy told him.
"Apparently, Le Vesconte and Captain Fitzjames are as thick as thieves. They knew each
other already when Hodgson met them, and apparently they could finish each other's
sentences..."
"Makes sense why he said Fitzjames was his Captain, then.", Hickey said.
"I don't understand why he hijacked the funeral like that, if that's what you're after.", Billy
added.

They were in his quarters, Hickey seeking him out after he had talked to the men a bunch.
Most of them were confused, and swore in their pathetic, blind devotion, that Captain Crozier
would never commit a murder, Le Vesconte must have personal reasons for slandering him
like that, and he deserved the lash for this, yes he did.
But officers weren't allowed to be lashed, which Hickey had only just found out about and
could only privately sneer at while outwardly pretending like he'd known all along.
Hickey was willing to bet, though, that the mood was quite different on Erebus. Le Vesconte
had to have a backing to do something like that, if he wasn't completely stupid, and that
Hickey couldn't say. Yet.
He wondered, however, if Fitzjames was going against Crozier now.
Did the two love-birds have a quarrel?
If they had, Crozier wasn't aware of it, or else he wouldn't have invited Fitzjames to talk to Le
Vesconte alone, followed by the two of them going to his cabin.
Was Fitzjames playing a double game? Or was the real fight between him and Le Vesconte?
"Who says I'm after anything?", Hickey asked Billy. "Maybe I simply wanted the pleasure of
your company."
Billy sighed. "You're always after something, Cornelius."
Hickey considered. "What if I told you that my special deal with the Captain was back on?"
Billy, who had been eyeing his bedspread critically, whipped up to face a grinning Hickey.
"Then I would tell you that you should be smarter than to get involved in the Captain's
affairs."
Hickey's grin deepened. "As far as I know, the Captain only has one affair, and he hides it
very badly."
"Yes, he must, for you to have caught on.", Billy said, then paused. "Cornelius? You're not
blackmailing the Captain, are you?"
Because he loved to be contrary, Hickey said: "And what would be so bad about that?"
Billy ran a hand through his hair. "You're going to give me grey hairs, worrying about you!",
he accused.
Hickey felt touched despite himself. He put a hand on Billy's arm. "I'm smarter than the
Captain, Billy."
"And that you think that is exactly your problem.", Billy said, but he didn't remove Hickey's
hand, much to the other's delight.

They hadn't talked about the Carnivale yet. Hickey wondered if Billy had forgotten his
confession of missing him, drunk as he had been.
"Anyway, we might have to make a decision soon.", Hickey said. "About loyalty."
"I'm loyal to the person who can get me home.", Billy replied. "Going on this entire cursed
expedition was a stupid mistake, but I would at least prefer to get out alive."
True that, Hickey thought.
"You don't want to find the Passage? See Hawai'i?"
"You know there are ships going to Hawai'i the other way, don't you? Anyway, why are you
so obsessed with that place?", Billy asked.
"My sources said that this journey would be faster than the other ships.", Hickey replied,
ignoring the other question.
"Parry overwintered in the Arctic twice. Ships get stuck in ice all the time. Did your sources
say anything about that?"
They decidedly had not. Hickey had long since begun to think that the real Cornelius Hickey
had not been the sharpest tool in the shed, much the pity.
Of course, Hickey didn't like to admit when he didn't know something, even to Billy.
Especially not to to Billy.
"I want to be free, Billy. Free of the rotten life I had before. Hawai'i sounds like a place where
I might achieve that." Hickey pulled out a cigarette. "I suppose I should've known it sounded
too good to be true."
"Not in my room.", Billy said, pointing to the cigarette.
"Really?", Hickey mocked, as he pulled a box of matches out of his pocket.
"Cornelius, I'm warning you."
"What are you gonna do to stop me?", Hickey challenged.
Billy glared at him and snatched the cigarette away from between Hickey lips, lightning fast.
"Give it back!"
"Forget it!"
More out of necessity than anything else Hickey knew how to hold his own in a fight, but
those skills only helped him if he truly wanted to hurt the other person.
Despite everything, he did want to stay on Billy's good side.

Rather clumsily, he threw himself at Billy to get the cigarette back, but Billy kept it out of his
reach. Then Hickey had the rather immature idea to start tickling Billy, because Billy was
ticklish, which resulted in them landing on a heap on the bed.
"Not fair, Cornelius!", Billy gasped between tears of laughter.
He relinquished the cigarette, but by now it had been crushed in his hand.
"We need to conserve supplies!", Hickey admonished Billy, who seemingly hadn't realised
yet that they were lying in his bed together, something he had never allowed before.
"I don't think the Captain meant your disgusting cigarettes."
"Every sailor smokes, how can you be so... prudish in that regard?", Hickey asked him.
"Well, I don't smoke.", Billy said. "What are you doing?"
This was his response to Hickey running his hand up Billy's arm in a caress meant to
tantalise.
"You said you missed me.", Hickey whispered, leaning closer.
Billy's eyes widened. "When?"
"At the Carnivale."
"I was blinding drunk at the Carnivale.", Billy said quickly, a blush appearing on his cheeks.
"Doesn't mean you weren't being truthful."
Hickey's hand was framing his neck now, thumb stroking his throat. Billy seemed to realise
only now how intimately entangled they were already, and he quickly jumped to his feet and
smoothed his clothes.
Hickey sighed in annoyance.
"We can't, Cornelius. I will not see either of us hanged."
"Who will tell on us? Even if we are caught, they will just go to the Captain or Fitzjames.
And they will do nothing."
Billy ran a hand through his hair. "How can you know that for sure? Fitzjames reported us
before."
Hickey, who didn't see any reason to get up from the bed, or even correct his casual lounging
position, replied: "Yes, but Crozier didn't do anything. And now that I know about them, too,
they're not going to dare-"
"Oh, they might, seeing as you told Franklin about them!"
Hickey sighed again. "Alright, fine. Have it your way."

It occurred to Hickey that he might convince Billy if he told about the entire murder, but he
didn't want to do that, not yet.
Not before he knew himself how he was going to proceed...
"Is there anything else you can tell me about Le Vesconte?"

Chapter End Notes

So, since this story is rather serious and high stakes I tried to let loose a little and wrote a
little something I'm going to publish soon, so if you're looking for something lighter to
distract you from this...
... get ready for a Fitzier coffeeshop AU!!! I felt like we could use one. It's not
completely plotless, and there is some drama (can't do without that) but it's definitely not
a matter of life and death...

Chapter 41: Francis
When the day came to abandon the ships, Francis felt suitably grave.
Yes, no one had mutinied against him yet, though Hickey had warned him that he shouldn't
trust anyone on Erebus in his reckoning.
Still, Francis had felt dangerously close to hopeless ever since Le Vesconte's speech at Sir
John's funeral.
Francis had to admit that that was mostly due to his continuous disagreement with James in
the beginning, yet it also went deeper than that.
At first, Francis had refused to consider James's idea of him telling Le Vesconte the truth. It
was preposterous, plain and simple.
Le Vesconte wouldn't believe him, and only think Francis insane afterwards.
But after the first evening with Le Vesconte in the brig had passed, James back on Erebus, he
had gone down with Jopson to relieve Edward.
"Won't you talk to him, sir?", Edward had asked.
As Francis had shaken his head, he had realised something: it wasn't just his pride that was
holding him back from even considering James's suggestion. It was fear.
He could barely talk about the horror of it in front of people he trusted; the idea of doing it in
front of someone who actively despised him was terrifying.
Francis had to admit, he knew what James meant when he had said that his honesty and
earnestness would convince Le Vesconte.
The problem was, he couldn't make himself vulnerable like that in front of him. He just
couldn't.
"I will not.", Francis said to Edward.
He had lain awake at night, thinking about James and Le Vesconte and his cowardice. He had
worried, how they were going to make it if Le Vesconte had managed to destroy his rapport
with the men.
On Terror, everything seemed alright, but as Hickey told him the next day, Erebus was a
different story.
"And on what do you base that claim?", Francis asked the Caulker's Mate.
Hickey cocked his head. "The nature of men. You simply don't have a strong foothold on the
loyalties over there. Even here, Sir John was revered, but the difference is, you are also

respected. Who on Erebus has seen more than a few glimpses of you?"
Francis nodded. Hickey was right. The question was, what could be done about it...
He should go over to Erebus and talk to the men, and do it soon. Perhaps if he delivered
something that was akin to his sermons on Terror, they would warm to him.
"Christ, we don't have time for this!", Francis groused. "We want to be leaving soon, and that
will be difficult enough..."
"What does the Lieutenant say?", Hickey asked.
Francis hadn't been paying attention. "Pardon?"
"Le Vesconte. What did he say to you, why he did it?"
Francis of course couldn't admit that he had as of yet not talked to Le Vesconte.
"He saw the deed.", he said curtly.
"Oh, that's not good.", Hickey replied. "But at least he didn't say something like that at the
funeral, just implied it."
Francis regarded Hickey. He had not forgotten what he had claimed in the other time, that he
had killed the real Cornelius Hickey in order to join the expedition.
Francis had wondered what he should do about it, but had come to the conclusion that now
wasn't the time to make an enemy of Hickey as well, and so he had done nothing.
The knowledge only served him to not underestimate Hickey ever again.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Francis had made the decision to take Hodgson and Irving with him on his way over to
Erebus. Edward was guarding Le Vesconte, and Francis still didn't want to replace him with
one of the Marines.
He knew that this was partly because he remembered Tozer being a part of the mutineers in
the other time, yet he couldn't tell himself he was to be trusted now.
"Will you make Dundy stand trial, back in England?", Hodgson asked him with barely
concealed worry.
"He would deserve it.", Irving cut in before Francis could answer. "He accused the Captain of
being a murderer!"
"In his grief, John.", Hodgson said. "You should know that the Lord asks us to forgive our
offenders."
"Yes, but-"

"I'm not going to make him stand trial.", Francis interrupted their argument. "I'm only
keeping him confined on Terror so he doesn't incite mutiny on Erebus."
"You don't trust Captain Fitzjames to keep him at bay?", Irving asked.
Francis sighed. "I have only the deepest trust in Captain Fitzjames. On the other hand, I don't
trust Le Vesconte."
Hodgson stepped up to him, looking earnestly pleading. "I understand your reasons, of
course, but I would beg you to remember that there was no malicious intent behind his
actions, only grief. Sir John's death was a blow to all of us."
"I will remember that.", Francis promised him.
When they had nearly reached Erebus, there was the sound of a musket being fired. They
immediately ducked and yelled, asking what was going on.
"It's the Captain, from Terror, and two Lieutenants!", Irving called, as if any person on the
ship wouldn't have been able to recognize them instantly, seeing as they had daylight.
"I'm sorry, Captain Crozier!", came the voice of Mr. Des Voeux from the railing. "We weren't
shooting in your direction, it's just that Mr. Pilkington thought he saw the beast, sir."
And so they went on board with an ominous feeling. Francis wondered if he truly had to fear
that Des Voeux had been lying.
"Summon all hands on deck.", Francis ordered the man once they had passed the railing.
Naturally, he would've wanted to talk to James first, but he knew it would look better if he
weren't seen to converse privately with him before speaking to the men.
James was one of the first to appear on deck, still in the process of buttoning his coat. He
went straight to Francis.
"Would you care to tell me what is going on?", he said quietly.
"I thought I might address the men.", Francis replied.
"I just dismissed them half an hour ago, after doing a big speech on your brilliance.", James
hissed. "And it was sorely needed, too."
Francis was beginning to see that perhaps he should've talked to James beforehand. Well.
What's done is done., he thought.
"Did Le Vesconte's speech do much damage?", he murmured to James.
James nodded, harried, but Francis could also see the truth in the sullen, mulish faces of the
men as they gathered.

"Dundy is very popular here. And Sir John, he is like a God. They already think you did
wrong by disagreeing with him, and rescinding his orders. You should've stayed on Terror,
Francis, and given me time to work on them." James cleared his throat multiple times. His
voice was barely there, no doubt taxed from the speech he'd had to do.
"I thought it better if they hear me explain in my own words that I'm innocent."
James just silently shook his head, but it was too late.
Francis faced the men, standing at the exact same spot Sir John had always been in when he
delivered his sermons on deck. Maybe that was a mistake, Francis couldn't judge it terribly
well.
He didn't know these men, not like he knew his Terrors.
He felt a distinct unease creep up in him.
"I came to make sure the preparations are going well.", he began. "I must say, in this time of
uncertainty, you have done splendidly and I commend you for it. Still, I wanted to clarify a
few things, because I'm sure the performance of Lieutenant Le Vesconte yesterday caused a
great deal of disquiet."
Over the years, Francis had developed a sense for his audience whenever he spoke. Initially,
he'd been surprised to see that holding a speech wasn't a singular affair, despite there only
being one speaker.
The audience always influenced the speech, and a good speaker worked with that, with the
mood that he sensed from his men.
Now, he looked into closed off faces, faces that only didn't seem hostile because they feared
his influence. Francis had never believed in ruling as Captain through fear. Discipline, yes,
but not fear.
"Yes, I quarreled with Sir John, as I'm sure you already know. But never did I do it because I
didn't respect him, nor because I sought some sort of personal advancement. I quarreled with
him because I was deeply worried for the fate of this expedition, and I saw it as my duty to
speak up, because I don't want a single one of you to freeze or starve."
Francis could see that the men weren't exactly warming to him, but they were curious for his
explanation.
He continued: "Sir John Franklin was a remarkable man. Everything I said about him at the
funeral was sincerely meant and true. But every man, myself included, can make mistakes.
My proposal to abandon the ships wasn't just favored by me, they are multiple experts who
advised us similarly. You can ask your Ice Master, Mr. Reid. It is the job of a good Second to
not only assist his First, but to think on his own two feet and if necessary, even question the
First's judgement. Sir John wanted me to do that, and he always appreciated my candor, even
in his anger."

This was a lie, but it hardly did anything one way or the other.
"I'm going to tell you something, something that many of you have suspected for a long time.
Sir John sought to keep the knowledge of it from you, and I agreed, for at the time there
wasn't anything we could do about it. It is true that you haven't been eating from the cans we
brought for months now, and that is because they are poisoned, all of them, with lead."
Francis paused to let that sink in. The men shared looks and murmured between themselves,
and Francis felt the mood change. There was fear, palpable in the air.
"We simply can't stay here for another winter. We can't. We want to find the Passage, but not
at the cost of our lives. And so we have to abandon the ships. The march will be difficult, I
will not lie. We will need the help of the Netsilik people to survive, but if we all make an
effort, we will survive. I want to bring every single one of you home."
Francis paused again, sighed, and continued gravely: "And once we are home, everyone who
thinks I am guilty of any transgression can say so at the court martial. I won't stop you. I
won't stop Lieutenant Le Vesconte, who deserves to live same as every single one of you."
James stared at him in surprise, before schooling himself. He wasn't the only one.
"First, though, we have to get home. Fort Resolution is far away, and we don't know what
dangers we'll encounter along the way. That's why I'm asking you to trust me, and Captain
Fitzjames, to lead you on this long, long walk."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
He dismissed the men, who went back to work on their venture with renewed desperation.
Few of them lingered, though, around Des Voeux and Fairholme.
Des Voeux finally walked up to Francis and asked him if he would release Le Vesconte.
Francis had dreaded that very question. On the one hand, it would be a gesture of trust that
would be good for his rapport with the men. On the other, Le Vesconte might destroy that
rapport single handedly if he was released back to Erebus.
On the long walk, other problems would hopefully keep them occupied enough for Le

He wasn't the only one still up, could see the light in Jopson's berth, for example.
There was something unsettling in the atmosphere, disquiet, as if Terror knew she would be
abandoned come morning.
At the ladder up, James paused. It was really late, and perhaps Dundy was sleeping. But then,
perhaps not.
James had to admit he had been avoiding him as well, unable to face his judgment.
Judgement he deserved.
Sighing, James took his lantern and climbed down into the hold, where Little was watching
Dundy, asleep over a book.
Francis had permitted him to sleep, but didn't want him to move from the door.
He jerked awake at James's footsteps, immediately alert.
"Everything is fine, Lieutenant.", James said. "I just want to talk to him."
Little nodded. "He's asleep."
James almost turned around then, but he decided not to be a coward. "Let me in."
Dundy was indeed asleep, or so it looked liked, lying as he was curled up on a stack of crates.
He took longer to stir, finally blinking up at James blearily, then with a closed off expression.
James was reminded of the first weeks of their acquaintance, where Dundy had disliked him
so fervently. Charlewood had told him to leave it alone, but James had not wanted to.
"You want everybody to be your friend.", Charlewood had said, shaking his head.
"Not everyone.", James had replied. "I'm merely convinced that Le Vesconte believes things
about me that aren't true, and I intend to rectify that."
"What do you want, James?", Dundy asked, bringing him back to the present.
"To see how you are."
Dundy looked at him a moment. "I'm fine. How are you?"

"You mean, how am I after I murdered my Captain?", James said. "I don't think it would
admirable if I felt right as rain."
"And, do you?"
"Of course not!"
Dundy hummed. He looked tired, but maybe that was only because he had just woken up.
"Visited Crozier, have you?", he asked.
James didn't deign that with a response. He felt the soreness in his backside all the more
acutely, heat rising to his cheeks.
"He told me he talked to you."
"He did.", Dundy said. "And I think he's either dangerously calculated or a madman."
"What if he is neither?"
Dundy sighed. "He really did a number on you."
"Regardless of how you feel about him-", James began. "-we all need to stick together to
survive, come morning. Please promise me that you're with me-"
"With you, always."
"-even if it means doing as Francis says."
Dundy sighed again. "I don't trust him. I'll never trust him."
"You don't have to. You just have to trust me.", James insisted.
He sat down across from Dundy on a crate, taking his hand. Dundy looked surprised at the
touch.
"Trust me.", James repeated. "Please?"
Dundy stared at their hands. James found himself thinking of all they had been through
together, the thousands of times they had strengthened their bond. Was it strong enough to
withstand these circumstances now?
"I trust you.", Dundy said at last. "You're a fool for loving him, but I trust you. I promise."
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
And so, the next day James said goodbye to Erebus, and climbed down the railing one last
time. He marched over to Terror, where everyone gathered.
Francis was waiting for him, sure as spring. They stood next to each other as Francis gave the
signal to start, and Little yelled "forward men!"

They started their laborious trek towards King William Land.
It had begun.
